cards.title: Harden release and CI hygiene for v1 credibility
cards.body: Audit finding: release/build hygiene does not yet match v1 seriousness. Align package versions, add actual CI/release workflows, make warnings fail, and make the default test path reliable in the documented environment. Evidence: Cargo.toml says 1.0.0 while flake.nix packages 0.1.0; docs/reference/versioning.md references .github/workflows/release.yml but no workflow exists; cargo check emits warnings; cargo test failed here because cc was missing outside the Nix shell.

Plan added 2026-06-22: release-ci-hygiene. No language decision required; next step is implementation on go.

cards.title: JIT tier-1b: own bytecode VM (replace Cranelift, zero runtime dep)
cards.body: Planned successor to the Cranelift tier-1: a Jet-owned register/stack bytecode VM (bytecode design + compiler from TIR + VM loop), roughly 5-20x over the tree-walking tier-0 interpreter with ZERO runtime dependencies, removing the Cranelift exception. Not native speed. FROZEN: pursue after Cranelift tier-1 is proven. Owner: plan to move to our own bytecode VM.

cards.title: JIT backend: own native JIT from scratch (master-of-all, eventual)
cards.body: Eventual Jet-owned native codegen backend (instruction selection, register allocation, x64 + aarch64, calling conventions, relocations, W^X executable memory, JIT hardening) replacing Cranelift AND the bytecode VM. Multi-year effort with miscompilation + security surface; justified only as the long-horizon master-of-all goal since production is AOT. FROZEN: post-v1 / far-horizon. Owner: then eventually our own native jit.

cards.title: Full HTTP core library — client + server (D-NETDEP1=A, owner-expanded mandate)
cards.body: Owner mandate (2026-06-26, expanding D-NETDEP1=A): Jet ships a full, complete HTTP library — both client AND server — as a core library, better than Go's net/http. D-NETDEP1's approved pure-Rust crate (ureq/minreq) is only the BOOTSTRAP backing c157's build-time fetch(url, sha256:); the native-ize end-state (Epoch-3 dep rule) is a first-party Jet/Rust HTTP stdlib. SCOPE: client (request/response, methods, headers, body, streaming, TLS, redirects, timeouts) + server (listener, router, handler, middleware, request/response types, graceful shutdown). The client+server API surface (naming + shapes) is SYNTAX/stdlib-surface design needing its own decision docs + ballots BEFORE code — drive from a real-world example per owner-anti-repetition + owner-decision-doc-style. NOT this card: c157's fetch backend (ships first against the bootstrap crate).

log.text: [created 2026-06-26] Opened from D-NETDEP1=A owner comment: "I want a full, complete http library, both server and client, better than go as part of the core libraries in jet." NEXT (PM pipeline): write+vet a plan (docs/plans or sidequests) driven from a worked real-world example; develop the client+server API-surface decision cards (request/response/handler/router/middleware naming + shapes), agent-review them, queue in the ballot. NO code until the API surface is ratified (owner-facing stdlib surface = syntax approval required). The native-ize obligation from D-NETDEP1 lands HERE: this library is the first-party replacement for the bootstrap HTTP crate.

decisions.title: Plugin substrate — sandboxed WASM vs native cdylib vs RPC
decisions.gist: How a `target: plugin` package is built and loaded so an untrusted third-party plugin is safe to load.
decisions.explainer: A package with `target: plugin` (the reserved keyword, E1210 today) compiles to a sandboxed WASM module the host loads and calls through a typed interface. The plugin runs isolated and can only touch what the host explicitly grants, so loading an untrusted plugin is safe by default with no `#Unsafe` gate — what I1 and the beginner experience demand. Native cdylib stays as a future expert opt-in layered on top, deferred to its own card so the safe default ships first. I6 cost named honestly: introduces a WASM runtime as a new stdlib external dependency (owner-gated, native-ize obligation) — tracked separately as D-DEP-WASM1; no plugin code is written until that lands.
decisions.story: The owner wants a plugin system where dropping in someone else’s plugin is safe out of the box, not an expert-gated unsafe load — the I1 footgun the default must never be.

options.name: Native cdylib + `#Unsafe`
options.detail: Every plugin load is an expert-gated unsafe FFI boundary. Rejected: makes the I1 footgun the default. Survives only as a future expert opt-in layered on top of B.
options.code: #Unsafe load("plugin.so")

options.name: Sandboxed WASM (chosen)
options.detail: `target: plugin` compiles to a sandboxed WASM module loaded through a typed interface; isolated, capability-gated, safe by default with no `#Unsafe`.
options.code: package { target: plugin }

options.name: Out-of-process RPC
options.detail: Plugin runs as a separate process spoken to over RPC. Rejected: highest latency, no shared typed state.
options.code: // spawn + RPC handshake per call

comparisons.note: Both run untrusted third-party plugins inside a WASM sandbox for exactly this safe-by-default reason.
Counter-example: native dynamic libraries are an unsafe FFI boundary every load — the expert path B keeps available, not the default.

decisions.title: WASM sandbox engine for plugins (wasmtime + Component Model)
decisions.gist: Which WASM runtime backs the D-PLUGIN1 sandbox.
decisions.explainer: Approve wasmtime as the runtime-side dependency that backs D-PLUGIN1=B’s plugin sandbox — the audited, widely-embedded (Zed/Shopify/Fastly/Envoy) secure WASM engine. It is Cranelift-based, so it reuses the dep already approved in D-JITDEP1 (no new codegen backend), and its Component Model delivers the typed host↔plugin interface (a `.wit` contract, deny-by-default capabilities) without hand-marshaling. Runtime-side only — I6 holds (never in `Source/`); hash-pinned in `.jet/lock`; carries the native-ize obligation whose frozen end-state is our own WASM runtime.
decisions.story: The owner needs a sandbox engine that is already audited and battle-tested rather than one built from scratch — standing up a security sandbox yourself spends the one resource (safety) you don’t.
decisions.inWild:
// .wit contract defines the typed host↔plugin interface
// wasmtime runs the module with deny-by-default capabilities

options.name: wasmtime + Component Model (chosen)
options.detail: Cranelift-based (reuses D-JITDEP1), audited, widely embedded; Component Model gives the typed `.wit` host↔plugin contract with deny-by-default capabilities.

options.name: wasmi
options.detail: Tiny pure-Rust core-wasm interpreter, closest to the I6 end-state — but hand-marshaled interface and interpreted speed. Rejected.

options.name: wasmer
options.detail: No Cranelift reuse, less-mature Component Model. Rejected.

options.name: Write our own now
options.detail: Standing up a security sandbox from scratch spends the one resource — safety — we don’t. Rejected; it IS the frozen native-ize end-state, just not now.

comparisons.note: All embed wasmtime as their production WASM sandbox; the Component Model is its typed-interface story.

decisions.title: HTTP backend for build-time fetch() + full HTTP library mandate
decisions.gist: Which HTTP backend powers comptime `fetch(url, sha256:)`; owner expanded to a full client+server HTTP core library.
decisions.explainer: Approve a small pure-Rust, blocking HTTP crate (`ureq`/`minreq` — no async runtime, no C) as a runtime-side dependency so D-CTEFFECT1’s Tier-1 `fetch(url, sha256:)` actually downloads, verifies against the `sha256:` pin, bakes the bytes in, and records `{url, sha256}` in `.jet/lock` for byte-identical builds. Owner-gated exactly like Cranelift, regex, sqlite, wasmtime: scoped, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation; I6 holds (never enters `Source/`). Owner expanded the mandate: the goal is a full, complete HTTP library — client AND server, better than Go’s `net/http` — as a Jet core library. The approved crate is the bootstrap; the API surface becomes its own design + ballot track (D-HTTPLIB1–4).
decisions.story: The owner doesn’t want just a fetch backend — he wants the whole HTTP stack to be first-party and best-in-class, with the crate as a temporary bootstrap toward a native Jet implementation.

options.name: Pure-Rust HTTP crate (chosen)
options.detail: Small blocking crate (`ureq`/`minreq`), runtime-side, owner-gated, hash-pinned. Owner-expanded into a full client+server HTTP core-library mandate.
options.code: fetch(url, sha256: "…")

options.name: Shell out to curl/wget
options.detail: Unvetted ambient tool, Windows gaps. Rejected.

options.name: git-only fetch
options.detail: Can’t fetch a plain file URL. Rejected.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Leaves the ratified `fetch` a stub. Rejected.

comparisons.note: All use a hash-pinned fetch (record url + sha256) so every machine’s build is byte-identical — the model adopted here.

decisions.title: `jet.http` server handler model — function-first mux
decisions.gist: Shape of the server request/response/handler/router surface for Jet’s first-party HTTP library.
decisions.explainer: Server handlers are plain `fn(req: Request) -> Response` functions registered on a `mux` value (`mux.get("/path", handler)`); route params via `req.params["id"]`; `http.serve(addr, mux)?` starts the listener. Typed extractors (B — Axum-style) and unified-fn / Rack-style (C) rejected: B adds a learning curve, C is most flexible but least discoverable. Part of the D-NETDEP1 full-HTTP-library mandate; see D-HTTPLIB2 (split `jet.http.client`/`jet.http.server`), D-HTTPLIB3 (HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2 + WebSocket in v1), D-HTTPLIB4 (rustls TLS). Ratified — not yet implemented; API surface design + bootstrap crate selection precedes code.
decisions.story: The owner wants the handler shape to be the most discoverable one a beginner could guess — a function that takes a request and returns a response, registered by route — not a framework-y extractor DSL.

options.name: Function-first mux (chosen)
options.detail: Handlers are `fn(req: Request) -> Response` registered on a `mux`; params via `req.params["id"]`; `http.serve(addr, mux)?`. Most discoverable.
options.code:
mux.get("/users/{id}", get_user)
http.serve(addr, mux)?

options.name: Typed extractors (Axum-style)
options.detail: Handler args are typed extractors (`fn(id: Path<String>)`). Rejected: medium learning curve.
options.code: fn get_user(id: Path<String>) -> Response { … }

options.name: Unified fn / Rack-style
options.detail: User-level routing inside one handler. Most flexible but least discoverable. Rejected.
options.code: fn app(req) -> Response { match req.path { … } }

comparisons.note: Same function-first model (`http.HandleFunc(pattern, fn)`) — the discoverability bar D-HTTPLIB1 aims to beat.
comparisons.code: http.HandleFunc("/users/", handler)

comparisons.note: Counter-example: typed extractors (option B) — powerful but a steeper first step.
comparisons.code: async fn h(Path(id): Path<String>) { … }

decisions.title: How do we spell a whole-graph effect prohibition?
decisions.gist: Should a function be able to forbid an effect across its entire reachable call graph, and how is that written?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF1 (the effect-propagation engine) is ratified and positive effects like #(Net) already flow up the call graph. A prohibition is that same walk run inverted; this decides whether to ship it and how it reads.
decisions.story: A security engineer ships a payment-signing routine that must never touch the network. She wants to read one annotation at the root and trust that no callee, however deep, opens a socket. Auditing the whole tree by hand on every change is exactly what she is trying to stop doing.

options.name: Per-effect prohibition #(no_net)
options.detail: A prohibition annotation names one effect the function and its whole reachable graph may not use. It is the exact inverse of the positive set and runs on the ratified propagation engine, so it costs no new machinery. Cleanest when the rule is 'this one capability, never here'.

options.name: Sealed allowlist #(only Io)
options.detail: Instead of forbidding one effect, declare the complete set the function may use; everything outside it is forbidden. Stronger guarantee (closes the door on all nine other effects at once) but you must restate the full whitelist, and it reads oddly when you only meant to ban one thing.

options.name: Reuse the empty set #()
options.detail: #() already means 'no effects at all'. Lean on it: if you want no network, write a pure function. But #() forbids all ten effects, so it cannot express 'no Net while Io stays fine' -- it is all-or-nothing, which fails the security engineer who still needs to log.
options.code:
#() fn pure_sign(o: Order) -> Receipt { return seal(o) }
// forbids ALL effects -- you cannot say 'no Net but Io is OK'

comparisons.note: Effect rows list exactly the effects a function may use; absence means forbidden, and total functions <> forbid all effects. Closed rows give the allowlist (option B) for free.
comparisons.code: fun total-add( x : int, y : int ) : <> int { x + y }   // <> = no effects allowed

comparisons.note: No native effect prohibition; the ecosystem fakes it with a deny-lint at the crate root. Borrow the `forbid` spelling precedent; note it is lint-level, not type-level.
comparisons.code: #![forbid(unsafe_code)]   // any unsafe anywhere in the crate is a hard error

comparisons.note: Abilities are tracked in the type; calling an ability not granted in scope is a type error -- a positive set whose complement is the prohibition.
comparisons.code: step : '{IO} Nat -> Nat   -- only IO is reachable; anything else won't typecheck

decisions.title: Does temporal ordering get its own surface, or fall out of typestate?
decisions.gist: Does enforcing the legal ORDER of a value's states need a separate state-machine surface, or does it already emerge from typestate transition edges?
decisions.explainer: D-STATE1 / D-STATE-DECL is ratified: states live in a `state` block and methods carry #Transition(A -> B) / #State(C), erased in codegen. The open question is whether ordering across many states needs its own surface or is already pinned by the transition edges.
decisions.story: A hotel-booking dev models a Reservation that is Pending before payment, Confirmed after, and only then CheckedIn. He wants check_in on a still-pending reservation to be a compile error, and he wants the legal order -- pay before check-in -- enforced too, not just the single current state.

options.name: Pure typestate -- edges ARE the machine
options.detail: Each method's #Transition / #State annotation is one edge of the state machine; the legal order emerges because the only path to a late state runs through the earlier ones. No new surface. The order is implicit, so a reader reconstructs it by scanning the methods rather than reading it in one place.

options.name: Explicit transition block
options.detail: List the legal edges once inside the state declaration; every method must match a declared edge or it is rejected. The machine is readable in one place and methods are checked against it, at the cost of stating each edge twice (once in the block, once on the method).

options.name: Typestate + a #timeline phase block
options.detail: Keep per-method transitions, and add a #timeline naming the ordered happy path for documentation and exhaustiveness checking. Best self-documenting surface; but it introduces a second place to keep in sync and risks drifting from the actual edges.

comparisons.note: Typestate via phantom type params: each state is a distinct type, methods consume self and return the next-state type. Ordering emerges purely from which methods exist -- the model behind option A.
comparisons.code: impl Door<Open> { fn close(self) -> Door<Closed> { Door { _s: PhantomData } } }

comparisons.note: A dedicated typestate language: states are declared first-class and transitions named explicitly on operations -- the precedent for spelling the machine out (option B).
comparisons.code: state OpenFile case of File { method CloseFile()[>>ClosedFile]; }

comparisons.note: Protocols encoded with an indexed state monad; the legal order lives in the type index, statically enforced. Powerful but heavy -- the ordering is in the types, not a separate block.
comparisons.code: check_in : ST m () [res ::: Reservation Confirmed :-> Reservation CheckedIn]

decisions.title: What surface declares a protocol, and what gets generated?
decisions.gist: How does a user declare a request/response protocol so the compiler generates ordered client and server stubs that reject out-of-order messages?
decisions.explainer: D-LIN1 (single-use/linear values) and D-STATE1 (typestate) are both ratified -- the two pieces session types need: a handle used exactly once per step, threaded through states. This decides only the declaration surface and what the compiler emits.
decisions.story: A network-protocol implementer writes a handshake -- client sends Hello, server replies Ack, then client sends Data, server replies Done -- once, as a type. She wants both a client handle and a server handle generated, and she wants code that sends a message out of turn rejected at compile time, not at runtime on a customer's machine.

options.name: A `protocol` block, compiler generates both handles
options.detail: Write the ordered exchange once; the compiler generates Handshake.Client and Handshake.Server handle types, each step consuming and returning the handle (linear + typestate underneath). One declaration, both sides, out-of-order sends caught at compile time. The clearest beginner surface.

options.name: Hand-written linear+typestate handle (no new keyword)
options.detail: No new syntax: the user writes a #SingleUse handle and annotates each method with #Transition by hand; the session-ness is derived from the ratified pieces. Maximum reuse, zero new surface -- but the user writes both client and server by hand and keeps them dual, which is the boilerplate a protocol declaration exists to erase.

options.name: Protocol-as-data, generated at comptime
options.detail: Describe the protocol as an ordinary value and have comptime read it to emit both handles. Maximally programmable (protocols can be built from data) but the exchange is no longer readable as a sequence -- it is a struct literal, which buries the one thing a reader wants to see.

comparisons.note: The session_types crate encodes protocols as nested type constructors and computes the dual by trait -- correct but unreadable type soup, and no generation. Borrow the duality idea, avoid the spelling.
comparisons.code: type Server = Recv<Hello, Send<Ack, Recv<Data, Send<Done, Eps>>>>;

comparisons.note: lchannels derives session types from a protocol description and generates a case class per state -- the closest prior art to option A's generate-both-sides approach.
comparisons.code: case class Hello(cont: Out[Ack]); case class Ack(cont: In[Data])

comparisons.note: First-class session types built into the language as a sequence of typed sends/receives. The academic reference; the operator spelling is cryptic, so keep the ordering readable.
comparisons.code: sig handshake : !Hello.?Ack.!Data.?Done.End

decisions.title: Does a type-position marker go before or after the type?
decisions.gist: When a plain value-tag like #Tainted decorates a type in a signature, does it sit before the type (#Tainted String) or after (String #Tainted)?
decisions.explainer: No gate clears this -- it is pure surface consistency, decidable today. Every other Jet marker is prefix (#Test fn, #Pure fn, #Unsafe block, #SingleUse struct); the only question is whether type-position tags match that or read better postfix.
decisions.story: A web dev marks form input #Tainted at the source and must write the type of a tainted string in a function signature. She needs one consistent spelling for #Tainted, #SingleUse, #NoCopy, and typestate markers -- the plain value-tags that decorate an existing type rather than minting a new one.

options.name: Prefix -- #Tainted String
options.detail: The tag comes before the type, matching every existing Jet marker (#Pure fn, #Test fn, #Unsafe, #SingleUse struct). One mental rule for all markers, wherever they appear. Reads as 'a tainted String'.

options.name: Postfix -- String #Tainted
options.detail: The tag follows the type, reading left-to-right as 'a String, tainted', like a refinement narrowing a base type. Arguably natural for qualifiers -- but it points the opposite way from every other #Marker in the language, so the reader now has two rules for where a marker lives.

comparisons.note: Outer attributes are prefix (#[test] fn foo). Jet's #Marker idiom already mirrors this; staying prefix keeps one rule.
comparisons.code: #[test] fn it_works() { assert_eq!(2 + 2, 4); }

comparisons.note: `const` may sit before OR after the type (const char* vs char* const), and allowing both spawned decades of reader confusion. The cautionary tale: pick one position.
comparisons.code:
const char *a;   /* pointer to const */
char * const b;  /* const pointer */

comparisons.note: Taint is a runtime flag (-T mode), not a type spelling -- shows the concept's value but offers no placement to copy; Jet makes it static and must choose a position.
comparisons.code:
#!/usr/bin/perl -T
my $clean = $1 if $tainted =~ /^([\w.]+)$/;  # untaint via match

decisions.title: Do dynamic Data trees get fluent accessors, and how far?
decisions.gist: Should reading an untyped Data/Json tree get fluent accessors that compose with `?`, or stay pattern-match-only?
decisions.explainer: No gate -- Data and its variants (.Null/.Bool/.Int/.Float/.Text/.Array/.Object) shipped with D-ENC-DYN1. This decides whether to add an accessor layer over the tree and how far it reaches.
decisions.story: A dev consumes a third-party JSON blob with no fixed schema, so the #[Codable] derive doesn't fit. Today he pattern-matches the Data tree by hand. He wants to pull config.server.port as an Int without a five-level nested match that buries the one field he came for.

options.name: Pattern-match only (status quo floor)
options.detail: Keep the shipped mechanism: walk the tree with value-dispatch and pull each level out by hand. Nothing new to learn or maintain, and it is fully general -- but reaching one deep field costs a tower of nested matches, which is exactly the friction the user is complaining about.

options.name: Pattern-match + minimal fluent accessors
options.detail: Keep pattern-match as the floor and add a small accessor set -- .field(name), .at(i), and the leaf coercions .int()/.text()/.bool()/.float() -- each returning a Result so `?` chains cleanly. Covers the common 'reach a field, read a scalar' path in one line; missing key or wrong variant is a normal err.

options.name: Full jq-like path query
options.detail: Add a path mini-language so a whole route is one string. Most powerful for ad-hoc digging, but it is a second grammar to learn and test -- a query DSL living inside string literals -- which collides with I8's one-canonical-way bar.
options.code:
cfg.query("server.port").int()?        // a path language inside a string
cfg.query("items[0].name").text()?     // a whole second grammar to learn

comparisons.note: serde_json::Value: indexing returns a Value and typed getters return Option (as_i64). Borrow the typed-getter idea; Jet returns Result so `?` composes instead of Option.
comparisons.code: let port = v["server"]["port"].as_i64().ok_or("missing port")?;

comparisons.note: encoding/json decodes to map[string]interface{}, forcing type assertions that panic on a wrong guess -- verbose and unsafe. The anti-pattern to avoid.
comparisons.code: port := m["server"].(map[string]interface{})["port"].(float64)

comparisons.note: A full path-query language: powerful but an entire second grammar -- precisely what option C would import and what I8 rejects.
comparisons.code: jq '.server.port' config.json

decisions.title: How does a function opt into deterministic replay?
decisions.gist: How does a user opt a function into deterministic replay, and what does the compiler guarantee about hidden non-determinism?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF1 is ratified and already tags the non-deterministic effects (#(Time), #(Rand), #(Net), #(Io)). This decides only the surface; the record/replay runtime harness is separate post-v1 build work, not decided here.
decisions.story: A game dev records a match's inputs and replays them to reproduce a one-in-a-thousand desync bug. He needs the compiler to guarantee that during replay nothing reads the clock, RNG, or network behind his back -- every non-deterministic source must be routed through something the replay harness can mock.

options.name: #Replayable marker (compile-time guarantee)
options.detail: A function marker rejects any reachable #(Time/Rand/Net/Io) that is not routed through a mockable capability -- the same inverse-propagation walk as D-PROP1. The compiler proves replay-soundness statically; the harness later swaps the capabilities. The guarantee lives in the type, so it cannot silently rot.
options.code:
#Replayable fn step(w: ^World, i: Input, clk: Clock) -> World { ... }
// any hidden clock.now() / rng in the reachable graph -> E0180 with the path

options.name: Library API over capability handles (no new syntax)
options.detail: No marker: the replay harness is just a library that passes mock capability handles, and the user routes non-determinism through them by convention. Zero new surface -- but nothing forces completeness, so one forgotten direct clock.now() silently breaks replay with no compile error.

options.name: Both -- marker for the proof, library for the harness
options.detail: Ship the #Replayable marker for the static guarantee AND the record/replay library for the runtime. The marker proves no hidden non-determinism; the library captures and plays back. Most complete story, and the two halves are naturally separable (the library is post-v1).

comparisons.note: Non-determinism is an effect you handle; a replay handler reinterprets rand/clock operations -- the model option A leans on, lifted to a marker over Jet's effect tags.
comparisons.code:
with handler { fun rand() { resume(replayed-value()) } }
fun () { simulate() }

comparisons.note: No language support; crates inject determinism by hand via trait objects and seeded RNG -- option B's manual capability passing, with no static completeness guarantee.
comparisons.code: fn step(w: &mut World, clk: &dyn Clock, rng: &mut StdRng) { /* ... */ }

comparisons.note: The record-replay debugger replays at the OS/runtime layer, orthogonal to the type system -- it is the harness half, showing the runtime piece is cleanly separable (post-v1).
comparisons.code: rr record ./game && rr replay   # deterministic playback, no source changes

decisions.title: Should the explicit-type binding form move the mutability marker onto the name (`name@ Type = val` / `name: Type = val`) and let `=` serve both bind and reassign?
decisions.gist: Today an explicit-typed binding carries two markers: a `:` for the type and a `@=`/`:=` for mutability (`name: Type @= val`). The owner's direction collapses that to one marker on the name (`@`=immutable, `:`=mutable), a bare type, and a plain `=`.
decisions.explainer: Amends S4 (`name: Type` annotation position) and reopens D-BIND2 (which fixed `@=`=immutable-bind, `:=`=mutable-bind, `=`=reassign-only per S17). The reopened rule is D-BIND2's `=`-is-reassignment-only invariant: under the WANT, `=` also binds whenever a mutability marker (`@` or `:`) precedes the name, so `=` becomes bind-or-reassign depending on the name's marker; the owner confirms this is intended and matches the Go/Odin/Pascal `:=` family. The INFERRED forms do not change: `name @= val` and `name := val` stay exactly as D-BIND2 ratified them. Sub-question for the owner: in the explicit immutable form `name@ Type = val`, the `@` now sits where loop-label and ref sigils also live; Card 'Labeled-loop suffix' is the consistency sibling, so decide them together. Scope note: the owner marked only the FIRST instance; ratifying applies the change repo-wide (canon.jet, syntax-decisions.md, the parser, Syntax.rs, and every explicit-typed binding in the examples), not just the two marked lines.
decisions.story: The owner wants the mutability decision to live in one place fused to the name, and the type to be optional and bare. Dropping the type then collapses cleanly back to today's inferred sigils: `name@ = val` is `name @= val`, `name: = val` is `name := val`. So only the explicit-typed spelling moves; the marker simply slides left onto the name and the type drops in between it and `=`.

options.name: WANT — marker on the name, bare type, `=` binds
options.detail: Explicit form: `name@ Type = val` (immutable) / `name: Type = val` (mutable). One mutability marker fused to the name, bare type, `=` binds-or-reassigns. Inferred `@=`/`:=` forms unchanged.
options.code:
nameImmut@ String = "Jet"    // immutable, explicit type
nameMut: String = "Jet"      // mutable, explicit type

options.name: HAVE — keep D-BIND2 (`name: Type @=` / `name: Type :=`)
options.detail: Status quo: type with `:`, mutability with the binding sigil `@=`/`:=`; `=` is reassignment only. The explicit form carries both `:` and the bind sigil.
options.code:
nameImmut: String @= "Jet"   // immutable, explicit type
nameMut: String := "Jet"     // mutable, explicit type

comparisons.note: `:=` declares-and-infers; a later bare `=` reassigns. The WANT generalizes that declare-vs-reassign split (both sharing `=`) to the explicit-type form.
comparisons.code:
name := "Jet"   // declare
name = "Go"     // reassign

comparisons.note: Both spell binding `:=`; Odin's `x: T = v` puts a bare type before `=` exactly as the WANT's mutable form does.
comparisons.code:
x: int = 5   // Odin: typed binding
y := 5       // inferred binding

decisions.title: Should loop labels write the `@` as a suffix (`outer@`) instead of a prefix (`@outer`), at both declaration and break/continue?
decisions.gist: D-LABEL1 + D-ATTR3 spell a loop label `@outer` (prefix) and target it with `break @outer`. The owner's direction flips the sigil to a suffix, `outer@`, everywhere it appears.
decisions.explainer: Directly REVERSES D-ATTR3 (ratified 2026-06-19, option B), which kept loop labels as an `@` prefix precisely so the language carries two marker sigils in two fixed positions; the plan flagged the mixed-sigil outcome as a trap and the owner chose the prefix with that flag visible. It also amends D-LABEL1 (which defines `@name loop` and `break @name`). Blast radius: the parser's label-position rule, Syntax.rs, the D-LABEL1 worked examples, and every labeled loop in canon.jet/examples; codegen still maps to Rust `'name:` labels unchanged. This pairs with the binding card (both push the owner's marker-suffixes-the-name direction), so decide them together for one consistent rule. Scope note: the owner marked only the FIRST instance; ratifying applies the change repo-wide, not just the marked block.
decisions.story: The owner wants the label sigil to hug the name the same way the binding marker does (`name@`), so the `@` reads as 'this name is special' and sits in one consistent position across the language rather than flipping sides between bindings and labels.

options.name: WANT — suffix label (`outer@`)
options.detail: Label sigil suffixes the name at declaration and at `break`/`continue`, matching the binding-card direction.

options.name: HAVE — keep D-ATTR3/D-LABEL1 prefix (`@outer`)
options.detail: Status quo: `@` prefixes the label at declaration and jump. Keeps the deliberately-chosen prefix position.

comparisons.note: Labels are a prefix with a leading sigil (`'outer:`), the opposite of the WANT's suffix.

Go and Java also label by prefix (`outer:`). No mainstream language puts the label sigil as a suffix on the name; the WANT's `outer@` is novel, justified by internal consistency with the binding card, not precedent.
comparisons.code:
outer:
for row := range g { ... }   // Go: prefix, like everyone else

decisions.title: Should match arms gain `|` value-alternation plus `||`/`&&` boolean combinators and paren grouping, replacing today's `||`-distributes-values rule?
decisions.gist: Today (S25) `400 || 404` in an arm distributes the comparison across values. The owner's direction splits the operators: single `|` alternates values, `||`/`&&` join a value-pattern with a real boolean expression, and parens group for clarity.
decisions.explainer: Reopens S25 (comparison distribution: `x == 1 || 2 || 3` re-applies the comparison to each plain value via `||`/`&&`). Under the WANT, `||` and `&&` stop being value-distributors and become boolean combinators, while a NEW single `|` takes over value-alternation (`400 | 404`). Also amends D-IF1/D-IF2's arm-head model, which today distinguishes a bare-value arm from a full-Bool-condition arm structurally by whether the head has a top-level comparison/logical operator; the WANT layers `|`/`||`/`&&`/parens on top of that and adds 'a left-value-less boolean uses the subject implicitly' (`500 | 501 || n == false`). Blast radius: the parser's arm-head grammar, S25's distribution machinery, every `||`-joined arm in canon.jet/examples, and the D-PAT1/D-PAT2 `&&` guard rule (which already uses `&&` for nested-pattern guards; confirm the two `&&` meanings unify cleanly). Sub-question: precedence of `|` vs `||`/`&&`, and whether parens are merely cosmetic or load-bearing. Scope note: the owner marked only the FIRST block; ratifying applies repo-wide. Option C offers a more conservative middle.
decisions.story: The owner wants arm heads to read like full predicates: alternate a few values with `|`, then optionally `&&`/`||` a boolean condition onto them, with parens available purely for visual clarity, and a bare boolean expression still implicitly compared against the subject.
decisions.inWild:
label @= if m {
    200 -> "ok"
    400 | 404 -> "client error"                 // `|` alternates values
    500 | 501 || n == false -> "server error"    // `||` adds a boolean; bare bool tests subject
    (600 | 601) && (n != false) -> "other"       // parens group; `&&` combines
    else -> "other"
}

options.name: WANT — `|` alternates, `||`/`&&` combine, parens group
options.detail: Full expressiveness: `|` value-alternation, `||`/`&&` combine with boolean exprs, optional paren grouping, bare boolean tests the subject implicitly.

options.name: HAVE — keep S25 (`||` distributes values)
options.detail: Status quo: `||` between plain values re-applies the comparison (S25); arm-level guards use `&&` on bound names (D-PAT). No single-`|` alternation, no paren grouping.

options.name: Middle — keep `||` value-join, add explicit guards
options.detail: Conservative compromise: keep S25's `||` for value-alternation, but add a separate guard clause (e.g. `if <bool>`) for boolean conditions instead of overloading `||`/`&&`/parens onto the head.

comparisons.note: `|` alternates patterns and a separate `if` guard adds a boolean, close to the WANT's split of value-alternation from boolean-combination, but Rust uses `if`, not `&&`/`||`, for the guard.
Pattern alternatives with `|` plus `if` guards; like Rust, it keeps alternation and the boolean guard in distinct syntactic slots rather than chaining `||`/`&&` into one head.

decisions.title: Should enum-variant patterns in match arms take a leading dot (`.Circle(r)`) to mark them as inferred-enum members?
decisions.gist: Today a match arm names the bare variant (`Circle(r) -> ...`) since the subject's type is known. The owner's direction adds a leading `.` (`.Circle(r)`) to read the variant as 'a member of the inferred enum'.
decisions.explainer: Amends S30 (variants declared/accessed as `Type.Variant`) and S31 (pattern tests, where the type prefix is dropped because the subject already pins it; note S31 also warns a bare name on the right is a variable if one is in scope, and tells you to qualify a unit variant as `Light.Red` to disambiguate, which the leading `.` directly addresses). Blast radius: the parser's pattern grammar, S31's bare-name-vs-variant rule, and every enum match arm in canon.jet/examples. Sub-question to raise: should the leading dot ALSO apply to value-position enum access, i.e. is `.Red` allowed where the expected type is known, alongside today's `Light.Red`? The mark only touches match arms; extending it to value position is a coherent but separate step the owner should rule on explicitly. Scope note: the owner marked only the FIRST instance; ratifying applies repo-wide.
decisions.story: The owner wants the leading dot to be the one consistent signal for 'inferred enum member', the same `.` that opens dot-construction (`.{ }`), so a reader instantly sees the arm is selecting a variant of the subject's type, not referencing some free name.

options.name: WANT — leading dot (`.Circle(r)`)
options.detail: Variant patterns in arms take a leading `.`, matching dot-construction and signalling inferred-enum-member resolution; also resolves S31's bare-name-vs-variable ambiguity.

options.name: HAVE — keep S30/S31 bare variant (`Circle(r)`)
options.detail: Status quo: arms name the bare variant; the subject's type supplies the enum. A bare name that shadows an in-scope variable must be qualified (`Light.Red`).

comparisons.note: Switch cases use leading-dot member syntax (`.circle`) because the matched type is known, exactly the WANT's model.
Counter-example: Rust match arms name the bare variant (`Circle(r)`), like Jet's current S31 form, no leading dot. Shows the WANT is a deliberate Swift-style choice, not the only convention.

decisions.title: Should the impl-trait separator be `.` (`impl Type.Trait`) instead of `:` (`impl Type: Trait`), for both plain impls and `using` forwarding?
decisions.gist: Today a trait attaches to a type with `:` (`impl Square: Shape2`), reusing the type-annotation/bound punctuation. The owner's direction switches to `.` so `impl FileErr.Fallible` reads 'FileErr's Fallible'.
decisions.explainer: Reopens S28, which EXPLICITLY rejected `impl Type.Trait` and chose `impl Type: Trait`, picking `:` deliberately to match type annotations (`x: Int`) and generic bounds (`<T: Comparable>`), and reserving `.` for namespace/method walks (modules, enum variants, `c.area()`). The WANT therefore overloads `.` onto a third job (trait-attach) that S28 kept separate. S28's own 'future relook' note anticipated owner interest in trait-attach sugar but, because `::` was spent on bindings, S83 reserved `~~` (`impl Point~~Trait`) for it; the owner now wants `.` instead of `~~`, so ratifying this also retires that reserved `~~` direction. Also amends S62 (trait delegation `impl Trait using field`), whose top-level spelling mirrors S28's separator. This card consolidates TWO owner marks ('Trait Implementation Syntax' and 'Trait Forwarding'): they are the same `:`-to-`.` change at two sites. Blast radius: the parser's impl-head grammar, S28's two impl spellings, S62 forwarding, and every `impl Type: Trait` in canon.jet/examples. Scope note: the owner marked only the first instance of each; ratifying applies repo-wide.
decisions.story: The owner wants the impl head to read possessively: `Type.Trait` is 'this Type's implementation of this Trait', and to apply that same separator uniformly to delegation (`impl App.Logger using logger`), so plain impls and forwarding stay visually identical.

options.name: WANT — dot separator (`impl Type.Trait`)
options.detail: `.` attaches the trait to the type for both plain impls and `using` forwarding; reads possessively as 'Type's Trait'. Overrides S28's explicit rejection of this spelling.

options.name: HAVE — keep S28/S62 colon (`impl Type: Trait`)
options.detail: Status quo: `:` attaches the trait, matching `x: Int` and `<T: Comparable>`; `.` stays reserved for namespace/method walks. The spelling S28 deliberately chose.

comparisons.note: No common language spells trait/interface implementation `Type.Trait`. Rust (`impl Trait for Type`), Swift (`extension Type: Protocol`), Go (implicit) all differ; Jet's current `impl Type: Trait` is closest to Swift's `:`. The WANT's `.` has no real precedent; its justification is the possessive reading, not prior art.

S28's 'future relook' floated a C++-ish `Type::Trait` feel; `::` was unavailable (spent on bindings), so the owner now reaches for `.` to get that member-of reading. But `::` in C++ is scope resolution, not interface impl, so even this is an analogy to the feel, not a true impl precedent.
comparisons.code: // C++: Type::member  — scope resolution, not trait impl

decisions.title: Confirm: `#grant`/`#layout` should be PascalCase `#Grant`/`#Layout`, a rubber-stamp of D-CASING1, with the lowercase spellings treated as doc/impl errors?
decisions.gist: The owner marked `#grant`/`#layout` to be PascalCased. D-CASING1 (ratified 2026-06-21) already requires EVERY `#`-marker to be PascalCase and even lists `#Grant` by name, so the lowercase spellings are pre-existing drift, and this is a confirmation rather than a new decision.
decisions.explainer: This ALIGNS with D-CASING1, not against it: D-CASING1's rule 1 is 'every `#`-marker is PascalCase' and its enumerated family explicitly includes `#Grant` (alongside `#Repr`, `#Transact`, `#NoCopy`, ...). Grep findings: (1) D-CASING1 lists `#Grant` PascalCase, yet D-SCAP1's later implementation note (2026-06-24, AFTER D-CASING1) wrote `#grant(Fs) { caps -> ... }` lowercase and the parser keyword is `KW_GRANT`; that lowercase impl/note is the drift to fix. (2) `#Layout` is NOT spelled out in any decision example: D-SOA1 and the D-SOA2A rename consistently wrote `#layout(columnar)`/`#layout(c)` lowercase, so `#Layout` was never explicitly PascalCased anywhere, but D-CASING1's blanket 'every `#`-marker' rule covers it. So `#Grant` is an open-and-shut rubber-stamp; `#Layout` is the same rule applied to a marker that predates the casing sweep and was simply never updated. Consolidates two owner marks (same change, two markers). Blast radius once confirmed: rename in the D-SCAP1/D-SOA1 impl + parser (`KW_GRANT`, the `#layout` family parse), Syntax.rs, ui snapshots, and every `#grant`/`#layout` in canon.jet/examples/docs. Option B exists only to let the owner say 'no, these two are intentionally grandfathered lowercase', which would itself be a carve-out from D-CASING1. Scope note: the owner marked only the first instance of each; ratifying applies repo-wide.
decisions.story: The owner wants markers to all draw the same attention as weighty, unique declarations: one casing rule, no exceptions, so `#grant`/`#layout` should look like `#Test`/`#Unsafe`/`#Repr`.

options.name: WANT — PascalCase (`#Grant`/`#Layout`), per D-CASING1
options.detail: Confirm both markers are PascalCase, treating the lowercase spellings as doc/impl drift from D-CASING1's existing blanket rule. Cheap rubber-stamp; no semantics change.
options.code:
#Grant(Fs) { caps -> ... }
#Layout(columnar) struct Particle { ... }

options.name: HAVE — lowercase grandfathered (`#grant`/`#layout`)
options.detail: Declare these two markers an intentional lowercase exception to D-CASING1. This would be a deliberate carve-out from the otherwise universal casing rule.
options.code:
#grant(Fs) { caps -> ... }
#layout(columnar) struct Particle { ... }

comparisons.note: The D-CASING1 follow-on already PascalCased exactly this kind of marker: `test`->`#Test`, `pure`->`#Pure`, `todo`->`#Todo`. `#grant`/`#layout` are the same move on two markers the sweep missed.
comparisons.code:
#Test "..." { ... }   // already PascalCased by D-CASING1
#Pure fn f() { ... }

comparisons.note: Counter-style: Rust attributes are lowercase (`#[derive]`, `#[repr(C)]`). Jet deliberately diverged via D-CASING1 to make markers read as weighty declarations, so 'Rust is lowercase' is not an argument to keep `#grant` lowercase here.
comparisons.code:
#[repr(C)]
struct CView { ... }   // Rust: lowercase attrs

decisions.title: Should a named test block write its name as a parenthesized argument `#Test("name") { ... }` rather than a bare adjacent string `#Test "name" { ... }`?
decisions.gist: Today a named test is `#Test "name" { ... }`, the marker followed by a bare string literal. The owner's direction parenthesizes the name (`#Test("name")`) so it reads as a normal marker argument.
decisions.explainer: Amends S43 (`#Test "name" { ... }` block, ratified 2026-06-12, amended through D-CASING1; note S43 already rejected `#[test]`-style attributes and `fn test_*` naming, so the bare-string form was a considered choice). Interacts with D-TEST1 (a parameterized `#Test fn name(...)` is a property test): the property-test form has NO string name (it draws its name from the function), so the paren form has nothing to wrap there. Sub-question to raise: does ratifying leave `#Test fn` untouched (recommended, there is no name string to parenthesize), or does the owner want some parenthesized form there too? Blast radius: the parser's `#Test` head grammar, S43, the `jet test` harness's name extraction, the E0052 teaching error, and every `#Test "..."` block in canon.jet/examples + ui snapshots. Scope note: the owner marked only the FIRST instance; ratifying applies repo-wide.
decisions.story: The owner wants `#Test` to take its name the way every other argument-carrying marker takes its args, in parens (`#Repr(C)`, `#Grant(Fs)`, `#Unit(usd)`), instead of the one-off bare-adjacent-string form, so the test marker is consistent with the rest of the marker family.

options.name: WANT — parenthesized name (`#Test("name")`)
options.detail: Name is a marker argument in parens, consistent with the rest of the argument-carrying marker family. The `#Test fn` property form stays as-is (no name string to wrap).

options.name: HAVE — keep S43 bare string (`#Test "name"`)
options.detail: Status quo: marker followed by a bare adjacent string literal; the considered S43 spelling that already beat `#[test]`-attribute and `fn test_*` forms.

comparisons.note: Attribute test cases carry their data as parenthesized arguments (`[TestCase("x")]`, `[Theory]`), matching the WANT's parenthesized-name shape.
comparisons.code:
[TestCase("reverses")]
public void Reverses() { ... }

comparisons.note: Counter-example: Rust's `#[test]` is a bare attribute with no argument; the test name comes from the fn name (like Jet's `#Test fn` property form). Shows the WANT's parenthesized name is an xUnit-family choice, not universal.
comparisons.code:
#[test]
fn reverses() { ... }   // no name argument

decisions.title: Add Verse-style structured task combinators (race / all / any) to the core concurrency surface?
decisions.gist: Concurrency is ratified as post-v1 (S53, direction A: tasks + channels). Before that surface is built, should Jet also adopt a curated set of high-level task combinators — race (first wins, rest cancelled), all (wait all), any (first success) — as part of the core async story, or leave that layer to library helpers? The combinator family vs the raw task/channel primitives are two distinct layers; this card decides the combinator layer only.
decisions.explainer: S53 ratified the task/channel primitives direction but deferred implementation. D-REACT1 ratified that reactivity is library-only, not a language mechanism. D-NET2 names async/concurrency as an Epoch 3 pillar. Adopting a combinator surface now (A) locks in semantics before the memory-capability model review the owner flagged as a prerequisite (see the S53 2026-06-19 caveat). A library-only path (B) means the combinators stay userland until the primitives ship and the model is clear. Deferring (C) explicitly acknowledges the ordering dependency and is the conservative gate. Touching S53/D-NET2 scope. No new I1/I8 issues in A itself, but wrong combinator semantics baked in early can constrain the memory-capability model.
decisions.story: I want to race two network requests and use whichever responds first, cancelling the other — one line, not a manual join-select loop. And I want to wait for all three background workers before I proceed. These patterns come up in every real async program.
decisions.inWild:
// Hypothetical — concurrency not yet implemented
let result = race.[fetch(url_a), fetch(url_b)]
let (a, b, c) = all.[load_config(), open_db(), start_cache()]
let first_ok = any.[try_primary(), try_fallback()]

options.name: Curated core combinators (race/all/any)
options.detail: Ship race/all/any as first-class core combinators over tasks, defined alongside the task primitives. Semantics: race cancels losers, all waits all (fails fast on first error), any returns first Ok (waits rest). Clean, learnable surface; Verse-proven. Risk: commits to combinator semantics before the memory-capability model review the owner required.

options.name: Library helpers only, no language surface
options.detail: The task/channel primitives ship bare; combinators live in a `jet.tasks` library module. Users compose race/all/any themselves or import them. No language commitment until the memory-capability model is settled. Downside: beginner experience is worse out of the box; the combinators end up there anyway, just not blessed.

options.name: Defer — decide after memory-capability model review
options.detail: Explicitly block this card on the memory-capability model review (S53 2026-06-19 caveat) and the broader async surface design. No combinators in core or library until the primitives and model are settled. Costs: roadmap gap, but avoids a mis-bet on semantics.

comparisons.note: Verse has race/sync/rush as built-in concurrent expression forms; they compose naturally with failure and are part of the core language, not a library.
comparisons.code:
race:
  result1 := fetch(url_a)
  result2 := fetch(url_b)

comparisons.note: Swift uses async let for parallel fanout and TaskGroup for dynamic sets; no single race primitive — you implement it with withTaskGroup and return-first logic.
comparisons.code:
async let a = fetch(urlA)
async let b = fetch(urlB)
let result = try await [a, b]

comparisons.note: Promise.race / Promise.all / Promise.any are library-level combinators — proven, widely understood, but live in the runtime not the language.
comparisons.code:
const winner = await Promise.race([fetch(urlA), fetch(urlB)])
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([loadConfig(), openDb()])

decisions.title: Allow explicit discard of a fallible result or secondary return value at the call site?
decisions.gist: Jet's `T ? E` model currently makes ignoring a fallible result a compile error (via `#MustUse` on fallible returns). Jai lets you silently ignore the `ok` secondary return. Should Jet add an explicit opt-out — a visible discard sigil at the call site — or hold the mandatory-handling line?
decisions.explainer: D-LIN1's `#SingleUse` handles must-consume values. `#MustUse` exists in the tag vocabulary (D-QUAL2 / syntax-decisions.md §tags). The question is specifically about `T ? E` fallible results: can a caller silence the error? Option B (explicit `_` discard) preserves I1 — it is visible and deliberate, not silent. Option C (Jai-style implicit ignore) violates I1: the default becomes silently dropping an error, exactly the footgun beginners must never hit. The decision also touches whether multi-return (multiple positional returns) is a separate open question; this card is narrowly about error/fallible-result discard only.
decisions.story: I'm calling a best-effort `log_audit_event()` that returns a `Bool ? IoError`. I know I can't do anything useful if it fails — I want to explicitly say 'I'm discarding this error on purpose' without a full `match` block.

options.name: Keep mandatory handling (status quo)
options.detail: All `T ? E` returns must be handled via `?`, `??`, or a `match`. The `_ = expr` trick panics at runtime in Jai; Jet's `#MustUse` makes it a compile-time error. Keeps I1 airtight. Callers who truly don't care use `?? ()` (discard to unit via the propagation chain) or a short `match`. No new surface.

options.name: Explicit discard sigil at call site
options.detail: Add a visible opt-out that suppresses the `#MustUse` error for that specific call. The sigil (e.g. a trailing `!_` or `!discard`) is mandatory — you can't accidentally suppress. Sema emits a lint (not an error) when used on a `#MustUse` result, pointing at what you dropped. Preserves I1: the footgun is opt-in and visible.
options.code:
log_audit_event(event)!_   // explicit discard; lint: "dropped IoError"
write_cache(key, val)!_    // same — intentional, not accidental

options.name: Jai-style implicit ignore
options.detail: Allow assigning only the success value, silently dropping the error: `content := read_file(path)`. Ergonomic but violates I1 — silent error loss is a footgun, and beginners will hit it constantly. Reject.

comparisons.note: Jai multi-return lets you capture only the first value, silently discarding `ok`. No warning. Ergonomic in expert hands, footgun for everyone else.
comparisons.code:
content, ok := read_entire_file("config.txt")
content := read_entire_file("config.txt")  // ok dropped silently

comparisons.note: Rust's `#[must_use]` makes ignoring a Result a warning, not an error; the escape is a `let _ = expr` assignment. Explicit but not a dedicated sigil.
comparisons.code: let _ = std::fs::write("f.txt", b"data");  // explicit drop, silences warning

comparisons.note: Go uses blank identifier `_` to discard any return value, including errors. Silent error discard is trivially easy and a pervasive Go footgun.
comparisons.code: content, _ := os.ReadFile("config.txt")  // error silently discarded

decisions.title: Inside `.{ }` / `T.{ }` literals, adopt Zig-style `.field = val` member syntax to enable LSP dot-completion?
decisions.gist: D-DOTCTOR1/2 (ratified 2026-06-25) established `T.{ }` and `.{ }` as the struct literal spellings with `field: val` syntax. This card reopens only the inside-the-braces field syntax: should fields use a leading dot (`.field = val`) to enable LSP completion when the user types `.`, or stay with the current `field: val` colon style?
decisions.explainer: D-DOTCTOR1=A (ratified, not yet implemented) uses `field: val` inside braces, matching named-parameter and record-update patterns elsewhere. Changing to `.field = val` would require a different tokenization rule inside literal braces (dot-name-equals vs name-colon) and amend D-DOTCTOR1. The LSP motivation is real: when a user types `.` inside `T.{ }`, completion engines can offer field names. However, LSP can also complete after the bare `field` token using the expected type from context — the leading dot is not strictly required for completion. Adding `.field =` also introduces a third sigil family inside braces. I8: if `field: val` and `.field = val` coexist, that is two ways to mean the same thing — reject unless one fully replaces the other.
decisions.story: I type `Server.{` and then `.` and the IDE shows me exactly which fields are available. It feels like autocomplete in a GUI form — the dot is the trigger that says 'I want a field name here'.

options.name: Keep `field: val` (status quo, D-DOTCTOR1=A)
options.detail: The ratified spelling stands. LSP completion is implemented in the server using the expected type from context — no dot trigger needed. Consistent with named-parameter syntax elsewhere. No I8 issue. Recommend.

options.name: Adopt `.field = val` Zig-style, replace `field: val` in literals
options.detail: Amend D-DOTCTOR1 so struct literal fields use `.name = value`. The leading dot is a uniform trigger inside any `{ }` context (struct literal vs block) that LSP and parsers can key on. Creates a syntactic split: `fn foo(field: val)` named args use colon, struct literals use `.field =`. Introduces inconsistency across two very similar contexts.

options.name: Allow both (reject — I8 violation)
options.detail: Permit either `field: val` or `.field = val` inside literals. Violates I8 — two spellings for one job. Beginners will encounter both in real code and wonder which is right. Reject.

comparisons.note: Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals uniformly. The leading dot is the LSP completion trigger and creates a consistent rule: dot-anything inside braces is a field init.
Rust struct literals use bare `field: value` with no leading sigil. IDEs complete field names from the struct definition without needing a dot trigger.

decisions.title: Add a blessed Jet stdlib type for loading/pending/unknown async states, or leave to user enums?
decisions.gist: Async UIs often need a four-state value: not-asked, loading, ok(T), error(E). Jet has `T?` (optional) and `T ? E` (fallible). Should Jet add a blessed `Loadable<T>` or `AsyncState<T, E>` enum in the stdlib, or leave this pattern to user-defined enums?
decisions.explainer: The four-state pattern is already expressible today with a user enum and a `match`. Adding a blessed type risks I8: it's a second optional-like container alongside `T?` and `T ? E`. A stdlib enum (B) is lower cost than a language keyword (C) and avoids I1/I8 issues, but it still adds surface area to the beginner namespace. The case for it is that UI/reactive code is a target domain (replace-Swift lens) and the pattern is ubiquitous enough to warrant a canonical name. The case against: one extra enum is not a hardship, and a blessed type could fragment — `Loadable` in one codebase, user enum in another, both in the stdlib docs.
decisions.story: Every screen in my app has a data-fetch lifecycle: not loaded yet, loading spinner, loaded data, error banner. I want a type that models this cleanly without me defining the same four-variant enum in every project.

options.name: Leave to user enums (status quo)
options.detail: No new stdlib type. The pattern is one enum away. Documentation in the cookbook shows the canonical four-variant shape so every project lands on the same idiom. Keeps surface small (I8). The reactive library (D-REACT1) can export its own `Signal<T>` without a generic Loadable. Recommend.

options.name: Ship a blessed `Loadable<T, E>` stdlib enum
options.detail: Add `jet.async.Loadable<T, E>` (or `jet.ui.AsyncState`) to the stdlib with variants Idle / Loading / Loaded(T) / Failed(E). Consistent naming across all Jet projects. Cost: adds a type to learn, risks being wrong for some use cases (no Idle? two error types?), and may become the 'official' way even when a user enum is clearer.

options.name: Language-level pending state / keyword
options.detail: Make `pending` a first-class language concept: `T | pending` or a `?~` suffix. Deep integration — the compiler knows what 'pending' means, enabling flow-sensitivity. Very high cost, hard to reverse, I8 concern (third optional-like mechanism), and the motivating UI use cases don't require language-level semantics. Reject.

comparisons.note: Elm has no stdlib Loadable; the community converged on a `RemoteData` package with four variants (NotAsked / Loading / Failure e / Success a). A library, not a language feature.
comparisons.code:
type RemoteData e a
    = NotAsked
    | Loading
    | Failure e
    | Success a

comparisons.note: Swift has no canonical async-state type. Every team defines their own. The fragmentation pain is real — it's one argument for a blessed stdlib enum.

decisions.title: Confirm lane-wise arithmetic for closed SIMD types only, and decide whether user vector types get component-wise operator opt-in?
decisions.gist: D-SIMD1/2 ratified lane-wise `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` on the built-in `F32x4`/`F64x2` lane types with operator overloading explicitly closed to user-defined types. D-LINALG1 blessed element-wise ops on `Vec2`/`Vec3`/`Vec4`/`Mat*` (same closed set). This card confirms that closure and decides whether to open a hook for user-defined structs to opt into component-wise arithmetic.
decisions.explainer: D-SIMD2 closed operator overloading to the built-in lane family. D-LINALG1 extended that closed set to linalg types. Both are ratified and implemented. The question is whether a user struct (e.g. a game `Color` or `Quaternion`) can opt into the same component-wise `+`/`-` via a blessed protocol/marker. Opening that gate is a different decision than confirming the closed set. I8 concern: blessed component-wise overloading could become a second way to write arithmetic on struct types (alongside plain method calls), and it touches operator soup territory. I1: user-defined operator overloading is an expert feature and must be opt-in.
decisions.story: I have a `Color.{ r: F32, g: F32, b: F32, a: F32 }` type. I want `c1 + c2` to add lanes automatically, exactly like `Vec4 + Vec4`. I don't want to write a `.add(other)` method.

options.name: Closed set only — no user operator overloading (confirm D-SIMD2)
options.detail: Lane-wise arithmetic stays on the compiler-provided types (F32x4/F64x2, Vec2/Vec3/Vec4, Mat*). User structs use method calls. Keeps operator semantics predictable, surface small, no expert escape needed. Recommend.

options.name: Blessed `#ComponentWise` marker for user struct types
options.detail: A struct marked `#ComponentWise` on all numeric fields gets compiler-generated `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` that apply field-by-field. Expert opt-in, no footgun (non-numeric fields are a compile error). Extends the SIMD/linalg precedent to user types. Downside: a new derivable behavior, another surface item to learn, and the component-wise result may surprise callers who expect a dot-product or magnitude.

options.name: Full user operator overloading
options.detail: Allow any type to define `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` freely via `impl Add for MyType`. Maximum flexibility. Operator soup, inconsistent semantics across crates, and the exact problem I8 is designed to prevent. Reject.

comparisons.note: Jai infers component-wise ops on structs whose fields are all the same numeric type — automatic, no annotation. Power-user magic that beginners hit unexpectedly.
Rust requires explicit impl of Add/Sub/Mul per type. Verbose, but semantics are always explicit and discoverable.

decisions.title: Maintain a short, living TS/Swift competitive-gap doc to guide roadmap prioritization?
decisions.gist: Jet's stated goal includes replacing TypeScript (typed web/app backends, client-server protocol) and Swift (iOS/macOS apps, protocol-oriented patterns). Should there be a short, maintained doc that enumerates the concrete gaps Jet must close to be a credible replacement — or should that analysis stay folded into the existing roadmap?
decisions.explainer: The replace-TS/Swift lens is already implicit in several open cards (typed client/server protocol, reactive UI, D-REACT1, plugin target). A standalone doc (A) makes the lens explicit and reviewable — each gap becomes a concrete feature requirement that can be cross-checked against the roadmap. The downside is another doc to keep current. Folding into the roadmap (B) avoids doc sprawl but buries the competitive reasoning inside milestone text. The doc is cheap to maintain if it stays short (one table of gaps) and is updated only when a gap closes.
decisions.story: When I'm deciding what to work on next, I want to be able to ask 'are we close enough to replace TS for a typed API server?' and get a concrete yes/no per capability — not re-derive it from the roadmap every time.

options.name: Yes — short living gap doc under docs/plans or docs/proposals
options.detail: A one-page doc: two sections (TS, Swift), each a table of concrete gaps with status (open card / ratified / deferred). Updated when a gap closes. No prose, just the table. Cross-linked from roadmap. Cheap to maintain; high signal for roadmap prioritization. Recommend.

options.name: No standalone doc — fold into roadmap
options.detail: Keep the competitive lens implicit in roadmap milestone descriptions. No new file. The gap analysis is redone informally each planning cycle. Lower maintenance burden but harder to track whether specific gaps are closing.

comparisons.note: Rust maintains explicit 'Rust vs C++ / Rust vs Go' comparison pages in the Reference and blog posts. They age but remain useful anchors for roadmap conversations.
comparisons.code:
// rust-lang.org/en/what/networking — maintained gap analysis
// https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch00-01-foreword.html

comparisons.note: Zig keeps a short 'Why Zig when there is already C, C++, and Rust?' page — concrete capability comparisons, not marketing. Maintained as a living doc.
comparisons.code:
// ziglang.org/learn/why_zig_rust_d_nim/
// Table: per-language, per-capability yes/no

decisions.title: Should Jet codify a written stdlib ergonomic-laws checklist?
decisions.gist: Stdlib API principles exist in practice but are not written down as a checklist. Without a rubric, new Core/std APIs are reviewed inconsistently and edge cases (e.g. misuse-resistant crypto, path objects) can slip through. This decision is whether to author a short, durable rubric doc that every new stdlib API must pass before merge.
decisions.explainer: The checklist would live in docs/ (not the spec) and be referenced in PR review. It codifies things we already believe — like 'make misuse a type error', 'never accept raw strings where a path object works', 'CSPRNG and PRNG must not share a namespace' — so reviewers have a checklist rather than relying on institutional memory. It has no syntax impact and no I8 risk. It does require someone to author and maintain it; the risk is it becomes stale or ceremonial. This is a process/docs decision, not a language feature.
decisions.story: I keep catching the same API shape mistakes in review — raw strings instead of typed path objects, functions that are easy to call wrong. I want a short checklist I can point to instead of re-litigating the same principles every time.

options.name: Author the rubric doc
options.detail: Write a short (~10 rule) stdlib ergonomic-laws doc in docs/. Reference it in contributing guidelines. Every new Core/std API must pass it before merge. Low cost, high leverage — catches the same mistakes that keep surfacing.

options.name: Leave principles implicit
options.detail: Keep relying on reviewer knowledge and existing docs. No new doc to maintain. Risk: inconsistent API surface as the stdlib grows and new contributors join.
options.code:
// Status quo: reviewer catches it or doesn't.
// jet.fs.read_file("./data.txt")  — raw string slips through in a time-pressured review

comparisons.note: Rust has a published API guidelines doc (rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines) that is explicitly required for std contributions. It catches naming, error handling, and ergonomics issues before they land.
Swift has a mandatory API design guidelines doc. Every new stdlib addition is checked against it, enforcing naming clarity and call-site readability.
comparisons.code:
// Swift guideline: "Prefer method and function names that make use sites form grammatical English phrases"
array.insert(x, at: i)   // not array.insert(i, x)

decisions.title: Should `jet fmt` preserve author-written grouping parentheses?
decisions.gist: Authors sometimes write parentheses to clarify sub-expression grouping even when they are not required by precedence rules. Currently it is unclear whether `jet fmt` strips these. The decision is whether the formatter should preserve or remove redundant-but-intentional parentheses.
decisions.explainer: This touches the formatter's normalization policy. D-FMT1 established single-line/multi-line preservation as respecting author intent; this is the same principle applied to grouping parens. The formatter-roundtrip-required memory note means any change here requires a stability test. Option A (preserve all author parens) is safest for intent but may accumulate noise. Option C (preserve only where precedence is non-obvious) requires the formatter to reason about precedence ranks — more complex but more principled. Option B (strip to minimal) matches classical formatter behavior but erases intent.
decisions.story: I wrote `(a + b) * c` and `jet fmt` rewrote it as `a + b * c` — technically the same but now I can't tell at a glance that the grouping was intentional. The formatter should not second-guess me.

options.name: Preserve all author parens
options.detail: The formatter never removes any parentheses the author wrote. Intent is always respected. Simple rule: if the author put parens there, keep them. Risk: accumulated unnecessary parens over time in auto-generated or refactored code.

options.name: Normalize to minimal parens
options.detail: Strip any parentheses that are not needed for correct parsing. Produces the most compact output. Risk: erases author intent and can silently change apparent meaning even when actual meaning is the same.

options.name: Preserve only non-obvious precedence parens
options.detail: The formatter keeps parens when operators of differing precedence are mixed across a threshold of 'obvious' (e.g. arithmetic vs bitwise, bitwise vs boolean). Strips parens that are redundant within a single precedence group. Requires a precedence-obviousness table but is the most principled option.

comparisons.note: Prettier strips all redundant parens by default. This is a known complaint — authors use parens for documentation and Prettier removes them silently.
rustfmt preserves most author parens, removing only the truly degenerate cases (double-parens around a literal). Generally considered the right call.
comparisons.code:
// rustfmt keeps: let x = (a + b) * c;
// rustfmt removes: let x = ((42));  → let x = 42;

decisions.title: Should `if x = 5` produce a dedicated teaching diagnostic?
decisions.gist: Writing `if x = 5` is a classic C-family footgun (assignment instead of equality check). Jet uses `==` for equality, so `=` in a condition position is either a grammar error or silently misbehaves. This decision is whether to add a dedicated what/why/fix diagnostic (per I4) rather than relying on a generic parse error.
decisions.explainer: If the grammar already rejects `if x = 5`, the fix is a targeted diagnostic that says 'this looks like assignment in a condition; did you mean `==`?' with a snippet fix suggestion. If it is not rejected, we need to add the grammar guard first. Either way, this is an I4 compliance item: every diagnostic needs a code, what/why/fix text, and a ui snapshot. No new syntax is introduced. This does not interact with any ratified decision but does touch the did-you-mean infrastructure. Cheap and high-value for beginners.
decisions.story: I came from C/Go and wrote `if count = 0` — I got a cryptic parse error with no hint that I meant `==`. A clear message would have saved me 10 minutes.

options.name: Teaching diagnostic with ui snapshot
options.detail: Confirm (or add) grammar rejection of `=` in condition position, then wire a dedicated diagnostic: error code, what/why/fix text, and a `tests/ui` snapshot. This is the I4-compliant path and costs very little — one sema/parser rule + one snapshot.
options.code:
error[E0310]: assignment in condition
  --> src/main.jet:2:4
   |
 2 | if user_count = 0 {
   |    ^^^^^^^^^^^   ^ this is `=` (assignment), not `==` (equality)
   |
help: did you mean `==`?
 2 | if user_count == 0 {

options.name: Leave as generic parse error
options.detail: Do nothing beyond the existing grammar rejection. Beginners see a raw parse error. Against I4 (no code, no what/why/fix, no snapshot) and against the beginner-first priority.
options.code:
error: unexpected token `=`
  --> src/main.jet:2:14
   |
 2 | if user_count = 0 {
   |              ^ unexpected

comparisons.note: Rust explicitly rejects assignment in condition and produces a dedicated error suggesting `==`. It has been a point of praise in beginner tutorials.
Swift removed assignment-as-expression entirely in Swift 3, with a compiler error: 'Use of unresolved identifier'. Later versions produce a clear 'assignment cannot be used as a value' message.

decisions.title: Should Jet ship default-on semantic-smell lints (float `==`, constant conditions, duplicate branches)?
decisions.gist: Several high-signal, low-false-positive lint families exist in the wild: comparing floats with `==`, conditions that are always true/false, and duplicate match/if branches. None are currently carded for Jet. This decision is whether to ship them, and if so at what default level.
decisions.explainer: Each lint family has different false-positive risk: float `==` is almost always a bug (rare legitimate uses, e.g. checking for sentinel NaN); constant conditions are high-signal with some legitimate uses in comptime-adjacent code; duplicate branches are nearly always a copy-paste error. I4 requires every lint to have a code, what/why/fix text, and a ui snapshot before shipping. Bundling all three into one ballot is a scoping choice — the owner may want to split. These lints would live in the sema pass and trigger on the AST; no new syntax is introduced. They interact with lint profiles if those exist.
decisions.story: I wrote `if result == 0.1` in a tight loop and got wrong answers for two hours. I want the compiler to catch that. And when I copy-paste a match arm and forget to update the body, I want a warning, not a silent bug.

options.name: Default-on for high-confidence, opt-in for noisy
options.detail: Float `==` and duplicate branch: default-on (W-code + snapshot). Constant conditions: opt-in (can legitimately appear in comptime-adjacent or debug builds). Each gets a code, message, and fix suggestion per I4. Split-shipping is allowed — float and dup first, constant conditions later.
options.code:
warning[W0210]: float equality comparison
  --> src/main.jet:5:4
   |
 5 | if measurement == 0.1 {
   |    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ floats rarely compare exactly equal
   |
help: consider an epsilon check: `(measurement - 0.1).abs() < f64.EPSILON`

warning[W0211]: duplicate match arm body
  --> src/main.jet:3:11
   |
 3 |     Err => { handle_success() }  // same body as arm on line 2
   |

options.name: All opt-in via lint profile
options.detail: Ship all three as opt-in lints under a `#lint(smell)` profile. Default build is silent. Teams that want them enable them. Lower beginner value — the point of these is catching mistakes before the author knows to look.
options.code:
#lint(smell)  // at file or module scope
// now float == and dup branch warnings are active

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't ship any of these yet. Build the lint infrastructure generically first, then add specific lints. Risk: the same bugs keep shipping in user code while we wait.
options.code:
// No lint. User ships:
if sensor_reading == 0.0 { … }  // silent, wrong

comparisons.note: clippy::float_cmp is a deny-by-default lint that fires on direct float equality. clippy::match_like_matches_macro and clippy::branches_sharing_code cover duplicate-body cases.
IntelliJ flags duplicate branch bodies in `when` expressions as a built-in inspection, default-on, with a quick-fix to merge arms.

decisions.title: Should Jet warn on confusable identifiers co-existing in the same scope?
decisions.gist: Two identifiers that look nearly identical in the same scope — `user` vs `users`, `l` vs `1` vs `I`, `O` vs `0` — are a readability and bug risk. Jet's did-you-mean infrastructure already computes identifier similarity; this is a question of whether to add a lint on top of it for identifiers that are simultaneously in scope.
decisions.explainer: This is a new lint, not an extension of did-you-mean (which fires on missing identifiers). The lint would fire at declaration time when a new identifier is shadow-similar to an existing one in the same scope. False-positive risk is real: `user` and `users` are commonly both legitimate in a scope (entity and collection). Homoglyph confusables (`l`/`1`/`I`) are higher-signal and narrower. Splitting them into two sub-lints may be cleaner. I4 requires code + snapshot for each. No new syntax. Opt-in default lowers friction.
decisions.story: I had both `user` and `users` in scope and spent 20 minutes debugging a function that was acting on the wrong one. A lint would have caught it at write time.

options.name: Default-on for homoglyphs only, opt-in for near-names
options.detail: Homoglyph confusables (`l`/`1`/`I`, `O`/`0`) are default-on: they are almost never intentional in the same scope. Plural/singular near-names (`user`/`users`) are opt-in: frequently legitimate. Two codes, two snapshots.
options.code:
warning[W0230]: confusable identifier names in scope
  --> src/main.jet:3:9
   |
 1 | let l = get_length()
 3 | let I = get_index()  // `I` and `l` are confusable
   |     ^

options.name: Opt-in for all confusable classes
options.detail: No default warnings. Teams that care enable the lint via profile. Lowest friction, but misses the safety-net value for beginners who most need it.
options.code:
#lint(confusable_names)  // enable at module scope
// now l/1/I and user/users checks are active

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't ship until the lint-profile infrastructure is fully landed. The homoglyph case is high enough signal that deferring it is a real cost to beginners.
options.code:
// No lint. User ships with l and I both in scope.
// Bug surfaces at runtime.

comparisons.note: clippy::similar_names fires on identifiers that differ by one character or transposition in the same scope. It is allow-by-default due to false-positive rate — the same reasoning that makes opt-in the safer default here.
The Unicode Consortium's confusable-characters table (tr39) is the standard dataset for homoglyph detection. Using it ensures coverage of Cyrillic/Greek lookalikes, not just ASCII pairs.

decisions.title: Should Jet build a copy-paste-drift lint, and if so, when?
decisions.gist: When N near-identical blocks exist in a codebase and one diverges from the rest, it is almost always a missed update. Detecting structural duplication with drift requires a semantic index to compare AST subtrees across a file or project. No such lint exists in Jet today. The question is whether to pursue it and at what phase.
decisions.explainer: This lint cannot be a single-file sema pass — it requires a global view of the codebase (cross-file AST similarity). That means it depends on the semantic-index API, which is not yet landed. Building it standalone (as a separate tool) avoids the dependency but creates a parallel infrastructure. The high false-positive risk (similar-looking code is not always copy-pasted) makes opt-in the right default. Given the dependency, deferring until the semantic-index API lands is the practical choice — but the decision to pursue it at all should be made now so it gets a slot.
decisions.story: I copy-pasted a validation block for three new fields, updated two of them, and shipped a bug in the third for six months. If the compiler had seen four nearly-identical blocks and flagged the diverging one, I would have caught it immediately.

options.name: Defer: plan it now, build after semantic-index lands
options.detail: Record the intent as a roadmap item gated on the semantic-index API. Once the index exists, build this as an opt-in lint on top of it — no standalone tool, no parallel infrastructure. This is the right sequencing: don't block, don't build twice.

options.name: Standalone external tool now
options.detail: Build a separate `jet dup-check` command that does its own AST traversal independent of the semantic index. Ships sooner but creates duplicate infrastructure that must be maintained and eventually unified. Against I8 (two mechanisms for the same job).
options.code:
$ jet dup-check src/
warning: near-duplicate blocks detected
