  src/validators.jet:3 and src/validators.jet:6 differ by 1 statement

options.name: Don't pursue
options.detail: High false-positive risk, complex implementation, depends on infrastructure not yet built. The cost may not be worth the benefit compared to other lint investments. Defer indefinitely.
options.code: // No lint ever. Users rely on code review to catch drift.

comparisons.note: SonarQube's CPD (copy-paste detection) engine runs as a separate analysis pass over the full codebase AST. It is effective but requires a project-wide index — the same dependency Jet would have.
comparisons.code:
# sonar-project.properties
sonar.cpd.exclusions=**/generated/**
# CPD fires on blocks > 10 tokens that appear 2+ times

comparisons.note: jscpd is a standalone copy-paste detector that works on token streams, not a semantic index. Fast but produces more false positives on intentional similar-looking code.
comparisons.code:
npx jscpd src/ --min-lines 5 --min-tokens 50
# Clone found: src/a.ts (12-18) ~ src/b.ts (34-40)

decisions.title: Should Jet define separate Display and Debug rendering hooks for types?
decisions.gist: Currently Jet has interpolation and formatting but no formal split between user-facing display and developer-facing debug rendering. Mixing these means types either over-expose internals (debug format shown to users) or hide detail from developers (display format too terse for diagnostics). The decision is whether to add two blessed protocol hooks — Display and Debug — as separate rendering contracts.
decisions.explainer: This touches the blessed-protocol-hooks system and interpolation. A Display hook would produce user-facing strings (clean, localized, intentional). A Debug hook would produce a full-detail dump for developer diagnostics (may include internal fields, addresses, raw values). These are distinct semantic jobs, so two hooks does not violate I8. The alternative — a single hook — forces a choice between user-legible and debug-useful. Auto-derive for Debug (like Rust) gives types a free diagnostic representation. Display requires explicit authoring. This is a moderate addition: two new hooks, changes to the interpolation surface (syntax for which to use), and auto-derive for Debug.
decisions.story: I print a `Request` in a log message and get raw bytes the user should never see. Then in a debug session I need those bytes and can't get them without changing the type. I need two different 'show me this' answers.

options.name: Two hooks: Display (explicit) + Debug (auto-derive)
options.detail: Add Display and Debug as two blessed protocol hooks. Debug auto-derives for any struct/enum (like Rust's #[derive(Debug)]). Display requires explicit impl — no default. Interpolation uses `{}` for Display and `{:?}` for Debug (or Jet-idiomatic spelling to be ratified separately). I8-safe: two distinct jobs.

options.name: Single rendering hook
options.detail: One hook, author chooses what to expose. Simpler surface but forces the author to commit to one representation that serves both users and developers — practically, they end up writing two helpers anyway and calling them manually.

options.name: Display only; Debug is auto-derived always
options.detail: All types get a Debug representation auto-derived (no hook needed). Display is the only explicit hook. Simpler for beginners — they only learn one thing to implement — but Debug cannot be customized (e.g. to redact sensitive fields like auth tokens).

comparisons.note: Rust has Display (impl fmt::Display) for user-facing and Debug (impl fmt::Debug, derivable) for developer-facing. The split is widely praised as the right call. {:?} and {:#?} select Debug in format strings.
Python has __str__ (Display) and __repr__ (Debug). __repr__ is auto-provided but often unhelpful. The split is standard but not enforced, leading to inconsistency.

decisions.title: Should the PRNG and CSPRNG APIs be structurally separated to prevent misuse?
decisions.gist: `core.random` (fast, seedable PRNG) and `jet.crypto` (CSPRNG) already exist but their naming and structural relationship may not make the security boundary unmistakable. Using a PRNG for secrets (session tokens, keys, nonces) is a critical security bug. The decision is whether to add structural guards — naming, types, lints — that make misuse a compile-time or lint-time error.
decisions.explainer: This is a misuse-resistant API design problem. The PRNG is not secret-safe; the CSPRNG is. If both are called `random`, a developer searching for 'random' may pick the wrong one. The fix is: distinct namespaces (already partially true), a type-level or lint-level guard that blocks PRNG output from flowing into crypto-context parameters, and clear naming. This interacts with D-STDRUBRIC1 (the ergonomic checklist would catch this pattern). A lint that fires when PRNG output is used where a CryptoRand is expected is the highest-value addition. No new syntax — this is API shape + a lint.
decisions.story: I grepped for 'random' and used `core.random.int()` to generate a session token. It looked right. Six months later a security audit found it. I want the compiler to tell me I'm using the wrong thing.

options.name: Distinct namespaces + typed outputs + misuse lint
options.detail: Keep `core.random` for PRNG and `jet.crypto.random` for CSPRNG. Give them distinct return types (`PrngBytes` vs `CryptoBytes`). Add a lint that fires when `PrngBytes` flows into a parameter typed `CryptoBytes` or any parameter named `token`, `key`, `nonce`, `secret`. Docs and error messages call out the distinction explicitly.

options.name: Single random module with a security flag
options.detail: One `random` module; caller passes a security level flag. Simpler API surface but violates I8 (one module doing two jobs with a flag) and makes misuse easy — the default flag is the unsafe one.

options.name: Status quo: docs and naming only
options.detail: Keep the existing split as-is. Add clearer documentation. No types, no lint. Risk: documentation is not read at the call site; misuse continues silently.

comparisons.note: Python's `secrets` module is explicitly for cryptographic use; `random` is for simulations. The naming makes the split clear. There is no lint — misuse is silent.
comparisons.code:
import secrets, random
token = secrets.token_bytes(32)   # correct
token = random.randbytes(32)      # wrong, no warning

comparisons.note: Go separates CSPRNG (`crypto/rand`) from PRNG (`math/rand`) at the package level. Different import paths make confusion less likely but not impossible. No lint either.

decisions.title: How deep should jet.time go — full civil-time + IANA zones, minimal instants-only, or status quo?
decisions.gist: A deterministic injectable Clock already exists. The question is whether jet.time should grow to cover civil dates (year/month/day), time zones via the IANA tz database, duration arithmetic, and calendar math. Without this, backend apps must reach for raw FFI or a third-party package for anything beyond Unix timestamps.
decisions.explainer: Full civil-time is table-stakes for any app backend (scheduling, billing, audit logs). The IANA tz database is a native dependency — the tz data file ships with the OS or must be bundled, touching the native-deps-nixpkgs interim pattern. Durations and calendar math ("next billing date", "30 days from now") are tightly coupled to civil dates; separating them creates an awkward API. The injectable Clock already handles determinism in tests; civil-time layers on top cleanly. This decision sets the boundary for a Core module, not a package — changing it later breaks source compatibility.
decisions.story: I'm writing an invoicing backend. I need to compute the next billing date 30 days from today, display it in the user's local time zone, and store it in UTC. With only Unix timestamps I have to do this by hand or pull in a package — and then my tests break because the clock isn't injectable.

options.name: Full civil-time in Core (recommended)
options.detail: Add Date, DateTime, Duration, Zone (IANA-backed) to jet.time in Core. Tz data sourced from the host OS (Nix: pkgs.tzdata; non-Nix: bundled fallback with a clear error if absent). This is the complete, non-fragmented API. Tradeoff: tz data is a native dep; adds ~2 MB of tz data to distribution.

options.name: Minimal Core (instants + duration) + tz as a package
options.detail: Core ships Instant and Duration only; civil dates and tz live in a jet.time.civil package. Keeps Core small but splits a naturally unified API — users writing any date-display code must always reach for the package. Tradeoff: forces two imports for common work, and the split API is harder to teach.

options.name: Status quo — don't expand jet.time
options.detail: Leave jet.time at the deterministic Clock / Instant layer. Users who need civil dates and tz use FFI or a community package. Appropriate only if Jet targets systems/embedded workloads where civil-time is irrelevant. For a general-purpose language this is a significant omission.
options.code:
-- Today: user must do this
import jet.ffi
let ts = ffi.libc.time(null)          -- raw Unix timestamp, no tz, no calendar

comparisons.note: stdlib time package ships full civil-time + IANA tz out of the box; tz data embedded or host-sourced. Widely considered the right call for a general-purpose language.
comparisons.code:
t := time.Now().In(time.LoadLocation("America/New_York"))
nextBill := t.AddDate(0, 0, 30)

comparisons.note: Rust stdlib has only Instant/Duration; civil-time requires the chrono crate (or time crate). This fragmentation is a common pain point — Jet can do better by including it in Core.
comparisons.code:
use chrono::{DateTime, Utc, Duration};
let next = Utc::now() + Duration::days(30);

decisions.title: Should we maintain a desugaring map doc that records what each surface feature lowers to?
decisions.gist: No written record currently exists of which surface features are sugar and what kernel form they lower to. This means different compiler passes may independently re-derive the lowering, and I8 (one canonical way to mean a semantic job) is enforced only by convention. The question is whether to create and maintain a small doc that makes these lowerings explicit.
decisions.explainer: A desugaring map disciplines I8 directly: if a new feature proposal would introduce a second mechanism that lowers to the same kernel form as an existing one, the doc makes that visible immediately. It also anchors the compiler-seams work (the 7-crate workspace under crates/) by giving each crate a clear contract for what it receives and emits. The doc is a living spec artifact, not a one-shot writeup — it must be updated whenever a surface feature is added or changed. Cost: author time per feature; benefit: prevents silent I8 violations and aids new contributors reading the compiler.
decisions.story: I'm reading the sema crate trying to understand what `for x in xs { }` desugars to. There's no doc — I have to grep through four files and guess whether the lowering is canonical or accidental. A one-page map would have answered this in ten seconds.

options.name: Maintain desugaring map in docs/spec (recommended)
options.detail: Create docs/spec/desugaring.md listing each surface form and the kernel AST node(s) it lowers to. Updated as part of the workflow loop (any feature that touches lowering updates the doc). Acts as an I8 guard and a contributor reference. No new invariant needed — fits the existing 'done means: tests pass, docs match behavior' standard.

options.name: Skip the doc
options.detail: Rely on code comments and grep to understand lowerings. Simpler now; becomes expensive as the surface grows. Leaves I8 enforcement purely implicit. Not recommended for a language that bills itself as having 'one canonical way to mean it'.
options.code:
-- current state: no single place to check
-- grep for_in Source/sema/*.rs  -- may return 6 files, no canonical answer

comparisons.note: The Kotlin spec maintains explicit desugaring rules for lambdas, for-loops, destructuring, and delegates. It is the authoritative reference for contributors and tooling authors.
GHC's 'desugaring' phase is formally documented in the Commentary wiki. Designers check it when evaluating new syntax for overlap with existing mechanisms.
comparisons.code:
-- GHC desugars do-notation:
-- do { x <- m; rest } => m >>= \x -> rest

decisions.title: Should Set<T> and Deque<T> ship in Core collections, or stay as packages or deferred?
decisions.gist: Core currently has Map and List (and presumably Array/Slice). Set and Deque/ring-buffer are absent. These are table-stakes data structures for nearly every non-trivial program — their absence forces users to reach for FFI or community packages for basic work. The question is whether they belong in Core now.
decisions.explainer: Set<T> requires a hashing or ordering story: hash-based Set needs a Hash constraint on T; ordered Set needs Ord. Both constraints exist in some form for Map already, so Set is a natural extension. Deque<T> is useful for queues, sliding windows, and BFS — a ring-buffer backing is the standard implementation. Shipping them separately means two packages and two import paths for what most languages expose as a single collections namespace. I8 applies: there should be exactly one Set type; adding both a Core Set and a package Set later is a violation. Decide the hashing story for Set alongside this decision.
decisions.story: I'm implementing BFS on a graph. I need a visited set and a FIFO queue. Without Set and Deque in Core I have to either fake a set with Map<T, ()> or pull in a package — both are annoying workarounds for things every language ships.

options.name: Ship Set + Deque in Core (recommended)
options.detail: Add Set<T: Hash + Eq> (hash-backed, unordered) and Deque<T> (ring-buffer) to jet.collections. OrderedSet<T: Ord> can be a follow-on. Ring buffer is the Deque backing — not a separate type (I8: one deque type). Hash/Eq constraints mirror Map's existing story; no new mechanism required.

options.name: Set only, defer Deque
options.detail: Ship Set<T> in Core now; treat Deque as a later addition or package. Useful if Deque is genuinely rare in initial target workloads. Tradeoff: BFS / sliding-window patterns still need workarounds; feels incomplete alongside Set.
options.code:
import jet.collections.Set

let visited: Set<str> = Set.new()
visited.insert("a")
print(visited.contains("a"))  -- true
-- still need List-as-queue workaround for BFS

options.name: Both as packages, not Core
options.detail: Ship Set and Deque as first-party packages (jet.collections.set, jet.collections.deque) rather than Core. Keeps Core minimal. Tradeoff: two extra imports for everyday work; fragments what should be a unified collections story; packages can't be as tightly integrated with type inference as Core types.

comparisons.note: set and collections.deque are both in the standard library. Their absence in a new general-purpose language would be conspicuous.
comparisons.code:
from collections import deque
visited = set()
queue = deque([start])

comparisons.note: Swift stdlib has Set<T> (hash-backed) but no Deque — that lives in swift-collections package. The omission is a known pain point; Jet can avoid it.
comparisons.code:
var visited = Set<String>()
// Deque requires: import Collections (package)

decisions.title: Should UUID (v4/v7) and base64/hex codecs ship in Core, or stay as packages or FFI-only?
decisions.gist: UUID generation and base64/hex encoding appear only in FFI examples today — there is no Core API for them. These utilities are ubiquitous in backend work (IDs, tokens, binary protocol data, serialization). The question is whether they belong in Core or in first-party packages.
decisions.explainer: UUID v4 requires a CSPRNG; UUID v7 requires the Clock (already injectable, so tests stay deterministic). Base64 and hex are pure-algorithm codecs with no dependencies. All four are used together frequently (e.g., generate a v7 UUID, store as base64 in a URL). Putting them in Core means one import; splitting them across packages means fragmentation for a very common task. The CSPRNG dependency for v4 is the main complexity — it must be a seeded/injectable source in tests (mirrors Clock). I8: if Core ships these, no package should duplicate them later. FFI-only status quo is a real footgun: users write their own unsafe wrapper or vendored code just to generate an ID.
decisions.story: I'm building a REST API. Every new record needs a UUID. Every token I issue needs to be base64-encoded. Right now I have to write FFI glue just to call uuid and base64 — that's not 'batteries included'.

options.name: Core: hex + base64 codecs + UUID v4/v7 (recommended)
options.detail: Ship jet.encoding (hex, base64 encode/decode) and jet.uuid (UUID v4 via CSPRNG, UUID v7 via injectable Clock) in Core. CSPRNG is system-sourced (/dev/urandom or OS equivalent) with an injectable interface for tests. No new language mechanism — pure library. Tradeoff: adds OS RNG dependency, but this is simpler and safer than leaving users to FFI it.

options.name: Split: UUID as a package, codecs in Core
options.detail: Ship hex/base64 in Core (no external deps), but UUID as a first-party package (jet.uuid). Sensible if embedded/WASM targets can't access a system RNG. Tradeoff: users generating IDs need an extra package; the most common use case is a two-import pattern.
options.code:
import jet.encoding.{base64}   -- Core
import jet.uuid.{UUID}          -- package

let id = UUID.v4()
print(base64.encode(id.to_bytes()))

options.name: Status quo: FFI only
options.detail: Leave UUID and encoding to FFI or community packages. Zero Core change. Not viable for a 'batteries included' language — generating a unique ID should not require unsafe FFI glue.
options.code:
-- current workaround:
let id_str = ffi.libc_uuid.generate()  -- unsafe, no test injection

comparisons.note: encoding/hex and encoding/base64 are stdlib. UUID is not (google/uuid package is the de facto standard) — a gap Go users commonly cite.
uuid and base64 are both in stdlib. UUID v4 uses os.urandom() by default. Considered the obvious right call.
comparisons.code:
import uuid, base64
id = uuid.uuid4()
print(base64.b64encode(id.bytes).decode())

decisions.title: Should Jet ship an exact base-10 Decimal type in Core plus a default-on lint against float money?
decisions.gist: There is no exact decimal numeric type in Jet today. Floating-point is the default numeric type for fractional values — a classic footgun for monetary arithmetic. The idea is to add a Decimal type and a lint that fires when float is used in a context that looks like money.
decisions.explainer: The float-for-money footgun is one of the most documented programming mistakes; it produces silent rounding errors in billing, accounting, and tax calculations. A default-on lint makes the safe path the effortless path (I1). Decimal requires a precision model choice: arbitrary precision (like Python's Decimal) vs. fixed-scale (like SQL DECIMAL(p,s)). Arbitrary precision is more flexible but harder to implement efficiently; fixed-scale is simpler and maps to most database types. The lint and the Decimal type are independent — the lint can ship without Decimal if needed, but both together close the footgun completely. I8: one Decimal type; do not later allow a second 'money' type that duplicates it.
decisions.story: I add up three prices: 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.7. The answer is 0.9999999999999999. My invoice is wrong and I didn't notice until a customer complained. If the compiler had flagged `price: float` with 'use Decimal for money', I'd have caught this at write-time.

options.name: Decimal in Core + default-on float-money lint (recommended)
options.detail: Ship Decimal (arbitrary precision, base-10) in jet.numeric. Ship a default-on lint E-FLOATMONEY that fires when a variable/field named price, cost, amount, total, fee, balance, tax holds a float. Lint is suppressible with #[allow(float_money)] for intentional uses. Tradeoff: arbitrary precision needs a bigint backing (native dep or pure-Rust implementation); lint has false positives for non-money float fields with money-sounding names.
options.code:
-- This triggers E-FLOATMONEY:
let price: float = 19.99
-- error[E-FLOATMONEY]: `price` holds a float; use Decimal for monetary values
--   hint: let price: Decimal = Decimal.from("19.99")

-- Correct:
let price: Decimal = Decimal.from("19.99")
let total = price * Decimal.from("1.08")
print(total.round_half_up(2))   -- "21.59"

options.name: Decimal as a package, no Core lint
options.detail: Ship Decimal as a first-party package (jet.numeric.decimal). No lint. Users who know they need it import it; others don't. Tradeoff: the footgun remains the silent default; beginners who don't know about float rounding will reach for float and get wrong answers.
options.code:
import jet.numeric.decimal.{Decimal}
let price = Decimal.from("19.99")   -- only if user knows to import it

options.name: Lint only, no Decimal type
options.detail: Add the float-money lint but don't ship Decimal — just suggest the user use an integer (cents) or import a community package. Tradeoff: the lint fires but has nowhere to point the user that's first-class. Incomplete solution.
options.code:
-- lint fires:
let price: float = 19.99
-- error[E-FLOATMONEY]: use integer cents or a decimal package
-- (but no built-in Decimal to offer)

comparisons.note: decimal.Decimal is in stdlib. No lint in the language itself, but the docs explicitly warn against float for money. Jet can enforce this mechanically.
comparisons.code:
from decimal import Decimal
price = Decimal("19.99")
total = price * Decimal("1.08")  # exact

comparisons.note: BigDecimal is in stdlib. No lint; beginners routinely use double for money and get burned. FindBugs/SpotBugs has a money-float check — but only in third-party tooling.
comparisons.code:
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99");
BigDecimal total = price.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.08"));

decisions.title: Should Jet ship a typed Path API with atomic write and dir-walk, replacing raw-string filesystem use?
decisions.gist: Jet has path and list_dir functions but treats filesystem paths as raw strings. Raw-string paths are a source of injection bugs, platform-specific separator errors, and silent overwrites on write. The proposal is a Path type with safe join/parent/extension methods, atomic rename-based writes, and a recursive walk iterator.
decisions.explainer: Path objects prevent the most common filesystem mistakes: concatenating paths with string + (gets separators wrong on Windows), writing to a file that another reader is mid-read (atomic write-rename avoids this), and forgetting to handle cycles in recursive traversal. The existing path/list_dir functions are thin wrappers; a typed Path doesn't break them but supersedes them as the canonical API (I8: one way to work with paths). Atomic write (write-to-temp then rename) is a single OS call sequence — no new language mechanism needed, just stdlib. Walk returns an iterator (lazy) with cycle detection. This decision sets whether Path is Core or a package.
decisions.story: I write a config file to disk. Halfway through the write, the process dies — the file is now corrupt and the app won't start. Atomic write would have prevented this. I also have a bug where I built a path with + instead of Path.join() and it broke on Windows. A Path type catches both.

options.name: Core Path type with join/parent/ext, atomic write, walk iterator (recommended)
options.detail: Ship jet.fs.Path as a Core type. Path.from(str) is the entry point. join(), parent(), extension(), stem() are pure methods. write_atomic() writes to a sibling temp file and renames. walk() returns a lazy iterator with cycle detection (symlink loop guard). Supersedes raw-string path helpers — those become teaching errors pointing to Path. Tradeoff: more API surface than raw strings, but each method does exactly one obvious thing.
options.code:
import jet.fs.{Path, WalkEntry}

let out = Path.from("/data").join("reports").join("2026.csv")
print(out.extension())    -- "csv"
print(out.parent())       -- Path("/data/reports")

out.parent().create_dir_all()
out.write_atomic("date,amount\n2026-01-01,100".to_bytes())

-- atomic: writes to /data/reports/.2026.csv.tmp, then rename
-- if process dies mid-write, original is never corrupted

options.name: Keep string paths + add helper functions
options.detail: Add path_join(), path_parent(), path_ext() as functions that operate on str. Add write_atomic(path: str, data: Bytes). No new type. Tradeoff: string paths remain passable where typed paths would catch errors; platform separator bugs persist; no type-level distinction between 'a path' and 'an arbitrary string'.

options.name: Status quo — raw strings, no atomic write
options.detail: Leave filesystem access as raw strings and non-atomic writes. Only appropriate if Jet targets embedded/WASM where filesystem APIs don't exist. For a general-purpose backend language, this leaves two real footguns: platform separator bugs and torn writes.
options.code:
-- current state:
let p = "/data/reports/" + "2026.csv"    -- separator hardcoded, breaks on Windows
file.write(p, data)                         -- non-atomic, can corrupt on crash

comparisons.note: pathlib.Path was added in 3.4 and is now the recommended way to work with paths. / operator for join, .stem/.suffix/.parent as properties. Atomic write not built in (requires tempfile + rename).
comparisons.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path.home() / ".config" / "myapp" / "settings.json"
p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
p.write_text(data)

comparisons.note: PathBuf / Path in std. push(), join(), extension(). Atomic write is a user pattern (write to NamedTempFile, persist). Jet can bake this in.

decisions.title: Should Jet ship library types for TTL-bounded cache entries and expiring secrets, or defer to tracked-uncertainty work?
decisions.gist: There are no first-class TTL/expiry types in Jet today. Cache entries that outlive their validity and secrets that stay in memory past their intended lifetime are both real hazards. The question is whether to address these now as library types (no language changes) or wait for a deeper 'tracked uncertainty' / freshness-effects system.
decisions.explainer: A TtlCache<K,V> and an ExpiringSecret<T> are pure library types — they wrap a value with a deadline derived from the injectable Clock (already exists) and return an error or zeroize on access past expiry. No language change is required. The alternative (a type-system-level 'expires' dimension that makes staleness a compile-time property) would require tracked effects and is on the roadmap as a larger research item. Coupling these two concerns delays the useful library types for a feature that may be years away. I1: ExpiringSecret should zeroize memory on drop and on expiry by default — the safe path is automatic. I8: if we ship TtlCache now, no second cache type later.
decisions.story: I cache a JWT public key. It has a 1-hour validity. Right now nothing stops me from using a cached key past its expiry — I have to remember to check the timestamp myself. An ExpiringSecret type would refuse access after the deadline and force me to handle the 'stale' case.

options.name: Library types now: TtlCache + ExpiringSecret (recommended)
options.detail: Ship jet.cache.TtlCache<K,V> and jet.security.ExpiringSecret<T>. Both take the injectable Clock so tests are deterministic. ExpiringSecret zeroizes memory on drop and on expiry (I1 — safe by default). TtlCache evicts lazily on access (no background thread needed). No language changes. Revisit type-level freshness tracking when tracked-uncertainty work matures.

options.name: Language-level 'expires' dimension (defer to tracked-uncertainty)
options.detail: Treat expiry as a type-level effect (a freshness dimension on values), so the compiler can statically flag use of a stale value. Powerful but requires tracked-effects work that is not yet designed. Ships nothing useful now; developers continue to handle expiry manually in the meantime.
options.code:
-- hypothetical future syntax (not ratified):
let key: Bytes @expires(1h) = fetch_key()
use_key(key)   -- compiler error if called >1h after binding
-- (not yet designed; shown only to illustrate the concept)

options.name: Defer entirely
options.detail: Ship nothing now. Developers track TTL manually with timestamps and conditional checks. No footgun prevention, no memory zeroization. Appropriate only if Jet targets workloads where caching and secrets are irrelevant.

comparisons.note: The secrecy crate wraps sensitive values in Secret<T> which zeroizes on drop. No TTL — expiry is still manual. Jet can do both in one type.
TTL caches are community packages in Go. No standard ExpiringSecret type. Secret zeroization requires explicit memset via unsafe. Jet can offer both safely and standardly.

decisions.title: Should Jet ship an official jet.raylib graphics package (FFI-bridge pattern) for cross-platform games and visual demos?
decisions.gist: No first-party graphics package exists in Jet today. Raylib is a C library covering 2D/3D rendering, input, audio, and windowing across Windows, macOS, Linux, and web. The proposal is an official FFI-bridge package (not in the compiler) that gives Jet programs a clean native-graphics story for games, tools, and flagship demos.
decisions.explainer: The FFI-bridge pattern is already established in stdlib (Archive.rs, Db.rs, FFI.rs) — a package emits bridge template text without adding a crate to the compiler's Cargo.toml (I6-safe). Raylib is MIT-licensed, actively maintained, and purpose-built for exactly this use case. A first-party package signals intent and ensures the bridge is idiomatic Jet (markers, error types, safe wrappers). Without it, the only graphics path is user-authored FFI glue — not something beginners can do. This is also a flagship vertical: a working Jet game demo is one of the highest-signal proofs the language is real. The package lives outside the compiler; a community package would be acceptable if the community existed, but it doesn't yet.
decisions.story: I want to build a small game in Jet to learn the language. Every other modern language has a tutorial path to a moving sprite on screen. Jet has nothing — I'd have to write my own C FFI bindings to even open a window. An official raylib package makes 'write a game in Jet' a realistic first project.

options.name: Official jet.raylib FFI-bridge package (recommended)
options.detail: Create a first-party package under the jet.* namespace using the FFI-bridge pattern (emits bridge template text; no Cargo.toml change in the compiler). Covers Window, Texture, draw, input, audio at minimum. Raylib is a native dep (C library) — sourced via nixpkgs on Nix; bundled raylib source fallback for non-Nix (raylib supports being compiled from source with no system deps). This is a package, not a Core module — opt-in only.

options.name: Leave to community packages
options.detail: Don't maintain a first-party raylib binding. Wait for community contributors to publish one. Tradeoff: the community doesn't exist yet; this leaves graphics entirely unaddressed for the foreseeable future. No flagship demo is possible without it. Not recommended while the ecosystem is empty.
options.code:
-- hypothetical community package (doesn't exist):
-- [dependencies]
-- raylib-jet = "0.1"  -- community-maintained, unknown quality

options.name: Plan an own renderer for later, nothing now
options.detail: Defer graphics entirely; plan a native Jet renderer (WebGPU or similar) as a future milestone. Tradeoff: a native renderer is a multi-year project; leaving graphics unaddressed now means no demos, no games, no visual flagship for years. The FFI bridge to raylib can coexist with a future native renderer — this option is false economy.
options.code:
-- no graphics today; future milestone:
-- jet.gfx (WebGPU-backed, post-v1)

comparisons.note: Odin ships vendor:raylib as a first-party vendor binding in the standard distribution. It is consistently cited as a reason developers try Odin for game prototyping. The binding is idiomatic Odin, not raw C.
raylib-zig is an official community package. Less tightly integrated than Odin's vendor binding but widely used for Zig game tutorials.

decisions.title: Should Jet distribute UI components as copy-in-and-own rather than a locked dependency?
decisions.gist: This decides whether Jet's UI component story follows a shadcn-style model: components are copied into user source and owned outright, not versioned behind a dependency. No UI component kit exists yet. This is a distribution model decision, not a component design decision — it gates what comes next.
decisions.explainer: The reactive-ui-stack decision (not yet ratified) must come first; this decision is downstream of it. The choice here shapes how jetpack handles UI components: a `jetpack add` command that copies source vs. a traditional dep that users don't own. Ownable distribution fits Jet's ownership ethos and removes forced upgrade coupling, but it means patches don't automatically propagate. It does not affect language semantics. Interact with: accessibility-by-default card (wherever that lands, accessible defaults ship in the component source the user now owns).
decisions.story: I want to use a button component. I run `jetpack add button`, it copies `components/button.jet` into my project, I read it, I change the hover color, and that's it — no fighting a library's theming API, no breaking upgrade.

options.name: Defer — wait for reactive-ui-stack decision
options.detail: Block this card until the reactive-ui-stack direction is ratified. The distribution model is meaningless without knowing what stack the components target. No wasted design work.
options.code:
// No component API to show yet.
// Unblock after reactive-ui-stack is decided.

options.name: Ownable kit via `jetpack add` (copy-in)
options.detail: jetpack copies component source into the user's tree. User owns it immediately. No version lock. Patches don't auto-propagate — user re-runs add or diffs manually. Fits I8 (one distribution path).
options.code:
$ jetpack add button
  Copied components/button.jet → src/components/button.jet
  You own this file. Edit freely.

options.name: Traditional versioned UI library dep
options.detail: Components live behind a jetpack dependency version. Users get updates automatically but fight theming APIs to customize. Standard model but conflicts with Jet's ownership ethos.

comparisons.note: Components are copied into your repo via CLI; you own and edit them. This is the direct model for option B.
comparisons.code:
npx shadcn-ui@latest add button
# copies components/ui/button.tsx into your tree

comparisons.note: Locked widget library; users customize via theme objects. Equivalent to option C — you fight the theming API rather than editing source.
comparisons.code:
// pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter

decisions.title: Should Jet add a `defer` keyword for scope-exit cleanup, or keep `core.scope.guard` as the only path?
decisions.gist: `core.scope.guard` already handles scope-exit cleanup. The question is whether a `defer` keyword should be added as the canonical spelling. Adding both violates I8 — two ways to do the same thing.
decisions.explainer: I8 forbids a second mechanism for the same semantic job without retiring the first. If `defer` ships, `core.scope.guard` must be demoted or removed. If it stays, the keyword is declined. The guard library form is already callable, composable, and consistent with other `core.scope.*` utilities. A keyword adds parse surface and teaches beginners a new control-flow concept that isn't in the type system. Interactions: D-SUGAR5 (nearby sugar declined); any RAII/destructor story is a related but separate decision.
decisions.story: I open a file and I want to make sure it closes when my function returns, even on error. I want to write `defer file.close()` at the top of the function and stop thinking about it.

options.name: Keep library guard only — no keyword
options.detail: Decline the keyword. `core.scope.guard` stays canonical. No new parse surface, no I8 violation, no migration cost. The ergonomic gap is one extra let-binding.

options.name: Add `defer` keyword, retire the guard
options.detail: `defer <expr>` becomes the canonical spelling. `core.scope.guard` is deprecated and removed on a migration path. Cleaner for beginners; requires parser + sema work and a deprecation cycle.

comparisons.note: `defer` is a keyword; it's idiomatic Go. Arguments stack LIFO. No library alternative.
`defer` is a keyword, runs at scope exit, used for cleanup. Similar motivation.
No `defer` keyword; cleanup is via RAII Drop. Library crates like `scopeguard` exist. Jet's `core.scope.guard` maps to this pattern.
comparisons.code:
use scopeguard::defer;
defer! { file.close(); }

decisions.title: Should Jet add a prelude opt-out directive, and/or let libraries mark names as prelude-injectable?
decisions.gist: The prelude auto-imports `print`, `input`, and a curated set. Two new ideas: (1) a user directive to opt out of the prelude, and (2) a library marker that puts names into scope without a prefix (`#builtin`-style). These can ship independently. This card decides both.
decisions.explainer: Opt-out lets expert users who want explicit imports take full control — a clean I1-compatible escape hatch. Library no-prefix injection is the riskier half: it lets any package pollute the default namespace, violates I8 (arbitrary second paths to a name), and defeats the prelude's curation. A library using this would look like Jet's own prelude to a beginner who can't tell the difference. Interactions: prelude `print`/`input` are ratified; this doesn't touch them. The `#builtin` marker is unratified scratch.
decisions.story: I'm writing a CLI tool with explicit imports everywhere for clarity. I want to put `#NoPrelude` at the top of my file and have zero implicit names — then import exactly what I use.

options.name: Opt-out directive only — no library injection
options.detail: Add a `#NoPrelude` file-level marker that disables auto-imports. Library no-prefix injection is declined (I8 violation — lets packages create arbitrary implicit paths). This is the minimal, safe escape hatch.

options.name: Both opt-out and library injection
options.detail: Libraries can mark exports with a `#Prelude`-style marker to inject names into callers' scope. Powerful but breaks I8 and the namespace contract — any dep can now shadow prelude names.

options.name: Neither — no changes
options.detail: Keep the current curated prelude with no opt-out. Expert users import on top of the prelude; the prelude names are always present. Simplest surface, least flexible.

comparisons.note: `#![no_std]` and `#![no_implicit_prelude]` opt out of std and prelude respectively. Expert escape hatch, not the default.
`{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}` disables the Prelude import per-file. Libraries then re-export curated sets (Protolude, Relude).
comparisons.code:
{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}
import Protolude

decisions.title: Should Jet ship a misuse-resistant crypto envelope (`seal`/`sign`) as the blessed default?
decisions.gist: Crypto primitives exist in some form. The question is whether Jet should provide a high-level `seal`/`open` + `sign`/`verify` envelope API that hides nonce, IV, and mode selection — with raw primitives gated behind the expert tier. This is a new API surface decision.
decisions.explainer: I1 (safe by default) directly motivates this: nonces, IVs, and cipher mode selection are where real-world crypto bugs live. A seal/open envelope (libsodium model) makes the correct choice automatic. Raw primitives remain available but live behind `@unsafe` or an explicit expert import, making misuse visible. Post-quantum agility is a downstream decision that sequences after this envelope shape is ratified. Interaction with the random-split card: the envelope must use a CSPRNG sourced from the ratified random API.
decisions.story: I want to encrypt a message to a recipient. I have their public key. I should be able to call `crypto.seal(message, recipient_key)` and get a ciphertext I can't misuse — no mode selection, no nonce wrangling, no IV parameter.

options.name: Seal/open + sign/verify envelope as default; primitives expert-gated
options.detail: Ship `crypto.seal`/`crypto.open` and `crypto.sign`/`crypto.verify` as the canonical API. Raw AES/ChaCha/RSA primitives require an explicit expert import. Misuse requires deliberate opt-in. Aligns with I1.

options.name: Expose primitives only — no envelope
options.detail: Ship AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, Ed25519 etc. directly. Users compose their own envelope. Maximum flexibility; maximum footgun surface. Conflicts with I1 for a default API.

options.name: Defer — wait for post-quantum agility decision
options.detail: Hold the envelope design until the post-quantum algorithm agility card is decided, so the envelope shape doesn't need to change. Delays a useful safe-by-default API.
options.code: // nothing ships yet

comparisons.note: The canonical misuse-resistant model: `crypto_box_seal` / `crypto_sign_detached`. No mode selection exposed at the default level.
comparisons.code:
crypto_box_seal(ciphertext, msg, msg_len, recipient_pk);
crypto_sign_detached(sig, NULL, msg, msg_len, sk);

comparisons.note: Provides `ChaChaPoly.seal` with automatic nonce. Still exposes AES-GCM with manual nonce as an alternative — two ways to seal.
comparisons.code:
let sealed = try ChaChaPoly.seal(data, using: key)
let opened = try ChaChaPoly.open(sealed, using: key)

decisions.title: Should Jet add an arbitrary-precision integer type (BigInt) to the standard library?
decisions.gist: No arbitrary-precision integer exists in Jet today. Fixed-width integers overflow silently in some contexts or trap. The question is whether to add a `BigInt` type — and if so, whether fixed integers auto-promote on overflow or whether BigInt is always explicit.
decisions.explainer: Sized integers are ratified (dsg9). The main design fork is overflow behavior: auto-promotion on overflow (Python model) vs explicit `BigInt` construction only. Auto-promotion is ergonomic but breaks the type: the return type of `+` on `Int` would depend on the value, not the type — incompatible with Jet's static type system. Explicit-only is the only safe fit. This also touches the decimal-money card: financial math may prefer `Decimal` over `BigInt` for exact representation. Interaction with I6: a BigInt implementation in std would use a Rust dependency unless native-implemented; owner approval required for any new I6 dep.
decisions.story: I'm computing a large factorial for a cryptographic key length check. The result doesn't fit in `Int64`. I want to write `BigInt(n).factorial()` and get the exact answer, not a wrapped or trapping result.

options.name: Core `BigInt` — explicit construction, no auto-promotion
options.detail: Add `BigInt` as a stdlib type. Fixed integers never auto-promote: `Int64 + Int64` stays `Int64` (traps or wraps per mode). BigInt is constructed explicitly. Fits static typing and I8.

options.name: Package-level only — not in core std
options.detail: BigInt ships as a first-party package (`jet.math.bigint`), not in core. Keeps std small; user opts in. Suitable if demand is narrow (crypto, scientific). Same explicit-only overflow contract.
options.code:
import jet.math.bigint.BigInt

let x = BigInt(2).pow(BigInt(128))

options.name: Defer — decide after decimal-money card
options.detail: The decimal-money card may clarify which exact-numeric niche BigInt fills vs Decimal. Deferring avoids shipping two overlapping numeric escape hatches.
options.code: // no BigInt yet

comparisons.note: Int auto-promotes to arbitrary precision on overflow. Ergonomic but makes integer type semantics value-dependent — not viable in a static type system.
comparisons.code: x = 2 ** 1000  # plain int, arbitrary precision automatically

comparisons.note: `BigInteger` is a standard library class, always explicit. Fixed ints overflow without promotion. Closest model to option A.
comparisons.code:
BigInteger x = BigInteger.TWO.pow(256);
BigInteger y = x.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(99999999L));

comparisons.note: No BigInt in stdlib. `Foundation` has none either. Third-party `BigInt` package required. Matches option B.
comparisons.code:
import BigInt  // third-party
let x = BigInt(2).power(256)

decisions.title: Should Jet ship grapheme-cluster iteration and Unicode normalization in the core standard library?
decisions.gist: Jet strings are Unicode-aware, but no grapheme-cluster iterator or normalization (NFC/NFD) API exists. Without these, user-facing text operations (length by visible character, string comparison) are incorrect for many languages. This is a new std API decision.
decisions.explainer: Grapheme clusters and normalization are distinct: you can ship iteration without normalization. Both require Unicode Character Database (UCD) tables, which are large (~1MB). Bundling in core std means every Jet binary carries this data; package-level avoids that for users who don't need it. The UCD tables must come from somewhere — a verified Rust crate via the FFI-bridge pattern is I6-compatible with owner sign-off, or native tables generated at build time. Interaction with native-deps memory: UCD is data, not a C lib, so the FFI-bridge pattern fits cleanly.
decisions.story: I'm building a text editor. I split the user's string on characters and the emoji with a skin-tone modifier counts as two — the cursor jumps wrong. I need `str.graphemes()` to iterate by visible cluster, not by codepoint.

options.name: Core: grapheme iterator + normalization (NFC/NFD)
options.detail: Both APIs ship in core std. UCD tables included in std via FFI-bridge or native. Binary size increases ~1MB. Correctness for user-facing text is a correctness concern, not an optional nicety.

options.name: Package-level (`jet.text.unicode`) — not in core
options.detail: Both APIs ship as a first-party package. Core strings remain lightweight. Users who need correct text processing opt in. Avoids mandatory UCD bloat for CLI tools, network code, etc.

options.name: Grapheme iteration only — defer normalization
options.detail: Ship grapheme iteration in core or package; defer normalization (NFC/NFD) to a later card. The two are independently useful and can ship in sequence.
options.code:
for g in s.graphemes() { ... }  // iteration ships
// normalization deferred

comparisons.note: Strings index by extended grapheme clusters by default. `String.unicodeScalars` gives codepoint access. Normalization via `String.decomposedStringWithCompatibilityMapping`.
comparisons.code:
let s = "caf\u{E9}"
print(s.count)  // 4, grapheme clusters
let nfc = s.precomposedStringWithCanonicalMapping

comparisons.note: No grapheme iteration in std. The `unicode-segmentation` crate provides it. Normalization via `unicode-normalization` crate. Both are explicit opt-in.
comparisons.code:
use unicode_segmentation::UnicodeSegmentation;
for g in s.graphemes(true) { ... }

comparisons.note: No grapheme iteration in stdlib. Third-party `grapheme` package or `unicodedata` for normalization only.
comparisons.code:
import unicodedata
nfc = unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s)

decisions.title: Which compression codecs should ship with Jet std, and how — alongside or separate from archive containers?
decisions.gist: `jet.archive` is the planned/in-progress archive container work (zip/tar). Compression codecs (gzip, zstd, brotli) are independent of archive containers — you can compress a stream without building a zip. This decides which codecs ship, where they live, and how they're sourced.
decisions.explainer: Archive containers and compression codecs are separate concerns: tar is a container, gzip is a codec, and a `.tar.gz` is both layered. Conflating them delays codecs behind archive work. The sourcing question is I6-relevant: gzip and zstd have well-maintained pure-Rust implementations; brotli is slower to stabilize. The FFI-bridge pattern (emit bridge template, don't add to jet Cargo.toml) is the I6-safe path for any Rust dep that needs owner sign-off. gzip and zstd are needed now (HTTP, network transfer, database wire formats); brotli is mostly web-server-side.
decisions.story: I'm writing a log aggregator that reads `.log.gz` files and writes compressed output to an S3-compatible endpoint. I need gzip decompress on read and zstd compress on write — I don't need to build a zip file.

options.name: gzip + zstd in std now; brotli later
options.detail: Ship gzip and zstd as `jet.compress.*` in std via FFI-bridge. brotli is deferred to a follow-on card. These two cover the dominant use cases (HTTP, database, log files). Each requires an I6 sign-off per dep.

options.name: All codecs as packages — nothing in core std
options.detail: gzip, zstd, brotli all ship as first-party packages users opt into. Keeps std minimal. Adds friction for common tasks that most applications need.

options.name: Archive-only — defer standalone codec API
options.detail: Ship only what `jet.archive` needs internally. No standalone `compress`/`decompress` API. Users who need codec-only access are blocked until a future card.

comparisons.note: `gzip`, `zlib`, `bz2`, `lzma` are in stdlib. `zstd` is third-party. Normalization of common codecs in std is the Python/Go model.
comparisons.code:
import gzip
with gzip.open('file.gz', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()

comparisons.note: `compress/gzip`, `compress/zlib`, `compress/flate` in std. zstd is a third-party package. gzip being in std is the clear expectation.
comparisons.code:
import "compress/gzip"
r, _ := gzip.NewReader(f)
io.Copy(os.Stdout, r)

decisions.title: Should Jet add a numeric type that carries and propagates error bounds (measurement ± uncertainty)?
decisions.gist: No existing Jet type tracks measurement uncertainty. Scientists and engineers who work with physical measurements need values like `9.8 ± 0.1` that propagate uncertainty through arithmetic. This is a new library type decision — no language change is proposed.
decisions.explainer: The tracked-uncertainty card (if it exists) and this card overlap: both concern numeric values carrying metadata. This card's scope is a pure library `Measurement<T>` type with `±` propagation — no compiler support needed, no language change. The main design question is whether it belongs in core std or a package. It's a niche use case (scientific computing, metrology) compared to general-purpose numeric needs. Interaction with decimal-money and `#Unit(usd)` markers: `Measurement<T>` would pair naturally with unit tracking but is independent of it. Interaction with BigInt: orthogonal.
decisions.story: I'm writing a physics simulation. I have a measured length `9.81 ± 0.02` m/s² and I want to multiply it by a time `2.5 ± 0.1` s and get back a value with the correct propagated uncertainty, without implementing error propagation by hand.

options.name: Package-level `Measurement<T>` — not in core std
options.detail: Ship as `jet.science.measurement` or similar first-party package. No language change. Users opt in. Scientific niche doesn't warrant core std footprint. This is the cleanest fit given I8 (one numeric type per job).

options.name: Core std numeric type with ± propagation
options.detail: Add `Measurement<T>` to core std. Every Jet program can use it without a dep. Overhead: adds a type that most programs never need; risk of I8 conflict with a future units/tracking story.

options.name: Defer — wait for tracked-uncertainty card alignment
options.detail: If a tracked-uncertainty card is already planned, align the two designs before shipping. Avoids two overlapping numerical metadata mechanisms (I8).
options.code: // nothing ships yet; defer to tracked-uncertainty card

comparisons.note: `uncertainties` is a third-party library. `ufloat` wraps a float with uncertainty; arithmetic auto-propagates. The direct model for option A.
comparisons.code:
from uncertainties import ufloat
x = ufloat(9.81, 0.02)
y = ufloat(2.5, 0.1)
print(x * y)  # 24.5 +/- 1.01

comparisons.note: `Measurements.jl` package. Operator overloading propagates uncertainty. Package-level, not in Base.
comparisons.code:
using Measurements
x = 9.81 ± 0.02
y = 2.5 ± 0.1
println(x * y)  # 24.525 ± 1.013

decisions.title: Add an opt-in GC library (`Gc<T>`) for cyclic heap data?
decisions.gist: Jet's default ownership model has no way to safely represent cyclic graphs (e.g. doubly-linked lists, graph nodes with back-edges) without unsafe or arena tricks. An opt-in library-level garbage collector — a `Gc<T>` handle — would let expert users manage cyclic data on a separate traced heap without touching the default model. This is New; no decision exists.
decisions.explainer: The core language stays ownership-based; users who import the gc library get a `Gc<T>` smart pointer whose backing allocation is traced and collected by a stop-the-world or incremental collector running on a side thread. All Jet code outside `@unsafe` remains sound: `Gc<T>` is a library type, not a language primitive. Blast radius: small — it's an opt-in import and does not touch sema, codegen rules, or the default allocation path. Prerequisite: the I6 exemption for the backing Rust GC crate requires owner approval (separate ballot). Interacts with I1 (must stay safe by default), arenas (c26), and single-use values (Gc<T> cannot be single-use).
decisions.story: I'm writing a compiler in Jet. My AST has parent-back-pointers. Ownership won't form a tree, and raw arenas need manual lifetimes. I want a `Gc<T>` I can opt into — cyclic, traced, safe — without giving up ownership everywhere else.

options.name: Opt-in `Gc<T>` library
options.detail: Ship a `gc` stdlib module with a `Gc<T>` traced handle. Ownership stays the default; `Gc<T>` is a deliberate expert import. Requires owner sign-off on the backing Rust crate (I6). The library itself is safe Jet; no language changes.

options.name: No GC — ownership + arenas only
options.detail: Keep the status quo. Users with cyclic data use index arenas (Vec<Node> + usize handles) or refactor to remove cycles. Simpler language surface; no I6 crate needed.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't decide now. Return when there's a concrete use-case (e.g. a real Jet program that can't be written cleanly with arenas). Keeps the option open without committing to an I6 dep.
options.code: // no change yet

comparisons.note: ARC is the default; cycles require `weak`/`unowned` annotations and the programmer must reason about them. No separate traced GC.
comparisons.code: class Node { weak var next: Node? }

comparisons.note: Community `gc` crate adds `Gc<T>` as a library; not in std. Same pattern Jet would follow.
comparisons.code:
use gc::{Gc, GcCell};
let a = Gc::new(GcCell::new(Node { next: None }));

decisions.title: Design the crypto envelope for algorithm agility now so PQ primitives can slot in later?
decisions.gist: The planned misuse-resistant crypto envelope (not yet shipped) will pick concrete algorithms. If we hard-code classical X25519 now, adding ML-KEM later means a breaking API change. The question is whether to design the envelope's internal seam for algorithm agility from the start, so hybrid X25519+ML-KEM can be wired in without user-visible changes when the primitives are ready. This is New/far-horizon and sequences after the crypto envelope card.
decisions.explainer: Algorithm agility means the envelope type carries an opaque algorithm identifier; the user picks a security tier (`#Classic`, `#Hybrid`, `#PostQuantum`) not a raw algorithm name — the implementation swaps the primitive behind the tag. This blocks on the crypto envelope card being decided first; don't implement either until that card lands. Blast radius: internal to the crypto stdlib module — no user-facing syntax change beyond the tier tags. Interacts with I6 (ML-KEM needs a vetted crate or native implementation, both require owner approval). NIST finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in 2024; X25519+ML-KEM-768 is the IETF hybrid draft.
decisions.story: I'm deploying a long-lived service today. I want to know that when post-quantum key exchange is ready, I change one tag and recompile — not rewrite my protocol layer.

options.name: Agility seam now, PQ algorithms later
options.detail: Design the envelope API with an opaque algorithm tier (`#Classic`, `#Hybrid`, `#PostQuantum`) rather than exposing raw algorithm names. Ship classical only; ML-KEM slots in when ready. User call sites never change. Requires sequencing after the crypto envelope card.

options.name: Classical only for v1, revisit later
options.detail: Ship the envelope with X25519 hard-coded. Defer agility design until PQ is actually needed. Risk: API break when PQ lands. Safe for near-term; technical debt for services with long key lifetimes.

options.name: Defer entirely
options.detail: Don't decide until the crypto envelope card is resolved. Keeps this off the plate; revisit as part of that card's follow-up.
options.code: // no crypto envelope yet; defer both

comparisons.note: Go 1.23 added X25519Kyber768Draft00 as a configurable curve ID; callers opt in by name, which is not agility — it's an extra parameter.
comparisons.code: cfg := &tls.Config{CurvePreferences: []tls.CurveID{tls.X25519Kyber768Draft00}}

comparisons.note: Separate crates for classical and PQ; no unified agility envelope in std. Applications compose manually.
comparisons.code:
use aws_lc_rs::agreement::{agree_ephemeral, X25519};
// ML-KEM is a separate crate, combined by hand

decisions.title: Add grouped and aliased selective imports (`use math.{a, b as c}`)?
decisions.gist: Today Jet users qualify names with the module path (`math.sin`) or use `use math` to bring the module itself into scope. There's no way to pull specific items out of a module without qualifying them, or to rename an import at the call site. This card adds `use math.{sin, cos}` (bring items into scope) and `use math.{sin as s}` (alias). New; no decision exists.
decisions.explainer: Selective imports do not conflict with the module-qualified path style — they are additive syntax. They complement D-MOD2/D-MOD3 without reopening glob imports (which D-MOD2 rejected with E0612 and a separate card covers). Single-item form `use math.sin` is a degenerate case of the grouped form; implementing grouped subsumes it. Aliasing covers the name-collision case. I8 check: this is one mechanism (selective bring-into-scope + optional rename), not two — the status-quo qualified path is a different job (no import needed), so no I8 conflict.
decisions.story: I use `math.sin` and `math.cos` in fifty places. I want `use math.{sin, cos}` at the top so the call sites read cleanly. And if two modules both export `encode`, I want `use http.{encode as http_encode}` to disambiguate.

options.name: Full grouped + aliased selective imports
options.detail: Allow `use mod.{a, b as c}` and `use mod.item`. Both grouping and aliasing land together; single-item is the degenerate case. Qualified paths still work; this is additive. Recommended — covers the full need in one mechanism.

options.name: Single-item only, no grouping or alias
options.detail: Allow `use mod.item` but not `use mod.{a, b}` or `use mod.{a as b}`. Simpler to parse; weaker — multiple imports need multiple `use` lines; no alias support.

options.name: Status quo — module-qualified paths only
options.detail: No `use` form for individual items. Users qualify every call or bring the module into scope with `use stats`. Small surface; more verbose at call sites.

comparisons.note: Grouped `use` with aliases is idiomatic Rust; very familiar to systems programmers.
comparisons.code: use std::collections::{HashMap, BTreeMap as OrdMap};

comparisons.note: `from mod import name as alias` is the standard form; grouping via parentheses.
comparisons.code: from math import sin, cos as cosine

decisions.title: Reopen wildcard imports (`use module.*`) rejected by D-MOD2?
decisions.gist: D-MOD2 rejected glob imports and wired E0612 to reject them with a clear error. The Ideas list proposes reopening `use module.*`. This is a Reopen decision: the prior rejection stands unless there is a compelling new argument.
decisions.explainer: E0612 was added deliberately: glob imports pollute the local namespace, make it impossible to know where a name came from without tooling, and break I8 (you can't tell which mechanism introduced a name). The new selective-imports card (D-SELIMPORT1) covers the actual need — bringing many names in without qualifying — without the namespace-opacity problem, by requiring the user to list the names. No new argument changes the D-MOD2 calculus. Reopening would require undoing E0612, which has a UI snapshot, and would conflict with I8.
decisions.story: I want `use math.*` so I can call `sin` without prefixing. (But: selective imports already give me `use math.{sin, cos}` with explicit names — is the glob form adding real value?)

options.name: Keep the rejection (status quo)
options.detail: E0612 stays. Selective imports (D-SELIMPORT1) cover the real need. No change. Recommended — the prior decision was well-reasoned; no new argument overturns it.

options.name: Allow glob with shadow warnings
options.detail: Lift E0612; emit a warning when a glob import shadows a local or another import. Weaker discipline than the current rejection; namespace opacity returns.
options.code:
use math.*          // warning: glob import — consider listing items
use geo.*           // warning: 'sin' shadowed by geo.sin
fn f() { sin(1.0) } // which sin?

options.name: Allow only for designated prelude modules
options.detail: A module can declare itself `prelude` and users can glob-import it. Niche mechanism; adds a concept (prelude designation) for marginal gain. Still violates I8 (two ways to introduce names).

comparisons.note: Glob imports are allowed but strongly discouraged in idiomatic Rust; clippy warns on them in most contexts.
comparisons.code: use std::collections::*; // works; not recommended

comparisons.note: `from mod import *` is allowed but considered an anti-pattern; it populates the namespace invisibly and breaks static analysis.
comparisons.code: from math import *  # works; linters flag it

decisions.title: Add a package-scoped visibility tier (`pub(package)`) between private and `pub`?
decisions.gist: Jet currently has two visibility levels: private (default) and `pub`. In multi-package payloads, there's no way to expose something to sibling packages without making it fully public to all downstream consumers. `pub(package)` (or an equivalent spelling) fills that gap. New/Reopen — S18/D-MOD3 did not define this tier.
decisions.explainer: Multi-package payloads (owner-ratified) create the need: an internal helper shared across packages in the same payload shouldn't appear in the public API. Without this tier, authors either duplicate code or over-expose it. Blast radius: visibility rules in sema, pack.jet scope resolution, and the `pub` syntax surface. The spelling `pub(package)` mirrors Rust's `pub(crate)`; alternatives like `pub.package` or a distinct keyword (`internal`) are on the table. This sequences after D-MOD3 and the payload multi-package work. I8: this is a new semantic tier, not a second way to do an existing job — no conflict.
decisions.story: My payload has three packages: `core`, `utils`, and `cli`. `utils` has helpers that `core` and `cli` need, but I don't want them in the published API. I need one more visibility notch.

options.name: `pub(package)` spelling
options.detail: Add `pub(package)` as the package-scoped tier. Matches Rust `pub(crate)` semantics; familiar to systems programmers. Spelling is consistent with the existing `pub` keyword.

options.name: Keep private + `pub` only
options.detail: Don't add a third tier. Authors who need cross-package internals make them `pub` and rely on documentation to signal "internal". Works for small payloads; breaks down at scale.

options.name: `internal` keyword spelling
options.detail: A distinct `internal` keyword instead of `pub(package)`. Slightly more readable for beginners; one fewer parenthesized qualifier. Adds a new keyword to the surface.
options.code: internal fn hash_intern(s: str) -> u64 { … }

comparisons.note: `pub(crate)` is the idiomatic crate-scoped tier; `pub(super)` scopes to the parent module. Both are well-understood.
comparisons.code: pub(crate) fn internal_helper() {}

comparisons.note: `internal` is a keyword meaning visible within the same Gradle module — analogous to `pub(package)`.
comparisons.code: internal fun hashIntern(s: String): Long = …

decisions.title: Add a distinct `namespace { }` spelling for in-file grouping, or keep `module name { }` only?
decisions.gist: Jet already supports `module name { }` for inline in-file grouping without a separate file. The Ideas list proposes a distinct `namespace { }` keyword as an alternative or replacement spelling. This would be a second syntax for the same semantic job — a direct I8 conflict. Reopen/New.
decisions.explainer: Inline `module name { }` groups items into a named scope within a file, which is exactly what a namespace block does. Adding `namespace { }` either means two keywords for identical semantics (I8 violation) or a subtle semantic distinction that must be invented and justified. If the motivation is that `module` implies a file boundary to readers, that's a documentation problem, not a language problem. Renaming `module` in-file to `namespace` (Option C) would be a breaking change to any existing code using inline modules. No new expressiveness is gained by a second spelling.
decisions.story: I have a big single file and want to organize it into groups — `math helpers`, `string helpers` — without splitting files. I write `module strings { }` today. Is that clear enough?

options.name: Keep `module name { }` only (status quo)
options.detail: No `namespace` keyword. One spelling for in-file grouping; I8 preserved. If the word 'module' is confusing, improve documentation or diagnostics. Recommended.

options.name: Add `namespace { }` as a second spelling
options.detail: Both `module name { }` and `namespace name { }` work. Breaks I8: two ways to mean the same thing. Adds surface complexity; no semantic gain.

options.name: Rename in-file modules to `namespace`
options.detail: Reserve `module` for file-backed modules only; use `namespace` for inline blocks. Breaks existing code; adds cognitive overhead distinguishing the two. Only worth it if the semantic distinction is load-bearing.

comparisons.note: `namespace` is the only grouping primitive; there's no module/namespace distinction in classic C++. C++20 modules are a separate mechanism, still coexisting with namespaces.
comparisons.code:
namespace math { double sin(double x); }
math::sin(1.0);

comparisons.note: Swift has no namespace keyword; grouping is done with `enum` (as a namespace) or plain `struct`. One mechanism for grouping is a consistent pattern.
comparisons.code: enum Math { static func sin(_ x: Double) -> Double { … } }

decisions.title: Reopen transparent type aliases (`alias X = Y`) — declined by D-SUGAR3?
decisions.gist: S14 rejected `def` aliases and D-SUGAR3 declined transparent type aliases (a name that IS another type, fully interchangeable). The Ideas list asks to reopen. A transparent alias adds no new type-safety — `alias Meters = f64` means `Meters` and `f64` are the same type everywhere, unlike a newtype which is distinct. The reopen needs a concrete pain case that newtypes can't cover.
decisions.explainer: Newtypes (`struct Meters(f64)`) give you a distinct type with zero runtime cost, which is strictly more informative than a transparent alias. Transparent aliases are useful mainly for shortening long generic type spellings (e.g. `alias Result<T> = T ? IoError`). That's a real but narrow need. If reopened, `alias` is the preferred keyword over `def` (S14 rejected `def`). I8 check: a transparent alias for shortening a concrete generic instantiation is a different job from a newtype (distinct type); no I8 conflict for that case. But an alias for a primitive (`alias Meters = f64`) duplicates the newtype job without the safety — that case should stay declined.
decisions.story: I have `T ? ParseError ? IoError ? NetworkError` all over my code. I want `alias AppResult<T> = T ? AppError` at the top. That's not a newtype — it's a spelling shortcut for a complex type expression.

options.name: Keep declined (status quo)
options.detail: No transparent aliases. Newtypes cover the type-safety use case. Verbose generic spellings are a minor pain. D-SUGAR3 reasoning stands.
options.code:
// no alias; users repeat the full type:
fn parse(s: str) -> Token ? ParseError { … }

options.name: Add `alias X = Y` for generic type shortcuts only
options.detail: Allow `alias` only for parameterized type expressions (e.g. `alias Result<T> = T ? E`). Reject bare primitive aliases (`alias Meters = f64` → use a newtype). Narrow, concrete, no I8 conflict for the generic case.

options.name: Add `alias X = Y` fully transparent
options.detail: Allow any type alias, including primitive aliases. Simple rule; but `alias Meters = f64` gives no safety over bare `f64` and creates a second way to introduce a type name, weakening the newtype story.
options.code:
alias Meters = f64  // Meters and f64 are identical — no safety gained
alias AppResult<T> = T ? AppError

comparisons.note: `type Alias = T` is fully transparent — no distinct type is created. Newtypes are `struct Foo(T)`. Both exist, but newtypes are the idiomatic safety tool.
comparisons.code:
type Meters = f64;         // transparent — no distinction
struct MetersNew(f64);     // newtype — distinct type

comparisons.note: `type` is transparent alias; `newtype` is zero-cost distinct. Haskell programmers reach for `newtype` whenever safety matters.
comparisons.code:
type Meters = Double       -- transparent
newtype MetersN = MetersN Double  -- distinct

decisions.title: Add maturity markers (`#Experimental` / `#Tested` / `#Hardened`) that propagate like effects?
decisions.gist: A maturity lattice lets library authors tag APIs with their stability level, and the compiler warns (or errors) when stable code calls experimental code without an explicit acknowledgment. New; no decision exists. The machinery would ride existing marker and effect-ceiling infrastructure.
decisions.explainer: Propagation rule: calling an `#Experimental` item taints the caller unless the caller also carries `#Experimental` or explicitly acknowledges with a suppressor (e.g. `#[allow(Experimental)]`). The lattice is `#Experimental < #Tested < #Hardened`; unmarked items default to some level (TBD — a separate question). Blast radius: sema (propagation pass), effect ceilings, doc output. Prerequisite: effect ceiling machinery needs to exist or be extended. This interacts with the effect-ceilings card. If the marker propagation model isn't yet shipped, a doc-only convention (Option B) costs nothing and covers 80% of the use-case until the machinery is ready. I1: no safety impact — this is purely about API stability signaling. I8: maturity signaling is a new job; no existing mechanism covers it.
decisions.story: I publish a library. `parse_v2` is solid; `parse_experimental` is still in flux. I tag it `#Experimental` and anyone who calls it without opting in gets a warning at their call site — not buried in a changelog.

options.name: Full propagating marker family
options.detail: Add `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as propagating markers riding existing effect machinery. Compile-time enforcement; IDE surfaces stability at call sites. Sequences after effect-ceiling machinery.

options.name: Doc-only convention now, propagation later
options.detail: Define `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as documentation-visible markers today (no compiler propagation). When effect-ceiling machinery ships, wire propagation. Low cost; covers the doc/tooling case immediately.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't decide until effect-ceiling machinery is finalized. Avoids designing the propagation model twice.
options.code: // no change; stability is communicated via doc comments only

comparisons.note: `#[unstable]` is a compiler-enforced gate in the standard library (nightly only); third-party crates use `#[deprecated]` or doc comments. No lattice propagation.
comparisons.code:
#[unstable(feature = "new_parser", issue = "12345")]
pub fn new_parser(s: &str) -> Ast {}

comparisons.note: `@RequiresOptIn` / `@OptIn` is a propagating annotation lattice — callers must opt in or the compiler warns. Very close to what Option A proposes.

decisions.title: Add named swizzle access on vector types (`.xyz`, `.wzyx`, `.xy`) — and if so, allow lvalue swizzles too?
decisions.gist: SIMD/linalg vector types exist and are ratified. Named swizzle access (`.xyz`, `.yx`, `.wzyx`) — reading or writing up to 4 lanes by name — is not yet ratified. This decides whether swizzles ship as first-class syntax or as methods, and whether write-swizzles (lvalues) are in scope.
decisions.explainer: Swizzle syntax is a subset of member access: `v.xy` would return a 2-element vector drawn from lanes x and y of `v`. It amends D-SIMD1/2. The bundle risk is separating vector-type support (done) from swizzle syntax (this card). Write-swizzles (`v.xy = .{1.0, 2.0}`) raise a second design point. Under I8, swizzle-as-method (`v.swizzle(X, Y)`) would be the only alternative that avoids new syntax — it is less ergonomic and is not how any shader/linalg library spells it. No existing ratified syntax conflicts here.
decisions.story: I'm writing a game renderer. I have a `vec4` color and I want the RGB channels as a `vec3` for a lighting calc. `col.rgb` should just work — the same as GLSL, Metal, or Zig's @shuffle. Typing `.swizzle(R, G, B)` every time is friction I don't need.
decisions.inWild:
let col: Vec4 = .{1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 1.0}
let rgb: Vec3 = col.xyz          // read swizzle
let rev: Vec4 = col.wzyx         // reverse channels
col.xy = .{0.0, 0.0}             // write swizzle (lvalue)

options.name: Blessed member swizzle (read + write)
options.detail: Generate `x/y/z/w` lane names and all N-choose-k swizzle combos as compile-time-resolved member accesses on vector lane types. Write-swizzles are lvalues. This matches shader-language and game-engine convention and needs no method call.

options.name: Blessed member swizzle (read-only)
options.detail: Same as A but write-swizzles are deferred — too complex to lower cleanly for overlapping lanes (e.g. `v.xx = ...`). Read swizzles cover 90% of the use case today.

options.name: Explicit method only
options.detail: Keep the surface minimal; expose `.x()`, `.y()` single-lane getters and a `swizzle(a, b, c, d)` method taking enum lane values. No new syntax. Verbose but I8-clean if swizzle syntax is genuinely new syntax over existing member access.
options.code:
let v: Vec3 = .{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}
let v2 = v.swizzle(Y, X)        // Vec2.{2.0, 1.0}

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Block swizzles until the semantic index and SIMD lowering paths are more stable. Ship single-lane `.x .y .z .w` getters only for now.
options.code:
let v: Vec3 = .{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}
let x = v.x                     // scalar, works today

comparisons.note: GLSL has read and write swizzles on all vector types; the four sets (xyzw, rgba, stpq) select the same lanes, aliased by convention.
Zig uses `@shuffle` as a builtin — functional but verbose; no dot-swizzle shorthand.
comparisons.code: const rgb = @shuffle(f32, col, undefined, [3]i32{0,1,2});

comparisons.note: glam generates named swizzle methods via proc-macro — `.xy()`, `.zyx()` etc. Explicit methods, not member access; write-swizzles absent.
comparisons.code:
let rgb: Vec3 = col.xyz();
let rev: Vec4 = col.wzyx();

decisions.title: Ratify a normalization contract for the content-addressed build cache?
decisions.gist: The build cache (BuildCache.rs / SHA256.rs) is partially implemented but its normalization contract — what counts as 'the same definition' for cache-key purposes — is not specified or tested. This decides whether we lock down a concrete contract now or leave it ad hoc.
decisions.explainer: Without a stated contract, two definitions that are semantically identical (whitespace change, renamed local, reordered doc comment) may or may not produce cache hits depending on implementation drift. A contract at the AST level (after parsing, before sema) is rename-sensitive by default but immune to whitespace and comment changes. Ratifying this establishes a correctness floor for all incremental build work and is a prerequisite for any cross-machine or reproducible-build guarantee. It touches BuildCache.rs, SHA256.rs, and the parser, and pairs with the content-addressed-definitions card.
decisions.story: I rename a local variable inside a function body. Nothing semantic changed. I don't want a cache miss — or worse, a stale hit — because the cache doesn't know whether that rename matters. I need to trust the cache.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, rename-sensitive
options.detail: Hash the canonical AST (post-parse, pre-sema): strip whitespace and comments, keep all names as-is. Two definitions with different local names get different keys. Simple to implement, easy to test, conservative (avoids false hits). Document the contract and add a normalization test.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, alpha-rename-invariant
options.detail: Before hashing, alpha-rename all locals to positional names (`_0`, `_1`, …). Two definitions differing only in local names produce the same key. More cache hits but more complex to implement and requires a stable renaming pass before sema.

options.name: Leave ad hoc in BuildCache.rs
options.detail: No ratified contract. The cache continues to work however BuildCache.rs happens to implement it. Risk: silent correctness bugs as implementation drifts; no test surface for the contract.
options.code:
// no contract — cache hits are implementation-defined
// renaming a local may or may not bust the cache

comparisons.note: Nix derives cache keys from a normalized derivation ATerm (no whitespace variation); it is rename-sensitive at the attribute level. A clear, auditable contract is what makes Nix's reproducibility claims trustworthy.
comparisons.code:
# derivation hash = SHA256(normalised-ATerm-of-derivation)
# whitespace irrelevant; attribute names are part of the key

comparisons.note: Rust's incremental hashes the HIR with stable IDs; local renames do not bust the hash because HIR is already resolved. Jet can choose either policy but must choose one.
comparisons.code:
// rustc stable-hashes HIR bodies; local var names are irrelevant
// to the incremental fingerprint

decisions.title: Build a jetdoc generator from the compiler semantic graph?
decisions.gist: Jet has doc comments and doctests but no tool that generates browsable API docs from the compiler's semantic graph. This decides whether jetdoc ships as an E3 deliverable built on the compiler seams, and whether doc-comment examples double as doctests.
decisions.explainer: A semantic-graph doc generator reads the sema index (types, signatures, trait impls, doc comments) and emits HTML/Markdown API docs with tested examples. It is an E3 testing/docs ergonomics exit criterion. It depends on stable compiler seams (the `jet-sema` seam crate and the semantic index API card).
