Doctests close the loop: example code in `/// ` blocks is extracted and run as tests. Without this, doc quality decays because examples are untested. This card does not cover the LSP or IDE dossier views (those are D-DOSSIER1).
decisions.story: I publish a Jet library. I want `jet doc` to generate browsable API docs from my doc comments the same way `cargo doc` does — and I want any `/// ` example to fail CI if it stops compiling, not just silently rot.

options.name: Build jetdoc on semantic index (E3 deliverable)
options.detail: Wire a `jet doc` subcommand to the stable sema index. Emit HTML (or Markdown) docs per module/type/fn. Extract `/// ` code blocks as doctests compiled via `jet test --doctests`. Gate on the semantic-index API card being stable first.
options.code:
$ jet doc
Building docs for mylib v0.1.0
Wrote: docs/api/index.html
$ jet test --doctests
running 3 doctests
test mylib::add ... ok
test mylib::mul ... ok

options.name: Hand-written docs only (status quo)
options.detail: No generated docs tool. Authors maintain hand-written Markdown. Examples rot unless CI runs them separately. Keeps the toolchain surface smaller but fails the E3 ergonomics criterion.
options.code:
// no jet doc subcommand; docs are maintained manually
// broken examples only caught if author adds a test by hand

options.name: Defer until semantic-index API is stable
options.detail: Explicitly defer jetdoc — don't ship in E3. Block it on semantic-index API ratification. This avoids building jetdoc twice if the index API changes, but delays the docs ergonomics exit criterion.
options.code:
// placeholder: jet doc --help
// Error: jetdoc not available until semantic index is stable (E4)

comparisons.note: rustdoc reads HIR/MIR and emits structured HTML. Doc tests (```` ``` ```` blocks in `///` comments) are compiled and run by `cargo test --doc`. This is the gold-standard baseline for jetdoc to match.
DocC compiles doc comments into a structured catalog; examples are verified at build time. Goes further than rustdoc with tutorials and interactive playgrounds.

decisions.title: Build a dossier / outline view that stitches scattered type members across files?
decisions.gist: Jet allows methods and impls of a type to live in multiple files. Today there is no editor view that collects all of a type's members into one outline. This decides whether to build that view, and whether to gate it on a stable semantic index API.
decisions.explainer: A dossier view would use the LSP and semantic index to show every method, field, and impl of a type in a single outline panel, regardless of which files they live in. It supports the Blueprint north-star (memory): type-directed authoring where you see the full shape of a type without hunting across files. It depends on the stable semantic-index API card — building it before that API is locked risks throwing the work away. It is purely tooling (no language surface changes) and does not block any compiler invariants, but it affects the LSP sub-system. D-BREADCRUMB1 is the companion card for in-editor phantom stubs.
decisions.story: I'm working on a large type that has impls spread across five files — rendering, serialization, physics. I want one panel that shows me everything this type can do, so I can navigate without grep. Like an Unreal Blueprint node, but for my entire type.

options.name: Build dossier as LSP code-lens / outline, gated on semantic index
options.detail: Add a dossier outline command to the LSP server, powered by the semantic index once its API is stable. The editor extension surfaces it as a sidebar panel or `Go to type outline` command. Gate: semantic-index API must be ratified and stable first.

options.name: Defer until semantic index API is stable
options.detail: Explicitly defer — mark the card as blocked on semantic-index API ratification. Then build it as option A describes. Avoids a rebuild if the index API changes significantly, but delays the Blueprint north-star ergonomic win.
options.code:
// no dossier view today
// unblock when D-SEMIDX1 is ratified

options.name: Skip (use grep / LSP workspace symbols)
options.detail: Don't build a dossier view. Authors use the standard LSP workspace-symbols search or text grep to find scattered members. Keeps LSP surface smaller but leaves the Blueprint north-star incomplete.
options.code:
// status quo: Ctrl+T → workspace symbol search
// results: all symbols matching query across all files

comparisons.note: The 'Structure' panel shows all members of the current class. It does not stitch across files (separate impls show separately). Jet's dossier would go further.
comparisons.code:
// Structure panel: shows fields + methods of current file's class
// multi-file impls are NOT stitched — you see one file at a time

comparisons.note: Blueprint shows every event, function, and variable on a class as typed pins in one graph. The dossier is the textual analog: one place to see the full type contract.
comparisons.code:
// Blueprint node: all inputs/outputs visible at once
// no hunting across multiple graph views for the same actor

decisions.title: Show phantom breadcrumb hints for methods defined away from the type body?
decisions.gist: When a type has methods defined in other files, the type's own source file shows nothing about them. Breadcrumb hints would inject phantom (non-editable) stubs near the type body in the editor, listing methods defined elsewhere. This is a companion to the dossier view.
decisions.explainer: Breadcrumb hints are LSP inlay hints or code-lens annotations injected at the type declaration site, listing methods defined in other files with clickable jump-to-definition links. They add no language semantics — purely a tooling overlay. They depend on the same stable semantic index API as D-DOSSIER1. Building both on the same index pass is efficient; building either before the index API is locked risks rework. Under I8, this does not add a new language mechanism — it is an editor affordance only.
decisions.story: I'm reading `model.jet` and I see `struct Player`. I know there are rendering and physics methods somewhere, but the struct body is silent. I want ghost text just below the struct telling me '+ 4 methods in render.jet, physics.jet' with jump links — so I don't have to grep.

options.name: LSP inlay / code-lens phantom stubs, gated on semantic index
options.detail: Emit LSP inlay hints or code-lens items at the type declaration listing away-methods. Clickable → jump to definition. Gate: same semantic-index API stability requirement as D-DOSSIER1. Build both on the same pass.

options.name: Defer (same gate as dossier view)
options.detail: Defer explicitly — blocked on semantic-index API ratification. Once that unblocks D-DOSSIER1, breadcrumb hints can ship in the same pass. Avoids piecemeal work and rework risk.
options.code:
// no phantom stubs today
// unblock with D-DOSSIER1 when semantic index is stable

options.name: Skip
options.detail: Don't add phantom stubs. The dossier view (D-DOSSIER1) already gives a type outline on demand; inline hints are redundant if the panel exists. Keeps LSP surface smaller.
options.code:
// status quo: type body shows only its own members
// use dossier panel or workspace search for away-methods

comparisons.note: C# Dev Kit shows 'X references' code-lens above methods and types. It does not show away-methods at the declaration site — closer to a reference count than a stub listing.
comparisons.code:
// 5 references  ← code-lens above the class
class Player { ... }

comparisons.note: Rust-analyzer emits inlay hints (parameter names, return types) but no phantom stubs for trait impls defined elsewhere. Jet breadcrumbs would go further for the multi-file impl case.
comparisons.code:
// inlay hints: parameter names and types inline
// no phantom stubs for impl blocks in other files

decisions.title: Add a first-class `workspace.jet` workspace manifest for multi-package repos, or reuse `pack.jet payload:`?
decisions.gist: Multi-package repos need a way to declare a set of member packages. `pack.jet payload:` already handles multi-package core sources. This decides whether to introduce a separate `workspace.jet` root manifest or rely on the existing `payload:` mechanism.
decisions.explainer: The `payload:` field in `pack.jet` lets a single package declare multiple member packages (memory: payload-multi-package-core-source). A `workspace.jet` would be a new top-level file with no associated package, purely grouping independent packages for a shared build/tooling context (shared lock file, cross-member `pub(package)` visibility, unified `jet build`). The key question is whether `payload:` semantics already cover the monorepo case or whether they differ enough to justify a new file type. Under I8, two files solving the same grouping job is a strike unless they cover genuinely different semantic territory. This was a live owner decision in Tower c156.
decisions.story: I have a repo with four separate Jet packages — a compiler, a CLI, a stdlib, and a test runner. I want `jet build` at the repo root to build all of them, with a single lock file and cross-package visibility. I don't want one of them to be the 'master' package that owns the others.
decisions.inWild:
# workspace.jet (proposed)
[workspace]
members = [
    "crates/compiler",
    "crates/cli",
    "crates/stdlib",
    "crates/test-runner",
]

# vs. pack.jet payload: (existing)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

options.name: Add `workspace.jet` (separate workspace manifest)
options.detail: A new top-level `workspace.jet` file with no owning package — purely a grouping manifest. Members are independent packages each with their own `pack.jet`. Supports a shared lock file, `pub(package)`, and unified `jet` commands. Clearest model for repos where no single package is 'the root'.
options.code:
# workspace.jet
[workspace]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all members
$ jet test --all      # tests all members

options.name: Reuse `pack.jet payload:` (no new file)
options.detail: The root `pack.jet` with a `payload:` section already declares member packages. Extend its semantics: if `payload:` is present with no `[package]` section, it acts as a pure workspace root. No new file type; I8-clean if `payload:` already covers this exactly.
options.code:
# pack.jet (workspace root, no [package] section)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all payload members

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't ratify a workspace surface yet. Multi-package builds work today by running `jet build` in each package directory. Defer until the lock-file and `pub(package)` designs are settled, so the workspace contract is informed by what it actually needs to coordinate.
options.code:
# no workspace manifest; run per-package:
$ jet build -C crates/compiler
$ jet build -C crates/cli

comparisons.note: Cargo uses a root `Cargo.toml` with `[workspace]` members list. The root may or may not also declare a `[package]`. Members share a `Cargo.lock` and `target/`.
comparisons.code:
[workspace]
members = ["crates/*"]
resolver = "2"

comparisons.note: npm uses a root `package.json` with a `workspaces` array. The root is itself a package. Closer to Jet's `pack.jet payload:` model than to a separate file.
comparisons.code:
// package.json
{ "workspaces": ["packages/*"] }

decisions.title: Add generic modules (ML-functor-style module parameterized by a type or value)?
decisions.gist: Jet has generic types and functions. Generic modules — a module parameterized by a type or value at the module level, instantiated to produce a new module — do not exist. This decides whether to add them or keep the surface at generic types and functions only.
decisions.explainer: ML-style functors let you write `module Map(K: Ord)` and instantiate it as `module IntMap = Map(Int)`. The result is a new module with all members specialized to `K = Int`. In Jet, generic types already handle the common case (`Map[K: Ord, V]`); generic modules go further by allowing module-level abstraction (sharing multiple related types, hiding implementation modules, enforcing interface contracts at the module boundary). Under I8, if generic types already cover the use case, a second mechanism is a strike. The complexity is high: module instantiation affects name resolution, the module graph, and comptime. There is no ratified syntax precedent in Jet for module-level generics.
decisions.story: I'm building a pluggable hash-map where the key comparison strategy is a module (not just a function). I want `module HashMap(K: KeyModule)` where `KeyModule` supplies `hash`, `eq`, and an associated `Error` type — none of which are cleanly expressible as a single generic type parameter.

options.name: Add generic modules (ML-functor style)
options.detail: Ratify module-level parameterization. A module can declare type/value parameters; instantiation produces a new named module. Requires new syntax, new name-resolution rules, and comptime integration. Only justified if a concrete use case cannot be served by generic types alone.

options.name: Keep generic types and functions only (status quo)
options.detail: The existing `Type[T: Trait]` and `fn foo[T: Trait]()` cover the overwhelming majority of parameterization needs. Module-level generics add complexity for a narrow use case. Reject until a concrete case proves generic types are insufficient. I8-clean.

options.name: Defer pending concrete use case
options.detail: Don't reject outright — park the card until a real Jet codebase hits the wall with generic types and functions and needs functor-level abstraction. Then revisit with a concrete motivating example.
options.code:
// deferred: no syntax or implementation
// reopen when a concrete stdlib or user case requires it

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are the canonical ML-functor. `module Map.Make(Ord)` produces a map module specialized to `Ord.t`. Widely used but notoriously hard to read for newcomers.
comparisons.code:
module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)
let m = IntMap.add 1 "one" IntMap.empty

comparisons.note: Rust has no module generics — generic types and traits cover the use case. This is the status-quo model Jet already follows; it has proven sufficient for a production systems language.
comparisons.code:
// No generic modules; use generic structs + traits:
struct HashMap<K: Hash + Eq, V> { ... }

decisions.title: Add variadic function parameters and spread syntax (`...xs` call spread, `[...a, ...b]` list spread)?
decisions.gist: Jet has no variadic function parameters and no spread syntax. D-FP6 deferred list spread. This decides whether to add all three (variadic params, call spread, list spread) under a single sigil, and which sigil to use — aware that fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` (S75) is already ratified.
decisions.explainer: Three related but separable features: (1) variadic params (`fn log(msgs: ...String)`), (2) call spread (`log(...msgs)`), and (3) list spread (`[...a, ...b]`). They share a surface sigil. The tension: fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` (S75) already provides one form of multi-argument application, and list spread overlaps conceptually with concatenation. Under I8, spreading must not duplicate what fan-out already does. The spread sigil (`...`) is the JavaScript/TypeScript convention; Jet has no precedent for it. A new sigil needs owner ratification. Variadics also affect codegen (Rust does not have variadics; lowering requires a slice or tuple approach).
decisions.story: I'm writing a logging function that takes any number of strings. I want `log("user:", name, "age:", age)` without building an array first. And when I have a list `parts` already, I want `log(...parts)` to expand it at the call site — not write a different function.

options.name: Add all three under `...` sigil
options.detail: Ratify `...` as the spread/rest sigil. Variadic params use `name: ...T` (rest position, last param only). Call spread uses `f(...xs)`. List spread uses `[...a, ...b]`. Lowers variadic params to a slice `[T]` in codegen. Must verify no overlap with fan-out S75.
options.code:
fn sum(ns: ...Int) -> Int { ns.fold(0, fn(a,b){a+b}) }
let xs = [1, 2, 3]
sum(...xs)                     // 6
let ys = [...xs, 4, 5]         // [1,2,3,4,5]

options.name: List spread only (re-open D-FP6)
options.detail: Ratify `[...a, ...b]` list spread only. Variadic params and call spread are deferred. Covers the most common non-function use case without touching function signatures or the call protocol.
options.code:
let a = [1, 2]
let b = [3, 4]
let c = [...a, ...b]           // [1,2,3,4]
// variadic fn params: still not available

options.name: Variadic params only (no spread sigil yet)
options.detail: Add variadic params (`name: ...T`) as a language feature; do not ratify a spread sigil. Call sites pass individual args or an explicit slice. Avoids ratifying `...` before deciding its full scope.

options.name: Keep deferred (status quo)
options.detail: Maintain the D-FP6 deferral. Fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` covers multi-application; explicit list construction covers concatenation. Add variadics only when a stdlib function genuinely needs them and there is no I8-clean alternative.

comparisons.note: TypeScript has rest params (`...args: string[]`) and spread in calls and arrays. The `...` sigil is overloaded across all three contexts; it is the most common model in modern languages.
Python uses `*args` for variadic params and `*seq` for call/list spread. Separate sigils (`*` vs `**`) for positional vs keyword. Functional but two-sigil complexity.
comparisons.code:
def log(*msgs): print(*msgs)
parts = ['a','b']
log(*parts)
all_ = [*parts, 'c']

decisions.title: Define a versioned public semantic-index query API?
decisions.gist: The compiler already builds a rich symbol database internally (Source/LSP/SymbolDB.rs: symbols, types, references, call graph). Right now that data is internal-only — no external tool can query it without forking compiler internals. This decision is whether to promote a stable, versioned subset of that data into a public API that tools (IDE plugins, impact analyzers, dossier, ask-your-codebase) can depend on.
decisions.explainer: A public semantic-index API is listed as an Epoch 4 exit criterion. It is the prerequisite for three other queued ideas — impact-analyzer (D-IMPACT1), codemods (D-CODEMOD1), and ask-your-codebase — all of which need reliable, versioned access to compiler facts. The API would live on top of the seam crates (compiler-workspace-seams: jet-sema, jet-foundation) and be versioned independently of the compiler internals. It does not change language semantics or surface syntax, so I1/I8 are not in play. Sequencing risk: if the internal SymbolDB layout changes significantly before the API is frozen, the versioning story becomes harder; starting the freeze now reduces that drift.
decisions.story: I'm writing a refactor tool. I need to know every call site of a function, the type of each argument, and which tests exercise it — without running the compiler myself. I want to query that from a stable interface that won't break when the compiler's internals change.

options.name: Versioned public API over seam crates
options.detail: Expose a stable, versioned query surface (symbols, types, references, call graph) as a public crate built on jet-sema/jet-foundation. Tools depend on the API version, not compiler internals. This is the E4 exit criterion and unlocks impact analysis, codemods, and dossier.

options.name: Keep internal-only
options.detail: No public API. External tools must parse source themselves or shell out to the LSP. Simpler for the compiler team; blocks all downstream tooling ideas indefinitely.
options.code:
// current state: tools use LSP textDocument/references
// (network protocol, not a typed query API, no type info)

options.name: Defer past E4
options.detail: Accept the E4 exit criterion slip. Useful if the internal SymbolDB is still in heavy flux and freezing it now would be costly. Leaves downstream cards blocked.
options.code:
// no change; D-IMPACT1, D-CODEMOD1, ask-your-codebase
// all remain blocked

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer exposes a public `ide` crate with typed queries (find_all_refs, go_to_def, call_hierarchy). Third-party tools depend on it. It is versioned separately from the compiler.
ts-morph wraps the TypeScript compiler API into a stable typed query surface. Tools use it for refactoring and analysis without touching compiler internals.
comparisons.code:
const refs = sourceFile.getReferencedSymbols();
refs.forEach(r => console.log(r.getDefinition().getFilePath()));

decisions.title: Build an impact / blast-radius analyzer on top of the semantic-index API?
decisions.gist: When you change a function signature, add a field, or rename a type, it is not obvious how many things break downstream. An impact analyzer reports the full blast radius of a proposed change — callers, dependent types, and affected tests — before you commit it. No such tool exists for Jet today. This decision is whether to build one, and whether to sequence it after D-SEMINDEX1.
decisions.explainer: This card has a hard prerequisite: the semantic-index query API (D-SEMINDEX1). Without a stable, typed query surface, the analyzer would have to duplicate compiler internals or use fragile text heuristics. If D-SEMINDEX1 is approved, this card can proceed immediately after. The tool is purely additive — it reads the index and reports; it does not change language semantics (I1/I8 not in play). Blast-radius reporting is also an input to the codemod system (D-CODEMOD1): you want to know the impact before you replay a codemod.
decisions.story: Before I rename `payments::charge` to `payments::bill`, I want to see exactly how many files change, which tests are affected, and whether any public API is broken — without actually making the change yet.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet impact payments::charge --rename payments::bill
Blast radius: 12 call sites across 4 files
  src/billing.jet:44  src/invoice.jet:19  ...
Affected tests: 3 (#Unit, #Integration)
Public API: yes — exported symbol

options.name: Build on semantic-index API, sequence after D-SEMINDEX1
options.detail: Implement `jet impact` as a CLI tool (and LSP hover/codelens) that queries the semantic index for callers, dependents, and test coverage. Sequence it after D-SEMINDEX1 is shipped. Clean separation: query layer does the work, this tool just renders it.
options.code:
$ jet impact auth::Session --change remove-field:token
Blast radius:
  8 read sites  (src/auth.jet, src/session.jet, ...)
  2 write sites (src/login.jet:71, src/refresh.jet:22)
  Tests affected: 5
  Breaking public API: no

options.name: Standalone, no semantic-index dependency
options.detail: Build the analyzer against compiler internals directly, not a public API. Faster to start but tightly coupled; breaks whenever internals change. Violates the intended seam-crate architecture.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until more of the tooling ecosystem is defined. Low cost now; leaves developers without blast-radius visibility indefinitely.
options.code:
// no tool; developer must trace call sites manually
// or rely on compile errors after the change

comparisons.note: `cargo tree --invert <crate>` shows reverse dependencies. rust-analyzer's 'find all references' is the per-symbol analog. Neither gives a pre-change blast-radius report with test coverage.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo tree -i serde --edges features
serde v1.0
└── my-crate v0.1

comparisons.note: IntelliJ's 'Find Usages' + 'Safe Delete' shows all usages and affected tests before a deletion. The closest existing art to what this card proposes.

decisions.title: Model refactors as named, shippable, reversible codemod objects?
decisions.gist: Today the LSP supports one-shot fixes and renames, but there is no way to package a refactor as a named, versionable object that can be shipped to a team, replayed on a different branch, or undone. This decision is whether to introduce a codemod object model — named transformations backed by the semantic index — as a first-class Jet tooling concept.
decisions.explainer: This card depends on the semantic-index API (D-SEMINDEX1) for reliable symbol resolution and on the impact analyzer (D-IMPACT1) for pre-flight blast-radius checks. It is also complementary to content-addressed definitions (if ratified): if definitions are content-addressed, a codemod can reference the pre- and post-image by hash rather than by name, making reversal exact. The codemod object model is pure tooling — no language syntax change, no I1/I8 impact. The risk is over-engineering: if one-shot LSP fixes cover 90% of real refactor needs, a full object model may be premature.
decisions.story: My team is upgrading an API across 30 files. I want to define the rename once, preview it, commit the codemod as a named artifact so others can replay it on their branches, and undo it cleanly if the API changes again.

options.name: Named codemod objects on top of semantic-index + replay log
options.detail: Define a `.codemod.jet` format: a named transformation (rename, signature change, pattern substitution) backed by semantic-index resolution. Include a replay log so it can be applied on a different branch and undone cleanly. Sequence after D-SEMINDEX1 and D-IMPACT1.
options.code:
$ jet codemod apply rename-charge.codemod.jet
Applying RenameCharge:
  modified: src/billing.jet (3 sites)
  modified: src/invoice.jet (1 site)
Log written: .jet/codemods/rename-charge.log
$ jet codemod undo rename-charge.codemod.jet
Reverted 4 sites

options.name: Keep ad-hoc LSP fixes only
options.detail: One-shot rename/fix via the LSP; no named objects, no replay, no undo log. Sufficient for small codebases; breaks down when a refactor spans branches or needs to be shared across a team.
options.code:
// LSP: workspace/applyEdit for a rename
// No replay, no undo, no sharing

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until D-SEMINDEX1 and D-IMPACT1 are proven in practice before designing the codemod model. Lower risk of over-engineering; delays the team-sharing use case.
options.code:
// no change; team shares refactor scripts
// manually (fragile, no semantic resolution)

comparisons.note: jscodeshift lets you write a transform function, apply it to many files, and share it as an npm package. No built-in undo or semantic resolution — it works on AST, not types.
`cargo fix` applies machine-applicable compiler suggestions automatically. Not user-authored, not named, not reversible — but shows the pattern of compiler-guided rewrites.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo fix --allow-dirty
Fixing src/main.rs (2 fixes applied)

decisions.title: Recover the original stored-reference note and decide if any ownership-vocabulary work remains?
decisions.gist: An older note flagged stored-reference fields and ownership vocabulary as needing a relook. Since then, capability sigils and `ref` hardening have landed. It is unclear whether the original note described a gap that is now closed, or whether real work remains. Before reopening ownership vocabulary, we need to know what the original note actually said.
decisions.explainer: This card is primarily a triage action, not a design decision. The risk of acting without recovering the note is either (a) reopening a topic that is already resolved — wasted design work — or (b) ignoring a real gap because it looks resolved on the surface. The ownership vocabulary touches I1 (safe by default); any change here must not make unsafe aliasing the default. The C FFI capability was previously reverted over exactly this concern (owner-design-kill-criteria). If recovery shows the gap is closed, close the card. If a real gap exists, a follow-on ballot handles it.
decisions.story: I wrote a note months ago about stored refs and ownership. I don't remember if I was tracking a bug, a missing feature, or an open design question. Before the team spends time on it, I need to know what I actually meant.

options.name: Recover the note, then decide — likely close as addressed
options.detail: Retrieve the original note from git history or archived docs. If capability sigils + ref hardening cover the concern, close the card as done. If a real gap surfaces, open a targeted follow-on ballot. This avoids both premature closure and wasted design work.
options.code:
$ git log --all --grep='stored ref' --oneline
# find the original commit/note
# review against current capability-sigil spec
# if covered: close card
# if gap: open D-REFRELOOK2 with specific concern

options.name: Reopen ownership vocabulary now
options.detail: Treat the card as active and design a new ownership vocabulary without recovering the original note. Risk: solving a problem that doesn't exist, or designing around the wrong problem.
options.code:
// premature — we don't know what gap
// the original note described

options.name: Close as done
options.detail: Declare capability sigils + ref hardening sufficient and close the card without recovering the note. Risk: a real gap gets silently dropped.
options.code:
// closes the card — acceptable only if
// we have high confidence the note is stale

comparisons.note: Rust's borrow checker enforces stored-reference rules at compile time. `&'a T` in a struct requires explicit lifetime annotation; no runtime aliasing allowed. The reference point for Jet's own guarantees.

decisions.title: Add generic coroutines as a lower-level primitive beneath @async/await?
decisions.gist: The current async plan is `@async`/`await`/tasks — a colored-function model. Generic coroutines (stackless or stackful suspend/resume with no function-color split) would be a more general primitive: async could be built on top of them, and other use cases (generators, cooperative scheduling, iterators over async data) would benefit too. The question is whether to adopt coroutines as the substrate now or keep `@async/await` as the only concurrency mechanism for v1.
decisions.explainer: The E3 async plan commits to `@async`/`await`/tasks as the user-facing model. If coroutines are introduced as the substrate, they do not necessarily become a user-visible surface — they could be a compiler-internal implementation detail. However, exposing them as a user primitive (for generators, custom schedulers, etc.) would be a significant surface addition. I8 applies: if coroutines can express everything async can, that's two ways to do concurrency — the design must draw a clear line. I1 applies: stackful coroutines require explicit stack allocation; that should not be the default. Function coloring (the 'red/blue function' problem) is the main pain point being addressed.
decisions.story: I'm writing a streaming parser. I want to yield tokens one at a time as I consume input, without converting my entire call stack to async. `@async` is overkill — I just need suspend/resume.

options.name: Keep @async/await for v1; revisit coroutines as substrate post-v1
options.detail: Ship `@async`/`await`/tasks as the only user-visible concurrency model for v1. After v1, evaluate whether to adopt coroutines as the internal substrate (not exposed to users) or as a full primitive. Keeps the surface small and learnable; defers the hard implementation work. Recommended for v1.

options.name: Add generic coroutines as the substrate async builds on
options.detail: Implement coroutines (stackless, compiler-managed) as the internal primitive; `@async`/`await` becomes sugar over them. User-visible surface stays the same for v1 but the implementation becomes more general. Higher implementation complexity now; enables generators and custom schedulers later without an additional primitive.

options.name: Expose coroutines as a full user primitive now
options.detail: Ship both `@async/await` and a user-visible coroutine/generator syntax. Risks I8 (two concurrency mechanisms) and surface bloat for beginners. Would need a clear, non-overlapping use-case boundary documented in the spec.

comparisons.note: Kotlin coroutines are the substrate for all async code. `suspend` functions, channels, flows, and structured concurrency all compile down to the same coroutine machinery. No function-color split at the primitive level.
Go goroutines are stackful; the runtime manages switching. No function coloring — every function can block. Simple model for users; high memory overhead per goroutine.
Python has both generator coroutines (`yield`) and async/await. The surface overlap is a known source of confusion; Python 3 deprecated the mixed form.
comparisons.code:
async def fetch():
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
        return await s.get(url)
# vs generators: def gen(): yield 1; yield 2

decisions.title: Adopt structured concurrency (nursery scope + cancellation + deadlines) as the canonical task-spawn model?
decisions.gist: Tasks exist in Jet but there is no lexical scope that guarantees all child tasks finish (or are cancelled) before the scope exits. Structured concurrency — a nursery or task group — provides that guarantee, preventing task leaks by construction. Cancellation propagation and deadline contexts are closely related. This is listed as an E4 exit criterion.
decisions.explainer: Unstructured `spawn` makes it easy to leak tasks: a function returns, its caller doesn't know tasks are still running, and errors from those tasks are silently dropped. A nursery scope closes that gap at the language level — you cannot exit the nursery until all children are done or cancelled. This pairs with D-COROUTINE1 (the async substrate) and D-RACEWIN1 (race combinators are a nursery operation). Cancellation and deadlines can be separate cards but are most useful alongside the nursery; the ballot here is for the nursery as the primary mechanism. I1 is relevant: unstructured spawn (the footgun) should not be the default — beginners should reach for the nursery first. The nursery model is proven in Trio (Python) and structured concurrency literature.
decisions.story: I'm making three API calls in parallel. If any one fails, I want the others cancelled immediately. If they all succeed, I collect the results. Today I'd have to manually track tasks and handle cancellation — I want the scope to do that for me.

options.name: Nursery scope as the canonical spawn model
options.detail: Define `nursery { }` as the only blessed way to spawn tasks. Unstructured `spawn` remains available for expert use but is not the default and produces a lint warning. Cancellation propagates automatically when the nursery exits with an error. Deadline context is a follow-on (separate ballot). This is the E4 exit criterion.

options.name: Unstructured spawn + manual join
options.detail: Keep unstructured `spawn` as the primary model; programmers join tasks manually. Familiar to Go/thread-pool users; makes task leaks easy to write and hard to detect. Not recommended as the default — violates the beginner-safe principle.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Accept the E4 exit criterion slip. Appropriate only if the async substrate (D-COROUTINE1) is not yet settled, since the nursery's cancellation model depends on how tasks are implemented.
options.code:
// no nursery; E4 criterion missed;
// task-leak hazard remains

comparisons.note: Trio originated structured concurrency. `trio.open_nursery()` is the only way to spawn tasks; the nursery guarantees all children exit before the block exits. Proven in production.
comparisons.code:
async with trio.open_nursery() as n:
    n.start_soon(fetch, url1)
    n.start_soon(fetch, url2)
# both done (or both cancelled) here

comparisons.note: `coroutineScope { }` and `supervisorScope { }` provide structured concurrency. `launch` inside the scope is the idiomatic pattern; cancellation propagates automatically.

decisions.title: Add try-both / keep-the-winner as a structured-concurrency combinator?
decisions.gist: Some patterns need to run alternatives concurrently and keep the first to succeed, cancelling the rest. Examples: fallback servers, speculative execution, hedged requests. Today there is no built-in mechanism; the transaction system (`#Transact`) handles rollback but not general success-racing. This decision is whether to add a `race` / `any` combinator and where it lives.
decisions.explainer: This card depends on structured concurrency (D-NURSERY1): a success-race is a nursery operation — spawn alternatives, cancel siblings when one succeeds. Implementing it as a standalone primitive risks I8 (two spawn mechanisms). The correct home is the concurrency combinator set alongside `all`, `any`, `first` — all of which are nursery-level operations. The distinction between first-done-race (returns the first to finish regardless of success/failure) and success-race (returns the first to succeed, retries on error) must be explicit in the API — they are different semantics and should have different names. `#Transact` rollback is orthogonal; this card is not about undoing state.
decisions.story: I have two CDN endpoints for the same asset. I want to fire both requests and use whichever responds first. The slower one should be cancelled. Today I'd write that manually with tasks and channels; I want a one-liner.

options.name: Fold into the structured-concurrency combinator set (race/any), sequence after D-NURSERY1
options.detail: Define `race(tasks)` (first to succeed) and `any(tasks)` (first to finish) as combinator functions in the concurrency stdlib, built on the nursery primitive. No new language syntax — just functions. Sequence after D-NURSERY1. Satisfies I8: one spawn mechanism, multiple combinators over it.

options.name: Standalone language primitive
options.detail: Add `race { }` as a first-class language block, separate from the nursery. Doubles the concurrency surface (I8 concern). Only justified if the nursery model cannot express racing cleanly.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until D-NURSERY1 is implemented and the combinator API is proven before adding racing. The manual pattern works; this is a quality-of-life addition.

comparisons.note: `Promise.any()` returns the first fulfilled promise; `Promise.race()` returns the first settled (either). The naming distinction maps directly to what this card proposes.
comparisons.code:
const result = await Promise.any([
  fetch(cdn1),
  fetch(cdn2),
]); // first success

comparisons.note: `select { }` expression picks the first channel or deferred that is ready. More general but more verbose than a `race` combinator.

decisions.title: Add a bare `undo` keyword for reversing operations, or keep `#Transact` as the sole reversal mechanism?
decisions.gist: The `#Transact` marker already provides transactional rollback. A bare `undo` keyword has been proposed as an alternative spelling — shorter, more imperative. D-SUGAR5 already declined a nearby cleanup-sugar proposal. This reopen asks whether `undo` offers enough over `#Transact` to justify adding it to the surface.
decisions.explainer: I8 is the decisive issue: `#Transact` and a bare `undo` keyword would express overlapping semantics. Unless `undo` covers a strictly different use case (e.g., reversing a single operation mid-function rather than rolling back an entire transaction), it is a second way to do the same job. The keyword would also consume a reserved word in the grammar. D-SUGAR5's rejection establishes a pattern: the owner has already declined nearby sugar. The status-quo is the recommended option unless a concrete use case is presented that `#Transact` cannot express.
decisions.story: I called `db.insert(record)` and now I want to undo just that one operation, not roll back an entire transaction. `#Transact` feels heavy for a single-op reversal.

options.name: Keep #Transact only; reject the undo keyword
options.detail: No new keyword. `#Transact` handles transactional rollback; rollback hooks handle per-operation reversal. The use case in the story is already expressible with a `#SingleUse` or rollback hook. Keeps the surface small; consistent with D-SUGAR5.

options.name: Add `undo` as sugar over #Transact
options.detail: Introduce `undo expr` as a built-in that calls the registered inverse of `expr`. Requires every reversible operation to register an inverse at the type level. Adds a keyword, a registration mechanism, and a new surface concept for a marginal gain over `#Transact` rollback hooks.

comparisons.note: Ecto.Multi composes operations that can be rolled back as a unit. No bare `undo` keyword; rollback is a first-class concept in the transaction type.
comparisons.code:
Multi.new()
|> Multi.insert(:record, changeset)
|> Multi.run(:side_effect, fn _, _ -> … end)
|> Repo.transaction()

comparisons.note: SQL uses explicit `ROLLBACK` within a transaction; there is no single-statement undo outside a transaction. The analogy maps to `#Transact` + rollback hooks.

decisions.title: Should arbitrary Jet values carry per-value version and conversion history?
decisions.gist: Jet already has schema-level snapshots and migrations for published data shapes. This card asks whether individual values should also carry a version tag and conversion history at runtime. That's a different layer: every value, not just schema-published types.
decisions.explainer: Schema versioning covers the "what shape did this type have at version N" problem for serialized/published data. Per-value history means each runtime value carries provenance of which version it started as and every conversion step it passed through. This is a much heavier runtime model — it affects allocation, copy semantics, and GC pressure for all values, not just schema-registered ones. It also overlaps the time-travel-history card (D-TIMETRAVEL1) and the ask-why card (D-PROVENANCE1). Adding it risks building three overlapping provenance/history mechanisms (I8 concern). The schema migration system is the ratified canonical path for versioned data shapes.
decisions.story: I want to know whether the User object I'm holding was originally a v1 or v2 schema shape and whether it went through the auto-migration — without logging that manually every time.

options.name: Keep schema-level versioning only (status quo)
options.detail: Per-value history is costly (extra allocation on every value), niche (most callers don't need it), and overlaps ask-why / time-travel cards already in the queue. Schema migrations cover the published-shape problem. Don't add it.

options.name: Opt-in versioned wrapper type
options.detail: A stdlib Versioned<T> that wraps a value and accumulates its conversion history. Zero cost for types that don't opt in. Requires a design for how conversions are registered and replayed.

options.name: Defer — wait on time-travel and ask-why outcomes
options.detail: Per-value history is a strict subset of what time-travel debugging (D-TIMETRAVEL1) and provenance tracking (D-PROVENANCE1) would provide. Decide those cards first; if one ships, this card collapses into it.
options.code: // No new surface; revisit after D-TIMETRAVEL1 / D-PROVENANCE1

comparisons.note: No per-value version tracking; schema versioning is handled by serde with manual version fields or crates like serde_versioned.
Every datom carries a transaction-time timestamp — the DB is the history. Per-value history is the storage model, not a type attribute.
comparisons.code: (d/q '[:find ?name ?tx :where [?e :user/name ?name ?tx]] db)

decisions.title: Should Jet add proof-based elision of bounds checks for proven-safe indexing?
decisions.gist: Jet indexes are bounds-checked by default (safe, I1). This card asks whether to add a path where static proof of in-range lets the compiler elide the runtime check — zero-cost for proven-safe code, full safety by default.
decisions.explainer: The default array indexing `arr[i]` panics on out-of-bounds — safe. Experts writing tight inner loops want to assert "i is in range" and get unchecked access without writing `@unsafe`. The cleanest route is to tie elision to the refinement-types machinery: when the type of `i` carries a bound proof (e.g., `i: UInt where i < arr.len`), the compiler can drop the runtime check. This is distinct from `@unsafe` manual elision, which carries no proof obligation. It is gated on refinement types being designed and ratified first (D-REFINE1 / c73xs2f). Adding it as a standalone `@unchecked` attribute risks two escape hatches (I8).
decisions.story: My inner-loop index is already validated before the loop — I don't want to pay for a redundant bounds check 10 million times, and I don't want to write @unsafe just because the compiler can't see the proof yet.

options.name: Proof-carrying elision via refinement types (rec, gated)
options.detail: When an index value's type carries a static range proof (from the refinement-types system), sema elides the check. No new syntax, no second escape hatch. Gate this decision on refinement types landing first.

options.name: Checked-only always
options.detail: Keep bounds checks unconditional forever. Safe, simple, but forecloses expert zero-cost paths. Correct for most code; a real cost for hot numeric loops.
options.code: // no change; arr[i] always checks

options.name: @unsafe manual elision only
options.detail: Allow @unsafe blocks to use a raw `.get_unchecked(i)` call. Expert opt-in with explicit audit obligation. Works today without new machinery but requires an @audit annotation and carries undefined-behavior risk if wrong.

comparisons.note: Default indexing panics; `get_unchecked` is unsafe and requires the caller to prove safety manually.
comparisons.code: unsafe { *arr.get_unchecked(i) }

comparisons.note: SPARK proves array index safety at compile time via contracts; bounds checks are elided when the proof succeeds — same model as option A.
comparisons.code:
pragma Assert (I in Arr'Range);
X := Arr (I);  -- check elided after proof

decisions.title: Should Jet add tracked uncertainty, freshness, and/or precision as first-class type dimensions?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether values should carry metadata dimensions like "this is an estimate", "this may be stale", or "this is accurate to ±5%". These are distinct axes. Option/taint already cover some failure and trust dimensions.
decisions.explainer: Three separate ideas are bundled: (1) numeric precision/tolerance (honest-numbers overlap); (2) freshness/staleness (TTL-secrets overlap); (3) general estimate vs exact (new). All three would require new type-level machinery or effect system extensions. Adding all three risks a proliferation of qualifiers on every value (I8: multiple overlapping mechanisms). Honest-numbers and TTL-secrets are already separate cards; freshness may belong there. A general qualified-value framework would be a large surface area that touches every numeric and IO type.
decisions.story: I'm pulling sensor readings with known tolerance — I want the type system to remind me that adding an exact price to a ±5% temperature doesn't give me an exact result.

options.name: Defer — let honest-numbers and TTL-secrets carry the axes they own
options.detail: Honest-numbers owns numeric precision; TTL-secrets owns staleness/freshness. Let those cards be decided first. A general uncertainty framework is too broad to ballot now without knowing what the specialty cards won't cover.
options.code: // no new surface; revisit after honest-numbers + ttl-secrets decisions

options.name: Pick one axis: freshness only
options.detail: Freshness ("is this value stale?") is the most concrete, most requested axis. Model it as a TTL marker on values that carry a timestamp and expire. Precision and estimate dimensions deferred.

options.name: General qualified-value framework
options.detail: A Qualified<T, Q> wrapper that lets any axis (estimate, stale, tolerance) be composed. Heavy design investment; risks becoming a parallel type system sitting on top of the real one (I8 concern).
options.code:
let temp: Qualified<Float, Tolerance(pct: 5)> = sensor.read()
let bad = temp + exact_val  // type error: mixing Tolerance + Exact

comparisons.note: Libraries like `rounded-hw` track precision as a type parameter but require opt-in; no standard freshness axis.
comparisons.code:
import Numeric.Interval
let x = 1.0 ... 1.1 :: Interval Double

comparisons.note: Tracks dimensional correctness (meters, seconds) but not uncertainty/staleness — orthogonal to this proposal.
comparisons.code:
[<Measure>] type m
let dist: float<m> = 5.0<m>

decisions.title: Should Jet add failure-aware comprehensions that auto-skip failed elements?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether collection-building expressions should have a mode that silently drops elements whose computation failed, collecting only the successes. Today there is no comprehension syntax; the iterator/adapter set is the planned path.
decisions.explainer: Auto-skipping failures in a comprehension is equivalent to `filter_map` with a fallible transform: keep elements where the function returns a value, drop the rest. Adding implicit skip-on-failure as comprehension syntax would be a second way to mean the same thing (I8 concern). The explicit adapter path — `iter.filter_map(fn)` or `iter.try_collect()` — is readable, composable, and doesn't hide control flow. Hidden skip-on-failure makes bugs silent: a whole class of elements can vanish with no error. This card is primarily about whether implicit skip warrants special syntax, not whether the operation exists.
decisions.story: I'm parsing a list of user-supplied URLs — some are malformed. I want the valid ones and want to silently drop the rest, without writing a manual loop.

options.name: Explicit filter_map / try_collect adapter (rec)
options.detail: Add `filter_map` and `try_collect` as standard iterator adapters under D-ITER1. No new comprehension syntax. Callers that want to skip errors call `.filter_map(fn)` explicitly — the intent is visible in the code.
options.code:
let valid_prices: [Price] = raw
    .filter_map(fn(s) -> Price? { parse_price(s) })
    .collect()

options.name: Comprehension syntax with implicit skip
options.detail: A `[expr for x in coll try]` or `[expr for x in coll catch skip]` form that drops failures. New syntax for something `filter_map` already expresses; hides control flow from the reader.
options.code: [parse_price(s) for s in raw try]   // silently drops bad entries

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Decide D-ITER1 (iterators) first. If filter_map lands there, this card is resolved without new syntax.
options.code: // no action until D-ITER1 settles the iterator adapter set

comparisons.note: List comprehensions with a conditional achieve the same thing explicitly; there's no built-in skip-on-exception in comprehensions (that would be a try/except in the expression).
comparisons.code: [parse(x) for x in raw if is_valid(x)]

comparisons.note: `filter_map` is the idiomatic path; `collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()` is `try_collect`. Both are explicit — no hidden skip.
comparisons.code: raw.iter().filter_map(|s| s.parse::<u32>().ok()).collect::<Vec<_>>()

decisions.title: Should Jet add a universal typed "hole" value that propagates through computation instead of failing?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether Jet should have a universal Hole<T> or similar missing-value sentinel that propagates silently through expressions. Jet already has Option<T>, Result<T,E>, and the T?E model for typed failure. This would be a second, distinct mechanism.
decisions.explainer: Option<T> and Result<T,E> make failure explicit: the caller must unwrap or propagate with `?`. A universal hole that flows through arithmetic and function calls is a different model — it defers failure to wherever the hole is eventually consumed. This is exactly what SQL NULL does, and the propagation behavior is the source of the most common class of SQL bugs. It also competes directly with Option<T> (I8). The main argument for it is ergonomics in data-pipeline code where many values may be absent; the counter-argument is that it hides which expression produced the hole.
decisions.story: I'm computing a derived column across a dataframe where some source cells are absent — I want the absence to flow through math without wrapping every step in `if let`.

options.name: Keep Option/Result/T?E — no universal hole (rec)
options.detail: Option<T> already expresses missing values. The `?` operator propagates failures explicitly. A universal hole hides the origin of the absence and creates a silent failure mode that Option was designed to prevent. Don't add it.

options.name: Blessed Hole<T> that propagates
options.detail: A stdlib type (not syntax) that propagates like Option but automatically across arithmetic operators via trait impl. Slightly less invisible than implicit NULL — the type is still named — but the propagation is implicit through ops. Risk: two ways to mean "absent" (I8).

options.name: Defer — revisit when dataframe/table stdlib is designed
options.detail: The strongest use case is dataframe/table operations. Design the table stdlib first; if column-absent semantics require a hole type, the design will surface it naturally.
options.code: // no action now; revisit with table/dataframe stdlib design

comparisons.note: NULL propagates silently through every expression. This is the canonical example of how invisible propagation creates bugs (NULL comparisons are always false/unknown).
comparisons.code: SELECT price * qty FROM orders  -- NULL * 5 = NULL silently

comparisons.note: Nullable types `T?` require explicit handling at each step; the compiler enforces it. Closer to Jet's current Option model.
comparisons.code: val total: Float? = price?.times(qty)

decisions.title: Should Jet add runtime value provenance tracking so you can ask a value where it came from?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether values should carry a provenance chain at runtime — recording which computations and inputs produced them — queryable by the developer. This is distinct from logging and tracing.
decisions.explainer: Provenance tracking means every value carries a graph of its origin: which function, which input values, which source location. At runtime this is expensive (extra allocation and pointer-chasing on every operation) unless it is debug-only or opt-in. The feature overlaps taint tracking (which tracks data flow for security purposes), the record-and-replay card (D-REPLAY1, which records full program execution), and the time-travel-history card (D-TIMETRAVEL1). Building a standalone provenance system risks a third overlapping mechanism for the same "where did this value come from" question (I8). Taint tracking tied to security already answers a subset; record-and-replay answers the rest for debugging.
decisions.story: I got a NaN in my physics sim. I want to point at the NaN and ask "which input caused this" rather than adding print statements everywhere.

options.name: Defer — rely on record-and-replay for provenance (rec)
options.detail: Record-and-replay (D-REPLAY1) makes every variable's history inspectable by replaying execution under a debugger. Provenance is a subset of that capability. Don't build a second mechanism — decide D-REPLAY1 first.
options.code: // no new surface; use D-REPLAY1 debugger to step back to NaN origin

options.name: Opt-in provenance wrapper for debugging
options.detail: A `Tracked<T>` debug wrapper that captures provenance on each operation, available in debug/test builds only. Zero cost in release. Useful but overlaps taint tracking if taint ever tracks data-flow edges.

options.name: Tie provenance to taint tracking
options.detail: Extend taint's data-flow graph to record computation edges, not just trust labels. Provenance becomes a query on the taint graph. Requires taint to ship first and expands its scope significantly.

comparisons.note: lineapy builds a computation graph of values post-hoc for data science notebooks; it's a library, not a language feature, and incurs significant overhead.
comparisons.code:
import lineapy
lineapy.save(result, "result")  # stores provenance graph

comparisons.note: Provenance can be modeled via Writer, but it's explicit and opt-in — every function in the chain must propagate the log.
comparisons.code:
import Control.Monad.Writer
compute :: Writer [String] Float
compute = do
  tell ["used sensor"]
  return 42.0

decisions.title: Should Jet build a standalone per-variable value history for time-travel debugging?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether the language/runtime should record a history of every variable's values during execution, queryable for debugging. This is the "rewind and inspect" debugging model.
decisions.explainer: Per-variable history is what time-travel debuggers provide: step backward through execution and inspect what a variable held at each point. The record-and-replay card (D-REPLAY1) covers this by recording the full execution trace deterministically and letting a debugger replay it. Building a separate value-history capture mechanism alongside record-and-replay would be a second mechanism for the same job (I8). The ask-why card (D-PROVENANCE1) also overlaps. The right call is to decide D-REPLAY1; if deterministic replay ships, time-travel debugging is a UI feature of the debugger, not a language-level mechanism.
decisions.story: My loop variable changed to an unexpected value at iteration 47 of 1000 — I want to rewind and see what it was at iteration 46 without adding a Vec to capture it manually.

options.name: Fold into record-and-replay (rec)
options.detail: Record-and-replay (D-REPLAY1) gives full execution history for every variable without any per-variable annotation. Time-travel inspection is a debugger UI feature on top of that recording. Don't build a parallel mechanism.
options.code:
// no new language surface
// jet debug --replay run.trace → step to iteration 47, inspect counter

options.name: Standalone opt-in history capture
options.detail: A `#[History]` marker on a variable that captures its value at each write into a debug-accessible ring buffer. Lighter than full replay; heavier than nothing; overlaps replay (I8).

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Gate on the debugger card (c144) and D-REPLAY1. No action until the debugger architecture is decided.
options.code: // no action; revisit after debugger card (c144) and D-REPLAY1

comparisons.note: Record-and-replay for native code; any variable's value at any point is inspectable by replaying — exactly what option A describes.
comparisons.code:
rr record ./my_program
rr replay  # then use gdb to step backward

comparisons.note: Elm's debugger records every message and model state; rewind is built into the dev server. A language-level property, not a separate annotation.
comparisons.code: -- enabled by `elm reactor`; no code annotation needed

decisions.title: Should Jet propagate latency deadlines implicitly through calls via the structured-concurrency context?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether a deadline or timeout set at a task boundary should flow automatically down the call graph — cancelling work when the deadline is exceeded — without callers threading a deadline parameter manually.
decisions.explainer: Structured concurrency (D-NURSERY1) gives Jet task-scoped lifetime management via nurseries. The `#Context` marker already carries cross-cutting values. Deadline propagation is a natural fit: the nursery or an ancestor sets a deadline; every `await` point inside checks it and cancels if exceeded. The alternative is explicit deadline parameters, which forces every function in the call graph to accept and forward a deadline — verbose and error-prone. A third option (a dedicated Deadline<T> type) risks being a second propagation channel alongside #Context (I8). The main design question is: is this a #Context field (automatic, invisible) or a first-class budget type (explicit, visible)?
decisions.story: My API handler has a 200 ms SLA. I want every downstream DB call and HTTP fetch it spawns to automatically cancel if the 200 ms window closes — without passing a deadline parameter into every helper function.

options.name: Deadline on #Context, enforced at await/IO points (rec)
options.detail: The nursery that spawns a task can set a deadline on #Context. Every await point inside the task checks it automatically. No parameter threading. Pairs cleanly with D-NURSERY1 cancellation.

options.name: Explicit deadline parameter
options.detail: Every function that does IO accepts a `deadline: Deadline` parameter. Visible, testable, easy to override per-call. Verbose: every helper in the call graph must forward the parameter.

options.name: Defer — design after D-NURSERY1 and #Context settle
options.detail: Deadline propagation is only well-defined once the nursery/context model is ratified. If #Context isn't the right carrier, this design will be wrong. Decide the concurrency primitives first.
options.code: // no action until D-NURSERY1 and #Context are ratified

comparisons.note: context.Context carries a deadline/cancel signal; every function in the call graph must accept and forward ctx. Correct but verbose — option B's model.
comparisons.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 200*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()
result, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)

comparisons.note: withTimeout cancels the entire coroutine scope automatically; inner coroutines inherit the deadline without explicit threading — closest to option A.

decisions.title: Should Jet add language-level support for approximate algorithms, or keep it a library concern?
decisions.gist: Some algorithms trade accuracy for speed under a policy or budget — HyperLogLog for cardinality, t-digest for quantiles, random sampling. The question is whether Jet provides any language machinery for this or leaves it entirely to library code. Currently nothing exists; this is a new idea with no card.
decisions.explainer: A language-level approximation layer would need some way to express accuracy budgets and propagate them — touching the type system, possibly the comptime system, and the standard library. A library-only answer is self-contained and additive: ship HyperLogLog, t-digest, reservoir sampler as stdlib modules with plain Jet types. The language-level route risks a second mechanism for numeric precision alongside the 'honest-numbers' direction and the budgets-as-types card, which would pressure I8. The library path respects I8 and does not require any new surface.
decisions.story: I'm building a dashboard that counts distinct users across billions of events. I need HyperLogLog — I don't want to implement it myself, and I don't want the language to secretly approximate things I didn't ask it to approximate.

options.name: Library-only (no language feature)
options.detail: Ship HyperLogLog, t-digest, reservoir sampler, and CountMinSketch as stdlib modules. No new language surface. Users pick the right sketch for their accuracy/speed tradeoff explicitly. Respects I8 — no second numeric-precision mechanism.
options.code:
import std.sketch.HyperLogLog

let hll = HyperLogLog.new(error_rate: 0.01)
events.each(fn(e) { hll.insert(e.user_id) })
println(hll.estimate())  // prints: ~2_847_391

options.name: Policy/budget-driven auto-approximation
options.detail: Add a language mechanism (annotation or block) that lets code declare an accuracy budget, and the compiler or runtime swaps in an approximate algorithm. Requires new language surface, interacts with the type system and honest-numbers direction, and risks violating I8 by creating a second precision-control mechanism.

options.name: Defer — decide after budgets-as-types and honest-numbers land
options.detail: Both budgets-as-types and honest-numbers will constrain what a language-level approximation mechanism can look like. Defer this card until those designs are stable so we don't have to rework it.

comparisons.note: Pure library: users import sketch types explicitly. No language approximation machinery. The dominant industry pattern.
Library-only: Reservoir, t-digest, etc. as plain structs. No language feature.

decisions.title: Should Jet automatically parallelize proven-pure maps/folds, or keep parallelism explicit?
decisions.gist: Sequential-looking maps and folds could be run in parallel when the compiler proves they are pure. D-REACT1 already rejected hidden async/reactive machinery in favor of explicit parallelism. This card asks whether auto-parallelism on pure pipelines is a different enough case to reconsider, or whether explicit par_* adapters are sufficient.
decisions.explainer: D-REACT1 established that Jet rejects hidden machinery that makes sequential-looking code run differently than it appears. Auto-parallelism is another instance of hidden machinery: a map that looks sequential would actually fork threads. This undermines predictability and debuggability, which the beginner experience depends on. The explicit adapter path (par_map, par_fold) is fully consistent with D-REACT1, keeps the performance model visible, and satisfies I8 — there is one way to mean parallel. The opt-in auto-parallel path requires the compiler to prove purity soundly, which interacts with the effects/dataflow system (not yet designed) and risks a silent footgun if the proof is wrong.
decisions.story: I have a list of 10 million records and I want to transform them in parallel. I don't want to think about threads — but I also don't want the language to silently decide my code is parallel when I'm reading it as sequential.

options.name: Explicit par_* adapters only (no hidden auto-parallelism)
options.detail: Ship par_map, par_fold, par_filter as explicit stdlib adapters. Sequential code is always sequential. Parallelism is always visible at the call site. Consistent with D-REACT1 and predictable for beginners.
options.code:
// Explicit parallelism — user chooses
let totals = orders
  .par_map(fn(o) o.subtotal * tax_rate)
  .par_fold(0.0, fn(a, b) a + b)
println(totals)  // parallel, visible

options.name: Opt-in auto-parallel on proven-pure pipelines
options.detail: Allow a pragma or block that permits the compiler to parallelize pure pipelines automatically. Requires a sound purity proof system (depends on effects/dataflow design). Opt-in means it isn't the default, which partially satisfies I1 — but it still makes code behavior non-obvious to a reader without knowing the pragma is active.

options.name: Defer — decide after effects/dataflow is designed
options.detail: Sound purity proof for auto-parallelism depends on the effects/dataflow system. Deferring keeps options open without committing to a surface that may need to change.
options.code:
// Status quo: no auto-parallelism; explicit par_map available
let results = items.par_map(fn(x) expensive(x))

comparisons.note: Explicit parallelism via par/pseq combinators or the parallel-strategies library. No hidden auto-parallelism in the language; all concurrency is opt-in.
comparisons.code:
import Control.Parallel.Strategies
result = parMap rseq transform items

comparisons.note: Auto-parallelism via @threads on loops — opt-in macro, explicit at call site. Not truly automatic; user annotates.

decisions.title: Should Jet build a query engine for structural/semantic questions over the codebase?
decisions.gist: A 'ask your codebase' query engine would answer questions like 'where can balance go negative?' or 'who mutates field X?' by running structured queries over the semantic index. No such engine exists today; this would ride the semantic-index API (not yet shipped). It is a new idea with no card.
decisions.explainer: This feature depends entirely on the semantic-index API existing and exposing the right dataflow/effects information. Without that foundation it cannot be built. If the semantic index is designed well, a query layer is a natural extension — it becomes the primary way to drive impact-analysis, refactoring tools, and the LSP. The crux here is not whether this is a good idea (it is) but whether to plan it now or wait until the semantic-index API is stable. Sequencing risk: if we design the query DSL before the index API is settled, the query layer will need to be reworked. The safe path is to ratify the semantic-index API first, then return here.
decisions.story: I refactored a shared Account struct and I want to know every path through the codebase where the balance field could go negative — not just 'who reads it' but 'who can write a negative value to it'.

options.name: Plan it now; build after semantic-index API is ratified
options.detail: Commit to the query engine as a first-class tool, define its shape in the plan, and gate implementation on the semantic-index API card. This secures a slot in the roadmap and ensures the index API is designed with queries in mind — avoiding an impedance mismatch later.

options.name: Defer — revisit after semantic-index API ships
options.detail: Do not design the query engine until the semantic-index API is stable and its data model is known. Lower design risk, but delays the roadmap slot.

options.name: Skip — leave to external tooling
options.detail: Expose the semantic index as a stable API and let external tools (scripts, plugins) build query engines on top. Jet does not own a query DSL. Saves scope but sacrifices a flagship differentiator.

comparisons.note: Cross-language semantic index with a graph query API. Query engine is a separate layer built on top of the index. Jet would follow the same separation.
comparisons.code:
// Kythe query (simplified)
/kythe/node?ticket=kythe://corpus?path=src/billing.go#balance

comparisons.note: Separate query language (QL) over a relational semantic model of the codebase. Flagship differentiator for security/refactoring at scale.
comparisons.code:
from MethodAccess ma
where ma.getMethod().getName() = "withdraw"
  and not ma.getArgument(0).isPositive()
select ma

decisions.title: Should Jet adopt content-addressed definition identity (Unison-style)?
decisions.gist: In Unison, a definition's identity is a hash of its body — not its name. Renaming is free; dependencies are immutable by hash. Jet currently identifies definitions by name within files (file-is-program model). This idea would replace or supplement name-based identity with content hashing. New idea, no card.
decisions.explainer: Content-addressed definitions conflict with Jet's file-is-program model where the source file is the authoritative artifact. A hash-based identity layer would require a persistent codebase database, a rename/alias management system, and tooling that understands both the hash identity and the human-readable name. This is a deep architectural commitment — not a surface feature. It also interacts with the build cache (content-addressed build cache card) and the codemods system. The benefit (free renames, immutable dependency identity) is real but Unison's model is controversial in practice: the codebase-as-database workflow is unfamiliar and tool support outside Unison's own tooling is thin. For v1 this is out of scope and likely incompatible with the file-is-program instinct.
decisions.story: I renamed a core function and now I have to fix 40 import paths. If the function's identity were its body hash rather than its name, the rename would be an alias move and nothing would break.

options.name: Reject for v1 — incompatible with file-is-program model
options.detail: Content-addressed identity requires a codebase database and breaks the assumption that source files are self-contained. Reject for v1. Invest in good codemods / LSP rename instead — that solves the pain without the architectural cost.

options.name: Adopt as an underlying identity layer
options.detail: Add a content-hash layer below the name layer: names are aliases over hashes, and the package system tracks definitions by hash. A large architectural commitment; requires resolving the file-vs-database tension before any other design work can proceed.

options.name: Far-horizon research — no current card
options.detail: Treat this as a far-horizon idea: log it, don't design it now, revisit post-v1 when the codebase model, package system, and build cache are stable. Lower risk than A while keeping the door open.
options.code:
// No current impact. Status quo applies.
// Revisit after: file-is-program model, jetpack, build cache finalized.

comparisons.note: Definitions identified by hash of their AST. Renaming is a metadata operation. Requires the Unison Codebase Manager — no plain text files as the source of truth.
comparisons.code:
-- Unison: renaming is an alias, not a rewrite
move.term math.square math.sq

comparisons.note: Build outputs are content-addressed by input hash. Works because Nix has a single central store. Jet's module/file model is less centralized.
comparisons.code:
# Nix store path encodes content hash
/nix/store/3a7f...-my-package-1.0

decisions.title: Should Jet define a generic database driver interface with parameterized-queries-only enforcement?
decisions.gist: Jet already has SQLite support in jet.db (c50). The question is whether to define a generic Driver trait that any database backend implements, with the interface enforcing parameterized queries only — making string-concatenated SQL structurally impossible. No generic driver interface exists today; this is the next step above the SQLite-specific API.
decisions.explainer: A Driver trait with a parameterized-only API eliminates SQL injection by construction — you cannot build a raw SQL string and execute it through the driver interface. This is a strong safety guarantee consistent with I1 (safe by default). The SQLite implementation (c50) becomes the first impl of Driver; Postgres, MySQL, and others would follow as stdlib or community packages. The interface design needs to cover: connection lifecycle, transactions (#Transact?), async vs sync, and error types. None of those require new syntax — they use existing Jet markers and the T ? E error type. The main risk is locking in a Driver shape before we know what async looks like in Jet; a sync-only v1 Driver is safe to ship now.
decisions.story: I want to write database code that works with SQLite in tests and Postgres in production, and I want the compiler to make it impossible to accidentally run string-interpolated SQL.

options.name: Define Driver trait + parameterized-only API; SQLite as first impl
options.detail: Specify a Driver trait with query(sql: &str, params: []Param) -> Result<Rows, DbError> and no raw-execute surface. SQLite (c50) is refactored to implement it. Safe by construction against SQL injection. Sync-only for now; async variant deferred until Jet's async story is settled.

options.name: Per-database APIs only; no generic Driver trait
options.detail: Keep jet.db as the SQLite-specific API. Each new database gets its own module with its own API. No shared interface. Simpler short-term; loses the cross-backend portability and the injection guarantee at the interface level.

options.name: Defer — design after async story is settled
options.detail: The right Driver shape depends on whether queries are sync or async. Wait until Jet's async/concurrency model is ratified, then design Driver once with the right shape. Risk: blocks any new database backends in the meantime.

comparisons.note: Generic DB interface with parameterized queries via ? placeholders. Drivers register themselves. No string-building API at the interface level — close to what Jet is proposing.
Macro-verified parameterized queries checked against a live DB at compile time. Stronger than Go but requires a live DB in CI — Jet's approach is lighter.

decisions.title: Should Jet formalize a `core ⊂ alloc ⊂ std` ring layering for embedded/no-runtime targets?
decisions.gist: Jet aims to cover servers, CLI tools, and microcontrollers. A three-ring library model (core: no heap, no OS; alloc: heap but no OS; std: full platform) makes the same code portable across those targets by controlling which rings a crate can use. No formal ring structure exists today; freestanding direction is mentioned but undesigned.
decisions.explainer: Without ring layering, every stdlib import implicitly requires a heap and OS syscalls. That blocks embedded targets and makes the 'same code from server to microcontroller' goal impossible without ad-hoc #[no_std] patches. The three-ring model (proven by Rust's core/alloc/std split) solves this cleanly: code written against core compiles anywhere; code that imports std is desktop/server only. Jet would express this as platform capabilities gated by which ring a module declares. This interacts with the explicit-allocation card (what 'alloc' means in Jet), the pack.jet platform target field, and the aarch64/QEMU CI work (c57). The ring declaration would live in pack.jet, not in source syntax — no new markers needed.
decisions.story: I'm writing a fixed-point math library. I want it to work on an STM32 microcontroller with no heap and on my server. Today I can't import it into a no-heap target because the stdlib isn't layered.
decisions.inWild:
// pack.jet for an embedded library — declares core ring only
[package]
name = "fixed-math"
ring = "core"  // no heap, no OS; portable anywhere

// pack.jet for a server app — full std available
[package]
name = "my-server"
ring = "std"

options.name: Define three rings in pack.jet; gate stdlib features by ring
options.detail: Formalize core (no alloc, no OS), alloc (heap, no OS), and std (full platform). A package declares its ring in pack.jet. Importing a higher-ring module from a lower-ring package is a compile error. No new source syntax — ring is a pack.jet field. Enables embedded targets and clarifies all stdlib dependencies.
options.code:
// Compile error: server module imported from core-ring package
error[E0410]: `std.net.TcpStream` requires ring `std`
  --> src/fixed_math.jet:3
  |
3 | import std.net.TcpStream
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  | help: this package declares ring = "core"; remove the import or raise the ring

options.name: Keep one std + ad-hoc freestanding; no formal rings
options.detail: Let embedded targets use #[no_std]-style ad-hoc exclusions without a formal ring model. Simpler to start; but every embedded user must manually audit what they can import, and there is no compiler enforcement. Does not scale.

options.name: Defer — design after explicit-allocation and platform-target cards settle
options.detail: The ring boundary between alloc and std depends on how Jet defines explicit allocation and what platform targets look like in pack.jet. Defer ring formalization until those are stable. Lower risk of rework.
options.code:
// Status quo: no ring layering; embedded targets blocked
// Revisit after: explicit-allocation card, pack.jet platform targets

comparisons.note: Three-crate split: core (no_std, no heap), alloc (heap only), std (full OS). Embedded crates use #![no_std] and import core/alloc explicitly. Proven model; Jet would encode this in pack.jet rather than source attributes.
No explicit ring layering: the standard library is structured so embedded code imports only the modules it needs. Import control is manual, not enforced by the build system.
comparisons.code:
const std = @import("std");
// Embedded: just don't import std.net, std.fs, etc.

decisions.title: Should Jet include a typed styling layer with compile-time CSS property and unit checks?
decisions.gist: A typed styling layer would let UI components declare styles using Jet types rather than CSS strings — catching wrong units (px vs em vs %), unknown properties, and invalid values at compile time. This rides the #Unit system and the reactive-UI stack. It is a new idea with no card.
decisions.explainer: Typed styles only make sense if Jet has a UI kit and a reactive component model. Both are still in the proposal stage.
